question: The Source Selection Decision Document for a construction Request for Proposal has just been signed and you now notice that the Davis-Bacon wage rate has just been modified. The award has not yet been signed by the contracting officer. What do you do?
answer:
You need to issue an amendment to all the offerors in the competitive range and provide them an opportunity to revise their pricing. Wage rates need to be up-to-date as of Day of Contract award for construction RFPs (FAR 22.403 — the RFO deleted 22.404-6, so this rule now sits at 22.403).

Cite: FAR 22.403.

question: You are the KO in a Source Selection and your higher leadership is now giving you direction which you believe is contrary to your legal guidance. How do you handle and what would you do?
answer: Discuss with leadership the reasoning for going the other way; discuss leaderships reasoning with legal; if still not sold, offer your reasoning for not agreeing with their proposed approach (follow-up with an email); if leadership "requires" their approach to be taken, have specialist work up contract in accordance with leadership approach; request that leadership sign off on contract and all associated documents; NEVER SIGN A CONTRACT YOU DO NOT FEEL COMFORTABLE SIGNING. MGT CANNOT MAKE YOU SIGN ANYTHING YOU FEEL IS NOT RIGHT.

question: A legally binding contract must contain what elements?
answer: Must involve two or more parties that have the capacity to contract. Must show agreement, including offer, acceptance, and mutual assent. Must show something of value changing hands between the parties to a contract, or other inducement that leads a person to make a promise. Must be for a legal purpose. Must be in the correct form.

DFARS DEV 225.7002 Restrictions on food, clothing, fabrics, hand or measuring tools, and flags.
225.7002-1 Restrictions.

(a) The following restrictions implement 10 U.S.C. 4862 (the “Berry Amendment”). Except as provided in subsection 225.7002-2 , do not acquire—

(1) Any of the following items, either as end products or components, unless the items have been grown, reprocessed, reused, or produced in the United States:

(i) Food.

(ii) Clothing and the materials and components thereof, other than sensors, electronics, or other items added to, and not normally associated with, clothing and the materials and components thereof. Clothing includes items such as outerwear, headwear, underwear, nightwear, footwear, hosiery, handwear, belts, badges, and insignia. For additional guidance and examples, see PGI 225.7002-1 (a)(1)(ii).

(iii)(A) Tents and the structural components of tents;

(B) Tarpaulins; or

(C) Covers.

(iv) Cotton and other natural fiber products.

(v) Woven silk or woven silk blends.

(vi) Spun silk yarn for cartridge cloth.

(vii) Synthetic fabric or coated synthetic fabric, including all textile fibers and yarns that are for use in such fabrics.

(viii) Canvas products.

(ix) Wool (whether in the form of fiber or yarn or contained in fabrics, materials, or manufactured articles).

(x) Any item of individual equipment (Product or Service Code (PSC) 8465) manufactured from or containing any of the fibers, yarns, fabrics, or materials listed in this paragraph (a)(1).

(2) Hand or measuring tools, unless the tools were produced in the United States. For additional guidance, see PGI 225.7002-1 (a)(2).

225.7002-2 Exceptions. Acquisitions in the following categories are not subject to the restrictions in 225.7002-1: 

(a) Acquisitions not exceeding $200,000, except for athletic footwear purchased by DoD for use by members of the Army, Navy, Air Force, or Marine Corps upon their initial entry into the Armed Forces 

(d) Acquisitions outside the United States in support of combat operations. 

(f) Acquisitions of food or hand or measuring tools (1) In support of contingency operations; or (2) For which the use of other than competitive procedures are approved on the basis of unusual and compelling urgency in accordance with FAR 6.103-2.

Self-Answer: The Berry Amendment, implemented in DFARS 225.7002, requires the Department of War to purchase certain items—such as food, clothing, textiles, tents, natural fibers, synthetic fabrics, canvas products, wool, and hand or measuring tools—only when they are grown, reprocessed, reused, or produced in the United States. It applies whenever DoW uses its funds to acquire these covered items, unless a specific exception applies, such as purchases under $200,000 (with limited exceptions), acquisitions made outside the U.S. in support of combat operations, or urgent/contingency acquisitions of food or tools.

question: Explain the “Bona Fide Needs” rule.
answer: The Bona Fide Need rule (law) requires appropriated funds be used only for goods and services for which a need arises during the period of that appropriation’s availability for obligation. The bona fide needs rule is a rule of appropriations law. It mandates that a fiscal year's appropriations be obligated only to meet a legitimate-or bona fide-need arising in (for sometimes before) the fiscal year for which the appropriation was made. It restricts this year's appropriated funds from being used to fund next fiscal year's requirements. For example, annual funds (such as operations and maintenance funding) appropriated for fiscal year (FY) 2014 are to be used to fund legitimate or genuine FY2014 needs and are not to be used to fund a need the agency won't actually have until FY2015.

question: What is an unauthorized commitment? What steps do you take in evaluating, processing and approving an unauthorized commitment?
answer:
An unauthorized commitment is means an agreement that is not binding solely because the Government representative who made it lacked the authority to enter into that agreement on behalf of the Government. The act of approving an unauthorized commitment is called a ratification. Unauthorized commitments may be ratified only when the conditions of FAR 1.405(c) are met. a) Use of appropriated funds, b) Provided to or accepted by the Government - received a benefit, c) Ratification official has the authority to ratify, d) Resulting contract must otherwise be proper, e) Price must be fair & reasonable, f) Funds are available and were available at the time the action occurred, g) The CO recommends payments, h) It is IAW other requirements and limitations

Cite: FAR 1.405(c).

question: What do you envision is the role of your CORs? When are you required to appoint one? What authorities are you allowed to delegate to your COR? What authorities are not delegable to the COR?
answer: A Contracting Officer's Representative (COR) is an individual designated by the Contracting Officer to act as their representative in the technical monitoring and surveillance of a contract. These individuals serve as subject matter experts and perform surveillance of a contract to insure that the goods and services obtained meet the government's acceptance standards. A COR may be designated other administration duties by the contracting officer. A COR should be nominated by the requirements official as early as practicable in the acquisition process. A COR assist in the technical monitoring or administration of a contract. (A) Contracting officers shall designate a COR for all service contracts, including both firm-fixed-price and other than firm-fixed-price contracts, awarded by a DoD component or by any other Federal agency on behalf of DoD. The surveillance activities performed by CORs should be tailored to the dollar value/complexity of the specific contract for which they are designated. The COR does not have the authority to take any action, either directly or indirectly, that could change the price/cost or fee, quantity, quality, scope, delivery schedule, labor mix or other terms and conditions of the contract and/or task order. Only the contracting officer has the authority to make such changes. CORs do not have contractual authority to issue directions or changes to any contract or purchase order that affects price, quality, quantity, delivery, or any other aspect that will change the terms and conditions of the contract. In cases where changes have been made by unauthorized personnel, the Procuring Contracting Officer (PCO) must be immediately notified. The PCO will then determine if the work performed was within the scope of the original contract. If the work is determined to be outside the scope of the contract, corrective action through the ratification process will be taken. CORs shall forward any correspondence received from the contractor to the PCO. COR restrictions and limitations include, but are not limited to the following: 1) COR authority may not be re-delegated. 2) Only DoD military or DoD civilian personnel may be appointed as CORs. Non-DoD personnel, including foreign nationals, shall not be appointed as CORs. 3) The COR shall not make any agreement with the contractor requiring the obligation of public funds. 4) The COR shall not sign any contract, including delivery orders, purchase orders, nor modify a contract, or in a n way obligate funds for the Government. 5) The COR shall not encourage the contractor by words, actions, or a failure to act to undertake new work or an extension of existing work beyond the contract period. 6) The COR shall not interfere with the contractor's management prerogative by "supervising" contractor employees or otherwise directing their work efforts. 7) The COR shall not authorize a contractor to obtain property for use under a contract. 8) The COR shall not allow government-furnished property accountable under one contract to be used in the performance of work under another contract. 9) The COR shall not issue instructions to the contractor to start or stop work. 10) The COR shall not order or accept goods or services not expressly required by the contract. 11) The COR shall not discuss acquisition plans or provide any advance information that might give one contractor an advantage over another contractor in future procurements.

-Verify and document that supplies/services meet contract requirements

-Review and approve invoices (when delegated)

-Report performance issues to the CO

-Maintain COR files and documentation

-All service contracts, unless oversight is retained by the KO

-Contracts with complex technical requirements

-Contracts requiring on‑site monitoring

-High‑risk or high‑value contracts

-Construction contracts (unless exempted by agency procedures)

-Must be a government employee (military or civilian); Contractor personnel cannot serve as CORs

Monitoring contractor performance, Inspecting and accepting supplies/services (if delegated), Reviewing and recommending approval of invoices, Verifying labor categories/hours worked, Tracking deliverables, Documenting performance, Reporting deficiencies to the CO

A COR may NOT: Make changes to the contract (scope, price, terms, schedule), Obligate funds, Sign or modify contracts, Direct the contractor to perform work not in the contract, Approve or negotiate contract modifications, Terminate a contract, Make final decisions on disputes, Authorize overtime or additional work, Commit the government to anything

question: Your contractor presents you with a request for equitable adjustment (claim). Describe your process/steps that you will take in evaluating, processing and approving a claim?
answer:
First you should notify your attorney that you have received an Request for Equitable Adjustment (REA). Then, you will need to determine whether the contractor's request has any merit. If you determine that the request has merit, you may attempt to negotiate a settlement with the contractor, involving your attorney as you deem necessary. If negotiating with the contractor is difficult, and the involvement of your program counsel has not helped, you may refer the case to legal for formal Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR). Formal ADR can be accomplished either before or after the issuance of a final decision. If you determine that the REA is without merit, you may still attempt to discuss the issues with the contractor prior to issuing the PCO's final decision. Once a stalemate has occurred and the claim can't be resolved at the PCO level, a final decision is issued and an appeal is processed. (FAR 52.243-1, 52.243-2 and 52.243-4 (Changes), DFARS 252.243-7002)

Cite: FAR 52.243-1; FAR 52.243-2; FAR 52.243-4; DFARS 252.243-7002.

DFARS 252.243-7002 Requests for Equitable Adjustment.

(a) The amount of any request for equitable adjustment to contract terms shall accurately reflect the contract adjustment for which the Contractor believes the Government is liable. The request shall include only costs for performing the change, and shall not include any costs that already have been reimbursed or that have been separately claimed. I certify that the request is made in good faith, and that the supporting data are accurate and complete to the best of my knowledge and belief.

question: Your customer has submitted a requirement and states that only one source can meet their requirements. Describe your process/steps that you will take in evaluating, processing and approving or rejecting a sole source acquisition? Discuss any differences in the process based on different threshold levels.
answer:
Ensure market research has been conducted seeking out alternative sources. If the procurement is greater than the SAT, a J&A is required. Review the J&A thoroughly. If under the SAT a limited source justification will be required. (FAR 6.103-1 & DFARS 206.103-170 / 206.104-71)

question: Your customer has submitted an urgent requirement and believes that we should limit the number of sources or go to only one source. Describe your process/steps that you will take in validating the urgency and either processing and approving a sole source/limited source J&A or denying it. Address any leniencies associated with urgency (synopsis, posting, etc.) if any.
answer:
Review the requirements for urgent procurements, FAR 6.103-2 -- Unusual and Compelling Urgency. Ensure the J&A includes: (1) The date the requirement was first known and the circumstances leading to urgency. 
(2) The quantity of items or services appropriate for the urgent procurement with supporting rationale. An urgent procurement should rarely, if ever, contain an option quantity. (3) The required product or service delivery schedule. (4) The reason(s) for delay in initiating the acquisition if the date the requirement identified was such that normal contracting and production lead times could have achieved delivery by the required date. 
(5) The harm (financial or other) to the government that would result if the required delivery dates are not met. Include estimated expenses the government would likely incur due to the delay, and explain the basis for this estimate. (6) If the requiring office is specifying the source(s) appropriate for this procurement, explain the expertise required and discuss the contractors' capability to meet the urgent requirement.
Synopsis not required if Unusual and Compelling Urgency. J&A's citing urgency shall be publically available 30 days after contract award.

Cite: FAR 6.103-2

RFO 6.103-2 Unusual and compelling urgency.
(a) Authority. 10 U.S.C. 3204(a)(2) or 41 U.S.C. 3304(a)(2).

(b) Urgency. Agencies may contract without providing for full and open competition when the agency's need for the supplies or services is of such an unusual and compelling urgency that the Government would be seriously injured, financially or otherwise, unless the agency is permitted to limit the number of sources from which it solicits bids or proposals.

(c) Period of performance. The total period of performance of a contract greater than the simplified acquisition threshold awarded or modified using this authority—

(1) May not exceed the time necessary—

(i) To meet the unusual and compelling requirements of the work to be performed under the contract; and

(ii) For the agency to enter into another contract for the required goods and services through competitive procedures; and

(2) May not exceed one year, including all options, unless the head of the agency determines that exceptional circumstances apply. This determination—

(i) Is separate from the justification and approval for the use of the unusual and compelling urgency authority and must be documented in the contract file;

(ii) Does not cover any subsequent modification that further extends the period of performance, except for options included in the original determination. Such extensions must be approved at the same level as the original determination.

(d) Documentation after award. The justification and approval for the use of this authority, as well as the determination described in paragraph (c)(2) of this section, may be made after contract award when making the determination before award would unreasonably delay the acquisition.

(a) A justification and approval must support procedures under 6.103, except 6.103-5 and 6.103-7.

(b) Contracting officers require the support of the broader acquisition team when making decisions regarding competition. question: How do you determine the most appropriate contract type? Give examples of when you would use the different types.
answer:
A wide selection of contract types is available to the Government and contractors to provide needed flexibility in acquiring the large variety and volume of supplies and services required by agencies. Contract types vary according to: (1) The degree and timing of the responsibility assumed by the contractor for the costs of performance, and (2) The amount and nature of the profit incentive offered to the contractor for achieving or exceeding specified standards or goals. (b) The contract types are grouped into two broad categories, fixed-price contracts, cost-reimbursement contracts. The specific contract types range from firm-fixed-price, in which the contractor has full responsibility for the performance costs and resulting profit (or loss), to cost-plus-fixed-fee, in which the contractor has minimal responsibility for the performance costs and the negotiated fee (profit) is fixed. In between are the various incentive contracts in which the contractor's responsibility for the performance costs and the profit or fee incentives offered are tailored to the uncertainties involved in contract performance. There are many factors that the contracting officer should consider in selecting and negotiating the contract type. They include the following: (a) Price competition. Normally, effective price competition results in realistic pricing, and fixed-price contract is ordinarily in the Government's interest. (b) Price analysis. Price analysis, with or without competition, may provide a basis for selecting the contract type. The degrees to which price analysis can provide a realistic pricing standard should be carefully considered. See FAR 15.404-1 (c) Cost analysis. In the absence of effective price competition and if price analysis is not sufficient, the cost estimates of the offeror and the Government provide the basis for negotiating contract pricing arrangements. It is essential that the uncertainties involved in performance and their possible impact upon costs be identified and evaluated, so that a contract type that places a reasonable degree of cost responsibility upon the contractor can be negotiated. (d) type and complexity of the requirement. Complex requirements, particularly those unique to the Government, usually result in greater risk assumption by the Government. This is especially true for complex research and development contracts, when performance uncertainties or the likelihood of changes makes it difficult to estimate performance costs in advance. As a requirement recurs or as quantity production begins, the cost risk should shift to the contractor, and a fixed-price contract should be considered. (e) Combining contract types. If the entire contract cannot be firm-fixed-price, the contracting officer shall consider whether or not a portion of the contract can be established on a firm-fixed-price basis. (f) Urgency of the requirement. If urgency is a primary factor, the Government may choose to assume a greater proportion of risk or it may offer incentives tailored to performance outcomes to ensure timely contract performance. (g) Period of performance or length of production risk in times of economic uncertainty, contracts extending over a relatively long period may require economic price adjustment or price redetermination clauses (h) Contractor's technical capability and financial responsibility (i) Adequacy of the contractor's accounting system. Before agreeing on a contract type other than firm-fixed-price, the contracting officer shall ensure that the contractor's accounting system will permit timely development of all necessary cost data in the form required by the proposed contract type.
Cite: RFO FAR 15.404-1.

(RFO PART 16) Contract Type / Risk Burden / When It’s Best Suited 
Firm‑Fixed‑Price (FFP) / Contractor / When requirements are stable, well‑defined, and the contractor can accurately estimate costs. Ideal for commercial items and routine services.

Fixed‑Price w/ Economic Price Adjustment (FPEPA) / Contractor (slightly less) / When requirements are stable but market conditions (e.g., labor rates, commodities) may fluctuate beyond contractor control.

Fixed‑Price Incentive (FPI) / Shared, leaning contractor /When the Government wants cost control but also wants to motivate efficiency or performance improvements. Useful for production contracts with measurable metrics.

Fixed‑Price w/ Prospective Price Redetermination / Shared /When long‑term performance is needed but future costs are uncertain (e.g., multi‑year supply contracts).

Cost‑Plus‑Incentive‑Fee (CPIF) /Shared, leaning Government / When requirements are not fully defined but incentives can drive cost or performance outcomes. Good for development efforts with measurable targets.

Cost‑Plus‑Award‑Fee (CPAF) / Government / When performance is important but difficult to measure objectively. Best for complex R&D or high‑touch service contracts where subjective evaluation is appropriate.

Cost‑Plus‑Fixed‑Fee (CPFF) / Government / When technical uncertainty is high and contractors cannot reasonably estimate costs. Common in early‑stage R&D or exploratory studies.

Time‑and‑Materials (T&M) / Government / When the scope cannot be precisely defined and the Government needs flexibility. Best for emergency repairs, troubleshooting, or short‑notice specialized labor.

Labor‑Hour (LH) / Government / Same as T&M but without materials. Used when only labor hours are required and the work cannot be estimated in advance.

Indefinite‑Delivery / Indefinite‑Quantity (IDIQ) / Depends on order type / When the Government needs flexibility in timing or quantity. Best for recurring needs with uncertain volume.

Requirements Contract / Mixed / When the Government wants a single source for all requirements but cannot predict quantities. Good for consumables or repetitive services.

Definite‑Quantity Contract / Mixed / When the Government knows the exact quantity but not the delivery schedule.

Letter Contract / Government / When urgent circumstances require work to begin before full terms are negotiated. Used sparingly due to high risk.

question: Your contract requires a modification. Address the different types of modifications that could be executed. Describe the steps you would take in executing the modification and include in your discussion the different modification authorities and what documentation would be necessary to support the modification action.
answer:
Only a contracting officer acting within their authority executes a modification; no one else may direct work belonging on one (RFO FAR 43.202(a), 1.402-1). My warrant must cover the cumulative contract value including the modification.

Types (43.203):
- Bilateral supplemental agreements, signed by both parties: equitable adjustments, letter contract definitization, other agreed changes; the only way to change a commercial contract (52.212-4(d)).
- Unilateral, signed only by me: administrative changes (43.201), change orders under the Changes clauses (43.301, 43.305), changes under other clauses such as Options, and termination notices.
- Only in-scope changes, including priced options evaluated in the competition, are exempt from Part 6 (6.001(c)); out-of-scope work needs competition or a J&A (6.103, 6.104).

Steps:
- Written requirement and scope determination; work someone already directed is a possible constructive change or unauthorized commitment (43.204, 1.405).
- Certified funds before adding money (43.205) and a SAM exclusions check (9.405-1(a)(2)).
- Price before execution if possible, or at least a ceiling (43.202(b)); certified data if the adjustment, counting increases and decreases, exceeds the contract threshold (15.403-3(b)(3)).
- Definitize change orders quickly, with a release (43.304); DoD unpriced change orders over $5 million need an NTE, a 180-day definitization schedule and a 50 percent obligation cap, or 75 percent after a qualifying proposal (DFARS 243.370).
- Sign the SF 30 (43.401) and report it in FPDS within three business days (4.301).

The VCE file (AFARS 5104.101(a)) must let a stranger rebuild the action (4.101): requirement, scope and funding records, exclusions check, option determinations (17.204-1(b)), analysis, objectives and PNM (15.408-1, 15.408-2), and signed SF 30s.

question:
Describe the different types of terminations available.
Address both non commercial (FAR Part 49) and commercial (FAR PART 12) terminations.
Discuss the termination procedures and remedies (if any) f each type of termination.
answer:
Termination for Default - The Government’s contractual right to completely or partially terminate a contract because of the contractor’s actual or anticipated failure to perform its contractual obligations. Termination for Convenience - The Government’s right to unilaterally terminate performance of work under a contract in whole or, from time to time, in part if the Contracting Officer determines that a termination is in the Government's interest.
Termination for Cause - This is an action that is only applicable to procurements accomplished under FAR Part 12 (under the RFO, commercial terminations are at FAR 12.304, formerly 12.403). It is essentially the commercial equivalent of a termination for default.
The Government may terminate a commercial contract, or any part thereof, for cause in the event of:
(i) any default by the Contractor, or
(ii) if the Contractor fails to comply with any contract terms and conditions, or
(iii) fails to provide the Government, upon request, with adequate assurances of future performance.

No-Cost Cancellation- This is an alternative to a Termination (Default/Cause/Convenience) for Contracts/Purchase Orders. This is essentially when the contractor and the Government agree to cancel or partially cancel a requirement without cost to either party.
Remedies: Cure Notice and Show Cause Notice. 
Cure Notice advises the Contractor of a problem and provides an opportunity to correct within a specified time limit. Must be at least 10 days remaining in the performance period to issue a Cure Notice. May be followed by a Show Cause. Show Cause directs the Contractor to show why he should not be terminated for default

Cite: FAR part 12 (commercial terminations at FAR 12.304); FAR part 49.

question: Discuss your understanding of SAM (System for Award Management Exclusions) and how / when it is to be utilized.
answer:
SAM is the System for Award Management at sam.gov. It is the single Government-wide entity registration, it carries the Exclusions record that replaced the old Excluded Parties List System, and since February 2026 it also holds the contract award data that used to live in FPDS. For this question the two uses that matter are registration and exclusions, and I keep them separate in my head.

First, registration. Offerors have to be registered and active in SAM when they submit an offer or quote, through award, during performance and through final payment. That is where I get the Unique Entity ID, the CAGE code, the banking data my payment office uses, and the annual representations and certifications. The policy is RFO FAR 4.203-1, and the provision at 52.204-7, prescribed at 4.208(b), puts the offeror on notice.

Second, exclusions. An exclusion record tells me a party is debarred, suspended, proposed for debarment, or declared ineligible under a statute or executive order. RFO FAR 9.405(e) tells me when to look: after bids, proposals or quotes come in, and again immediately before award, because the record can change while I am evaluating. An active exclusion is conclusive - it is not a judgment call. I cannot solicit offers from, award to, or consent to a subcontract with an excluded party, and under 9.405-1 I cannot add new work, exercise an option or otherwise extend an existing contract with one, unless the agency head makes a written compelling-reason determination - and in the Army that determination belongs to the Army Suspension and Debarment Official, not to my chain.

Practically, I put a dated system record of the check in the file, I match on the Unique Entity ID and not just a name, and if an exclusion appears after award I apply the continuation rules at 9.405-1: the current contract may generally continue, but nothing new goes to that contractor without the compelling-reason determination. I also use SAM as a market research tool - entity search for capability and socioeconomic status, and the contract award data for what was bought before and from whom.

Cite: RFO FAR 9.404 (exclusions in SAM), 9.405 and 9.405(e) (effect of listing; when to check), 9.405-1 (continuation of current contracts), 9.104-1 (responsibility standards); RFO FAR 4.203-1 and 4.208(b) with provision 52.204-7 (SAM registration); AFARS 5109.405(a) (the Army SDO makes the compelling-reason determination).

question: You have received competitive proposals in an LPTA situation. How would you determine the prices to be fair and reasonable.
answer:
In an LPTA, price reasonableness rests on competition, and I document it with price analysis, not cost analysis.

First I confirm I have adequate price competition: two or more responsible offerors, competing independently, submitted priced proposals that meet the solicitation's requirements, and award goes to the technically acceptable offeror with the lowest evaluated price. Under RFO FAR 15.403-2, once prices are based on adequate price competition I must not obtain certified cost or pricing data.

Then I do price analysis under RFO FAR 15.404-1. The primary technique is comparing the proposed prices received in response to the solicitation to each other. I back that with at least one independent check:
- The IGE, which AFARS 5107.90 requires above the SAT.
- Historical prices paid for the same or similar services.
- Market research, published price lists, and pricing trends.

I look at the whole field, not just the acceptable offers, because every price tells me what the market says. I check for unbalanced pricing under 15.404-6 when there are options or multiple CLINs, and I sanity-check an unusually low price so I am not awarding to an offeror that misread the requirement.

Two traps. If only one offer came in, DFARS 215.202-71 applies: if the solicitation allowed fewer than 30 days for proposals I consult the requiring activity and resolicit for at least 30 more days; otherwise I determine the price fair and reasonable under 215.202-71(c), which can mean asking for data other than certified cost or pricing data, and I document why. If the only technically acceptable price is far from the others, I write down why competition still supports it or I lean on the other techniques. For commercial services, RFO FAR 12.204 says the same: I must determine the price fair and reasonable and, whenever possible, base that on competitive quotations or offers.

The determination goes in a signed price analysis memorandum in the file.

question: You have received competitive proposals in a trade-off situation. You are required to evaluate realism as well as the reasonableness of the cost/price. How would you evaluate each each of these.
answer:
Two different questions, two different analyses. Price reasonableness asks whether the price is too high, that is, whether the Government would pay more than it should. Cost realism asks whether the proposed cost is too low, that is, whether it reflects what performance will actually cost under that offeror's own technical approach.

For reasonableness I use price analysis under RFO FAR 15.404-1. In a competitive tradeoff, adequate price competition is normally my primary basis: I compare the proposed prices to each other, to the independent Government estimate, to historical prices paid, to published or market prices, and to parametric yardsticks. I only go to cost analysis under 15.404-2 if competition does not establish reasonableness or the action requires certified cost or pricing data without an exception.

For realism I do a cost realism analysis under RFO FAR 15.404-3. It is required for cost-reimbursement contracts, and I may use it on competitive fixed-price incentive or other competitive fixed-price work in exceptional cases: the requirement is new and offerors may not fully understand it, there are quality concerns, or past experience shows proposed costs led to quality or service shortfalls. Either way the solicitation has to say I will do it. With the technical evaluators I go element by element: do the labor categories, hours, rates, materials and ODCs match the offeror's proposed approach and the PWS?
- Cost-type: I adjust to a most probable cost, and that is what the SSA uses in the tradeoff.
- Fixed-price: I do not adjust the price. An unrealistic price feeds the performance-risk or technical rating, or a responsibility question, exactly as the solicitation said it would.

What keeps me out of a protest: evaluate only the way the RFP said I would, apply the same method to every offeror, and document both analyses in the price evaluation and the source selection record.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.404-1 (price analysis), 15.404-2 (cost analysis), 15.404-3 (cost realism analysis), 15.104 and 15.202 (price or cost evaluated in every competitive source selection), 15.103-1 (tradeoff approach).

question: Address the importance of acquisition planning. What are some things that you, as a KO, can do to assist the customer in acquisition planning? Additionally, discuss when formal acquisition planning is required.
answer: To ensure that the Government meets its needs in the most effective, economical, and timely manner. An acquisition plan is required at the following thresholds: $50M or more for production or services for all years, or $25M or more for any fiscal year; $10M or more for development.

7.102 - Requirements

(a) Agencies must perform acquisition planning for all acquisitions. Agencies should establish procedures to determine when a written or oral acquisition plan is required (see 7.103). (1) Information is available for making informed decisions at each step in the acquisition process;

(2) There is clear support for all actions taken;

(3) Necessary information is available for reviews or investigations; and

(4) Essential facts are available in case litigation arises.

(b) Acquisition plans must promote and provide for:

(1) Acquisition of commercial products or commercial services, whenever feasible. If available commercial products or services do not meet agency needs, acquire nondevelopmental items, to the maximum extent practicable (10 U.S.C. 3453 and 41 U.S.C. 3307).

(2)Full and open competition (see part 6). When using an exception to full and open competition, obtain competition to the maximum extent practicable for the procurement.(10 U.S.C. 3206(a)(1)and 41 U.S.C. 3306(a)(1)).

(3)Selection of the appropriate contract type to fulfill the agency’s needs.

(4)Use of existing contracts, if appropriate, including interagency and intra-agency contracts, to fulfill the requirement, before awarding new contracts (see part 8).

1. Research and Development - $10M

question: When do you perform market research, why is it necessary, and how is it documented? Describe some of the market research techniques.
answer:
Techniques include:
1. Contacting knowledgeable individuals in Government and industry regarding market capabilities to meet requirements.
2. Reviewing the results of recent market research undertaken to meet similar or identical requirements.
3. Publishing formal requests for information in appropriate technical or scientific journals or business publications.
4. Querying the Government-wide database of contracts and other procurement instruments intended for use by multiple agencies and other Government and commercial databases that provide information relevant to agency acquisitions.
5. Participating in interactive, on-line communication among industry, acquisition personnel, and customers.
6. Obtaining source lists of similar items from other contracting activities or agencies, trade associations or other sources.
7. Reviewing catalogs and other generally available product literature published by manufacturers, distributors, and dealers or available on-line.
8. Conducting interchange meetings or holding pre-solicitation conferences to involve potential offerors early in the acquisition process.

question: How do you determine if a small business category is applicable to your procurement? What documentation is needed to support this determination? What are different categories in the small business program?
answer:
I start with market research, because the small business decision is really a market research decision. Under RFO FAR Part 10 I find out who can do the work, and I assign one NAICS code and its SBA size standard to the requirement, per RFO FAR 19.103 and 13 CFR 121. That tells me what small means for this buy.

Then I apply the set-aside rules in RFO FAR 19.104-1. Above the micro-purchase threshold, if I have a reasonable expectation of offers from two or more responsible small businesses that are competitive on price, quality and delivery, I set it aside. That is the rule of two. If I do not set it aside, I have to document why. Before I default to a total small business set-aside I look at the socioeconomic programs first: 8(a) under 19.108, HUBZone under 19.105, service-disabled veteran-owned under 19.106, and women-owned and economically disadvantaged women-owned under 19.107. Each has its own set-aside and sole-source authority and its own SBA certification requirement.

Documentation in my file:
- The market research report showing the sources I found and their size status.
- The NAICS code and size standard, stated in the solicitation.
- The DD Form 2579, Small Business Coordination Record, reviewed by the small business specialist for actions over the micro-purchase threshold, except under-SAT total small business set-asides (RFO DFARS PGI 219.102(g)(1)); if I reject the specialist's recommendation it goes to the SBA procurement center representative, who can appeal.
- My set-aside determination, or the written reason for not setting aside.
- The offeror's size and socioeconomic representations in SAM, plus SBA certification for 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB and WOSB awards, and the SBA acceptance letter for an 8(a) sole source.
- A subcontracting plan requirement when the action will exceed $900,000, or $2 million for construction (RFO FAR 19.109).

The categories: small business, small disadvantaged business, 8(a) participants, HUBZone, service-disabled veteran-owned and veteran-owned, and women-owned and economically disadvantaged women-owned small business. One note from an OCONUS office: RFO FAR 19.000(b) says I must apply Part 19 in the United States and its outlying areas and may apply it outside them, and RFO DFARS 219.104-70(b)(2) says the 19.104-1(a) set-aside requirement does not apply to acquisitions excluded from SBA procurement center representative review, which under 219.102-70(a)(4) and (5) includes awards under a Status of Forces Agreement and acquisitions both awarded and performed outside the United States. So for a Korea or Germany award I confirm the local set-aside practice with my policy shop before I set aside.

Cite: RFO FAR 19.000(b), 19.102, 19.103, 19.104-1, 19.105 through 19.109; RFO DFARS 219.102-70(a), 219.104-70(b)(2) and PGI 219.102(g)(1) (Class Deviation 2026-O0037 Rev 1); 15 U.S.C. 644(j); 13 CFR 121.

question: One of your specialists is new to contracting policies and procedures and asks you to explain a "D&F". How would you describe a D&F?
answer: A prerequisite to taking certain contracting actions. The "determination" is a conclusion or decision supported by the "findings". Determination and Findings” means a special form of written approval by an authorized official that is required by statute or regulation as a prerequisite to taking certain contract actions. The “determination” is a conclusion or decision supported by the “findings.’’ The findings are statements of fact or rationale essential to support the determination and must cover each requirement of the statute or regulation.

question: If a contractor is included on the List of Parties Excluded from Federal Procurement and Nonprocurement Programs, what are the rules on continuation of current contracts with the contractor?
answer:
Authority: FAR 9.405 -- 1. Agencies may continue contracts or subcontracts in existence at the time the contractor was debarred, suspended, or proposed for debarment unless the agency head or a designee directs otherwise. 2. Ordering activities may continue to place orders against existing contracts, including indefinite delivery contracts, in the absence of a termination. 3. Agencies shall not renew or otherwise extend the duration of current contracts (i.e. exercise options), or consent to subcontracts, unless the agency head or a designee authorized representative states, in writing, the compelling reasons for renewal or extension.

Cite: FAR 9.405; FAR 9.405-1

question: Describe the Anti-deficiency Act (ADA) and list some actions that would constitute a violation of it. What are the potential penalties for a violation of the ADA?
answer: The Anti-deficiency Act means that Government officials have no authority to obligate or spend funds unless the funding is available prior to the obligation occurring. Some of the violations of the ADA include: a. Obligation in excess of available funds. b. Expenditure in excess of available funds. c. Involving the Government in a contract or obligation in advance of appropriations. d. Improper augmentation of appropriations e. Accepting most voluntary services. Administrative discipline including suspension without pay and removal from job, criminal prosecution (if knowing and willful violation) - up to two years imprisonment and $5,000 fine, and the contract may be declared null and void, although the contractor may still be owed compensation.

question: You are a PCO and a new trainee comes to you seeking advice. answer: 1. Active - appropriation is available for obligation & disbursement. 2. Cancelled - no longer available for any purpose. Expired appropriations are cancelled at the end of the 5th full fiscal year following expiration.

question: The COR has reported to you that the contractor has failed to deliver a service per the contract requirements. What actions should you take as the Contracting Officer in this instance?
answer: Contact the customer/COR first to confirm that the services were not performed. Would reach out to the contractor to understand why the services weren't performed, ie: Fact finding. The goal is to ensure that no one on the Government side provided direction that they did not have the authority to direct the contractor and to get the contractors story. From there, we have a couple of options, assuming no Gov't direction was provided. 1. Could issue a cure notice, which gives the contractor 10 days to cure the failure, if they do not, I could terminate for default. That is pretty aggressive, especially if we still need the services because getting another contractor in would obviously result in a break of service. The second approach would be to send a PCO letter and ask them for consideration for an extension in order to complete the performance. The considration is usually monetary, but other possibilities could be discussed. For either scenario, legal would also have to be involved.

question: What is VCE PCF and why is it important? As a contracting officer, what steps will you take to personally ensure data being reported is accurate?
answer:
VCE PCF is the Virtual Contracting Enterprise Paperless Contract File - the Army's electronic contract file. AFARS directs contracting officers to use the VCE tools throughout the acquisition process, and the PCF module is where the documents that manage the acquisition are stored, accessed and routed, filed to the Army Cabinet Index folder structure so every file looks the same. When I say a document is in the file, I mean it is in PCF - with two exceptions: classified material, which never goes into VCE, and documents that already live in PIEE or the contract-reporting system of record (now SAM.gov contract data, formerly FPDS-NG), which I reference rather than duplicate.

It matters for three reasons: it is the file RFO FAR 4.101 requires me to keep - a comprehensive record of the transaction history that supports decisions, reviews, investigations and litigation; it is what an auditor, protest counsel, a claims attorney, or my successor reads when I am not there; and the data in it feeds Procurement Management Reviews and the reporting leadership uses to make decisions.

The integrity point is the one I would emphasize at a board. Bad file data is not an administrative problem, it is a defensibility problem. A missing sole-source justification or an undated exclusions check is how a good award becomes a sustained protest.

What I personally do, and I do mean personally, not delegate and forget:
- I file to the Army Cabinet Index as the action progresses, not at closeout. If it happened this week it goes in this week.
- I do not sign until I have walked the file myself. Before award I open PCF and confirm the justification, the responsibility determination and dated exclusions check, the price reasonableness determination, the funding document, and the legal and other required reviews are present and legible.
- I reconcile system data to the document. The award value, dates, NAICS, competition and set-aside codes in the contract action report in SAM.gov have to match the signed instrument, and I check the two against each other rather than assuming the system pulled it right.
- I self-audit a small sample of my own files every month against the Cabinet Index and the PMR checklist, and I fix findings before someone else finds them.
- I train and spot-check my specialists and CORs, and I give feedback on the file the same way I give feedback on a negotiation. When I take over a portfolio I inventory open actions and file status first.
- When something cannot be in PCF - classified or otherwise restricted - I put a signed memorandum in the file saying what exists and where it is held.

Cite: RFO FAR 4.101 (contract files), 4.308 and 4.309 (closeout; storage, handling and retention); AFARS 5104.101(a) and AFARS PGI 5104.101 (VCE tools and the PCF; before the June 2026 AFARS revision this text was AFARS 5104.802(f)). Confirm the current Cabinet Index version and the PMR checklist with your contracting operations chief and the local VCE/PCF administrator.

rfo.notes: Reviewed 14 Sep 2026. 4.101, 4.308-1/-2 and 4.309 read on the RFO Part 4 page. The AFARS was reissued for the RFO: in the combined AFARS PDF on army.mil (Part 5104 revised 30 Jun 2026) the contract-file rule is 5104.101(a) - use VCE tools throughout the acquisition; VCE not for classified documents; see AFARS PGI 5104.101. The PCF detail (PCF module for storing, accessing and routing documents; KO ensures PCF holds all appropriate documents; PIEE/FPDS-NG system-of-record rule; Army Cabinet Index) was read from the pre-revision AFARS 5104.802(f) text still displayed on acquisition.gov (rev. 11 Jul 2025) and is presumed to now sit in PGI 5104.101, which was not fetched. The PMR checklist and Cabinet Index version are local.

key_points: VCE PCF is the Army's electronic contract file; AFARS 5104.101 directs use of the VCE tools and the PCF module, filed to the Army Cabinet Index; 'in the file' means 'in PCF'.
Exceptions: classified material never goes in VCE; documents already in PIEE or the contract-reporting system of record are referenced, not duplicated.
File integrity is a defensibility issue - protests, claims, audits, PMRs and successor KOs all run on that file (RFO FAR 4.101).
Load documents as the action progresses; do not sign until you have walked the file yourself: justification, dated exclusions check, price reasonableness, funding, required reviews.
Reconcile the SAM.gov contract action report (value, dates, NAICS, competition and set-aside codes) against the signed instrument.

question: What is a Quality Assurance Surveillance Plan (QASP) and when is it required?
answer:
A Quality Assurance Surveillance Plan is the Government's plan for how we will check that the contractor is meeting the performance standards in the PWS. It is a Government document, not a contractor document. It lists the work that requires surveillance, the performance standard and acceptable quality level for each task, the surveillance method - hundred-percent inspection, random sampling, periodic inspection, customer complaint - who performs it, normally the COR, how results are documented, and what happens when performance falls short: corrective action requests, a contract discrepancy report, deductions, and ultimately the contract remedies.

When is it required?
- RFO FAR 46.401: a QASP should be prepared in conjunction with the statement of work and must specify all work requiring surveillance and the method of surveillance.
- RFO FAR 46.103: the activity responsible for the technical requirements prescribes the quality requirements, which for a service contract means the QASP.
- DFARS 246.401: the need for a QASP must be addressed and documented in the contract file for every contract except those awarded using simplified acquisition procedures, and for services the contracting officer should prepare one.
- DFARS 237.872 and PGI 237.872: QASPs are prepared with the PWS, SOW or SOO, tailored to the performance risk of the contract type and the work, include surveillance of the Combating Trafficking in Persons clause, and are retained in the file.
- RFO FAR 37.102-1: a performance-based service contract needs a PWS with measurable performance standards, and the QASP is what makes them enforceable.

In practice, every service contract above the SAT gets a QASP built with the PWS, the COR is trained to it before award, and I review it so the surveillance matches the risk: lighter for firm-fixed-price commercial services, heavier for cost-type or mission-critical work.

Cite: RFO FAR 46.103, 46.401, 37.102-1; DFARS 246.401, 237.872; DFARS PGI 237.872.

Contents: what to surveil, standard/AQL, method, who (COR), documentation, remedies.
RFO FAR 46.401: prepared with the SOW/PWS; 46.103: the requiring activity prescribes it for services.
DFARS 246.401: addressed and documented in the file for every contract except SAP; services should have one.
DFARS 237.872 / PGI 237.872 (was 237.172): prepared with the PWS, SOW or SOO, tailored to risk, includes trafficking-in-persons surveillance, retained in the file.

question: How do you determine what clauses to include in a solicitation / contract?
answer:
I do not pick clauses from memory. I let the FAR system pick them and then I verify every one. Every provision and clause in part 52 has a prescription in parts 1 through 51 that says when it is required, required-when-applicable, or optional, RFO FAR 52.101(e) points me to the provision and clause matrix at subpart 52.3, which sorts them by contract type as required, required-when-applicable, or optional, and for the last two I go back to the prescribing text to decide. So the clause set is driven by the characteristics of the acquisition:
- What I am buying: a commercial product or service under part 12, where the 52.212 series does most of the work and only statute-based clauses ride along; noncommercial supplies or services; construction; A-E; R&D.
- How I am buying it: simplified procedures (13.204), negotiated (part 15), sealed bidding (part 14), or an order under an existing vehicle where the parent contract's clauses already apply.
- Contract type: fixed-price, cost-reimbursement, T&M or labor-hour each carry different payment, allowable-cost, changes and termination clauses.
- Dollar value: many clauses key off the micro-purchase threshold, the SAT and other statutory thresholds.
- Special features: options, Government property, service contract or construction labor standards, small business set-aside, Buy American and trade agreements, cybersecurity, key personnel, and for us OCONUS the DFARS 225 and theater clauses plus host-nation and currency considerations.

Tools: the provision and clause matrix at RFO FAR subpart 52.3 and the acquisition.gov Smart Matrix, the DFARS 252 and AFARS 5152 matrices, and the contract writing system's clause logic. I answer its questions honestly and still read the output, because the system only knows what I told it. I incorporate by reference where I can (52.102), complete fill-ins and alternates (52.104, 52.105), and organize under the uniform contract format (15.109) when it applies. Before release I get a second set of eyes from a specialist or peer review, and legal at the required thresholds.

Leadership point: I teach my team why a clause is there, not just that it is. A clause with no prescription, or a prescription with no clause, is a red flag I want them to catch before the solicitation goes out.

Cite: RFO FAR 52.101(e), 52.102, 52.104, 52.105 and subpart 52.3; 12.205; 13.204; 15.109; DFARS part 252 and AFARS part 5152 clause matrices.

rfo.notes: RFO Part 52 section titles (52.101 Using Part 52, 52.102 Incorporating provisions and clauses, 52.104 Procedures for modifying and completing, 52.105 Procedures for using alternates, subpart 52.3 Provision and Clause Matrix) and the 52.101(e) matrix sentence re-confirmed on acquisition.gov 14 Sep 2026; 12.205, 13.204 and 15.109 are verified crosswalk entries. DFARS 252 / AFARS 5152 matrix references are general and were not re-fetched.

question: What is unbalanced pricing, and how should you address it?
answer:
Unbalanced pricing is when the total price is allocated across the contract line items or contract parts in a way that does not reflect an equitable distribution of costs. Typical patterns: a front-loaded base period with cheap option years, an inflated mobilization or first-article line with understated production lines, or on an IDIQ, high prices on the items the offeror thinks we will actually order and nominal prices on the rest.

Why I care: it creates two risks. Payment risk, because the Government ends up making what amounts to an advance payment for work it has not received yet. And performance risk, because once the profitable line items are done the contractor has no incentive to finish, or the evaluated price is not the price we will really pay if options or quantities do not materialize the way the offeror bet they would.

How I address it, per RFO FAR 15.404-6:
- Analyze every offer that has separately priced line items or subline items and look for line items that are significantly over- or understated compared with the IGE, other offers, and historical prices.
- If I find it, I assess the risk to the Government: could it advance funds, could it drive a walk-away, does it distort the evaluated price.
- I may reject an offer if the unbalancing poses an unacceptable risk to the Government. Under sealed bidding I may reject a bid whose line item prices are materially unbalanced (RFO FAR 14.306-3(g)).
- If it is mathematically unbalanced but not materially unbalanced, I document why the risk is acceptable and I may address it in discussions.
- I protect the Government up front by structuring the solicitation well: realistic quantity estimates, separately evaluated options, and payment terms that do not pay ahead of performance.

I document the analysis in the price negotiation memorandum or source selection record so the decision is defensible in a protest.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.404-6 (was 15.404-1(g)); RFO FAR 14.306-3(g) (was 14.404-2(g)).

rfo.notes: Both RFO numbers verified on acquisition.gov/far-overhaul (Part 15 page shows 15.404-6 Unbalanced pricing with the definition and reject-if-unacceptable-risk language; Part 14 page shows 14.306-3(g)). Patterns: front-loaded base year, inflated mobilization/first-article lines, IDIQ items priced to expected order mix
Risks: advance-payment (payment) risk and performance/walk-away risk; evaluated price may not equal price paid
Analyze all offers with separately priced line items; assess risk; may reject if unacceptable risk
Sealed bidding: may reject materially unbalanced bids (RFO FAR 14.306-3(g))
Mitigate in solicitation design and document the analysis in the PNM/SSDD

question: Explain the difference between suspension and debarment.
answer:
Both are exclusion actions taken by the agency's suspension and debarment official to protect the Government, not to punish, and neither is a contractual remedy. The difference is timing, evidentiary standard, and duration.

Suspension is the immediate, temporary action. The standard is adequate evidence of a cause - an indictment, or an information charging a criminal offense, is adequate evidence by itself - plus an immediate need to protect the Government. It takes effect right away, before the case is fully developed. It runs up to twelve months; an Assistant Attorney General can ask for one six-month extension, so eighteen months is the cap unless legal proceedings have been initiated within that period.

Debarment is the considered, longer-term action. It follows a fact-based proceeding, the standard is a preponderance of the evidence, and the period is commensurate with the seriousness of the cause - generally not more than three years, up to five for Drug-Free Workplace Act violations.

There is also a middle state: proposed for debarment. The moment the SDO issues the notice, the contractor is excluded during the proceeding, so the practical effect at the contracting table is the same as a debarment.

What is identical is the effect, and that is what I care about as a KO. All three create an exclusion record in SAM. Excluded parties cannot receive new awards, I cannot consent to a subcontract with them, and I cannot add new work, exercise an option or otherwise extend an existing contract, unless the agency head makes a written compelling-reason determination - in the Army, that is the Army SDO. Existing contracts may generally continue, but nothing new goes to them. Both actions can extend to affiliates and to named individuals when the SDO includes them.

My role is not to suspend or debar. My role is to check exclusions before award, document it, and refer conduct that warrants action through my chain and legal counsel. In the Army the Procurement Fraud Branch of the Contract and Fiscal Law Division, U.S. Army Legal Services Agency, processes the referral and recommends action to the Army SDO, and the Army notification procedures are in AFARS PGI 5109.406-3 and 5109.407-3. Separately, I record the facts in the responsibility record so other KOs see them.

Cite: RFO FAR 9.406 (debarment; 9.406-3(d) preponderance standard, 9.406-4 period), RFO FAR 9.407 (suspension; 9.407-2(b) indictment as adequate evidence, 9.407-4 period), RFO FAR 9.404 (exclusions in SAM), 9.405 and 9.405-1 (effect of listing; continuation of current contracts); AFARS 5109.402(c), 5109.405(a) and AFARS PGI 5109.406-3.

rfo.notes: Reviewed 14 Sep 2026. Subpart 9.4 numbering and the 9.406-3(d), 9.406-4, 9.407-2(b) and 9.407-4 rules read on the RFO Part 9 page (12 months; one 6-month extension at AAG request; 18-month cap unless legal proceedings initiated; 3 years / 5 years). The draft had the suspension rule backwards ('extendable to eighteen months if legal proceedings are initiated, and longer if DOJ requests it') - corrected. key_points: Both are protective, not punitive, and both are decided by the suspension and debarment official - not by the KO; neither is a contractual remedy.

Suspension: immediate, on adequate evidence (an indictment or information suffices, 9.407-2(b)); up to 12 months, one 6-month extension at an Assistant Attorney General's request, 18 months maximum unless legal proceedings were initiated in that period (9.407-4).
Debarment: follows a fact-based proceeding on a preponderance of the evidence (9.406-3(d)); generally not more than 3 years, 5 for Drug-Free Workplace Act violations (9.406-4).
Proposed for debarment excludes the contractor during the proceeding - same practical effect at the contracting table (9.405).

Identical effect: SAM exclusion record; no new awards, no subcontract consent, no new work, options or extensions absent a compelling-reason determination - in the Army, by the Army SDO (AFARS 5109.405(a)).
KO role: check exclusions before award, document it, and refer through the chain and counsel; Army referrals run through the Procurement Fraud Branch (AFARS 5109.402(c), PGI 5109.406-3).

question: What should you do if you have any suspicion of any ethics violation or fraud? How do you mentor and train your customer on ethics and fraud concerns?
answer:
If I suspect fraud or an ethics violation, I do not investigate it myself and I do not confront the contractor or the employee. I preserve the record, hold any pending action the suspicion touches, and report through the right channel the same day.

For a procurement integrity issue - source selection or bid and proposal information leaking, or an employee talking jobs with an offeror - RFO FAR 3.104-7 tells me what to do: determine whether it affects the pending award. If it does, I forward everything promptly to the HCA, through my chief and legal; if I conclude it does not, I still report it to the official Army procedures designate, who can disagree and send it to the HCA. The HCA decides whether to proceed, investigate, refer to CID or the IG, or recommend voiding the contract.

For suspected fraud - false claims, false certifications, kickbacks, bid rigging, product substitution - AFARS 5109.406-3 requires me to contact the local Procurement Fraud Advisor in the servicing legal office, who sends the Procurement Flash Report under AR 27-40 paragraph 8-5, and to send everything the PFA needs through the HCA; the report reaches the suspension and debarment official through the Procurement Fraud Branch. If the chain of command is the problem, the DoD IG hotline and Army CID are always open. I write down what I know and when I learned it, and if the flash report recommends suspension or debarment I withhold funds coming due on that contract unless the HCA or the debarring official directs otherwise.

For gratuities or personal conflicts I go to the ethics counselor under the Joint Ethics Regulation.

Mentoring the customer is prevention, and I do three things:
- At the post-award conference I brief CORs and the requiring activity on mandatory disclosure under RFO FAR 3.1003 and the hotline poster policy at 3.1002, on gifts, and on why they cannot direct the contractor.
- I teach with real cases: the COR asked to sign a receiving report for work not done; the program office steering a follow-on to the incumbent; the vendor offering lunch during evaluations.
- I make it easy to raise a concern early and without blame, because the cheapest fraud case is the one that reaches me as a question.

Cite: RFO FAR 3.101-1, 3.104-7, 3.1002, 3.1003; AFARS 5109.406-3; AR 27-40 chapter 8; DoD 5500.07-R (Joint Ethics Regulation); 41 U.S.C. chapter 21.

question: What is an organizational conflict of interest as it relates to contractor (or provider) access to acquisition information? Give an example.
answer:
An organizational conflict of interest exists when, because of other activities or relationships, a contractor is unable or potentially unable to render impartial assistance or advice to the Government, its objectivity in performing the work is or might be impaired, or it has an unfair competitive advantage. The three classic types are impaired objectivity, biased ground rules, and unequal access to information. This question is about the third one.

Unequal access means a contractor, through its work for the Government, obtained nonpublic information that gives it a competitive edge in a later competition: another company's proprietary data, the independent Government estimate, the acquisition strategy, draft evaluation criteria, budget data or source selection information. RFO FAR 9.505-4 addresses access to proprietary information, and 9.505-2 covers a contractor that helped write the specification or PWS, which is biased ground rules but usually carries an information advantage as well.

Example: an advisory support contractor works inside the DPW or program office helping draft the acquisition plan and IGE for the follow-on base operations contract. It sees the funding profile, the draft PWS and the evaluation approach. If that company or an affiliate later proposes on the follow-on, it has unequal access. That is an OCI even if nobody did anything wrong.

As the KO, under 9.504 I identify it early, during acquisition planning and market research, and I avoid, neutralize or mitigate it: exclude the firm from the competition, accept a Government-approved mitigation plan with firewalls and non-disclosure agreements, or release the information to all offerors so the advantage disappears. I document the analysis in writing with legal, put the OCI provisions and any mitigation requirement in the solicitation (9.507), and if it cannot be mitigated and award is still in the Government's interest, only the agency head or designee can waive it under 9.503. If the nonpublic information is source selection information, the Procurement Integrity Act rules at RFO FAR 3.104 apply on top of the OCI rules.

Cite: RFO FAR 9.501, 9.502, 9.503, 9.504, 9.505, 9.505-2, 9.505-4, 9.506, 9.507; RFO FAR 3.104; 41 U.S.C. chapter 21.

question: What is the difference between and Agency Protest and a GAO protest?
answer:
FAR RFO 33.104 Protests to the agency
Preaward: Any alleged solicitation improprieties must be protested within 10 days of when the alleged impropriety was known or should have been known. A contract may not be awarded until the agency resolves the protest, unless a written justification is made for urgent and compelling reasons, or award is determined in writing to be in the best interest of the Government.
Postaward: (a) If a protest is received, within 10 days after contract award or within 5 days after a debriefing date offered to the protester under a timely debriefing request in accordance with 15.505 or 15.506, whichever is later, then the contracting officer must immediately suspend performance, pending resolution of the protest within the agency, including any independent review by a higher level official, unless continued performance is justified.
(b)Continued performance may be justified upon a written finding that there are urgent and compelling reasons, or continued performance is determined in writing to be in the best interest of the Government.
FAR RFO 33.105 Protests to GAO
Preaward: (a) If the agency receives notice of a protest from GAO before award, then a contract may not be awarded unless the head of the contracting activity authorizes contract award and performance.
(b) The head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, may authorize contract award and performance upon a written finding that—
(1) Urgent and compelling circumstances which significantly affect the interest of the United States will not allow waiting for a decision from GAO; and
(2) Award is likely to occur within 30 days of the written finding.
Postaward: (b)(1) If the agency receives notice of a protest from the GAO within 10 days after contract award or within 5 days after a debriefing date offered to the protester for any debriefing that is required by 15.505 or 15.506, whichever is later, then the contracting officer must immediately suspend performance or terminate the awarded contract, unless the head of the contracting activity authorizes contract performance.
(2) The head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, may authorize contract performance, upon a written finding that—
(i) Contract performance will be in the best interests of the United States; or
(ii) Urgent and compelling circumstances that significantly affect the interests of the United States will not permit waiting for the GAO's decision.
(Citation note: the RFO text of 33.104-3 and 33.105-3 still cross-references 15.505 and 15.506; under the RFO the preaward debriefing section is 15.206-2 and the postaward debriefing section is 15.301.)

Cite: FAR 33.104 (protests to the agency); FAR 33.104-3 (postaward stay); FAR 33.105 (protests to GAO); FAR 33.105-2 (preaward); FAR 33.105-3 (postaward); FAR 15.206-2 and FAR 15.301 (debriefings)

question: Describe a Cure Notice and when you would use one as a KO.
answer:
If a contract is to be terminated for default before delivery date, a "cure notice" is required by the Default clause. Before using this notice, it must be ascertained that the amount of time equal to or greater than the period of "cure" remains in the contract delivery schedule or any extension to it. If the amount of time remaining in the contract delivery schedule is not sufficient to permit a "cure" period of 10 days or more, the Cure
Notice should NOT be issued, instead a "Show Cause Notice" may be issued.

deck_notes.text:
RFP FAR 49.607 Delinquency notices
​Cure notice. If a contract is to be terminated for default before the delivery date, a "Cure Notice" is required by the Default clause. Before using this notice, it must be ascertained that an amount of time equal to or greater than the period of "cure" remains in the contract delivery schedule or any extension to it. If the time remaining in the contract delivery schedule is not sufficient to permit a realistic "cure" period of 10 days or more, the "Cure Notice" should not be issued. The "Cure Notice" may be in the following format:
Cure Notice
You are notified that the Government considers your ____ [specify the contractor’s failure or failures] a condition that is endangering performance of the contract. Therefore, unless this condition is cured within 10 days after receipt of this notice [or insert any longer time that the Contracting Officer may consider reasonably necessary], the Government may terminate for default under the terms and conditions of the _______ [insert clause title] clause of this contract.
(End of notice)
RFO FAR 12.304 Terminations. (RFO FAR Part 12 Acquisition of Commercial Products and Commercial Services)
(a) General. Follow the procedures in this section and the termination paragraphs of the clause at 52.212-4, when terminating contracts for commercial products or commercial services. Do not use the procedures in part 49.
(b) Termination for cause.
(1) Before terminating a contract for cause, send a cure notice to the contractor, unless the reason for the termination is late delivery.
(2) When a termination for cause is appropriate, send the contractor a written notification regarding the termination. At a minimum, this notification must include—
(i) A statement that the contract is terminated for cause;
(ii) The reasons for the termination;
(iii) Which remedies the Government intends to seek or give a date by which the Government will inform the contractor of the remedy; and
(iv) A statement that the notice constitutes a final decision of the contracting officer, and that the contractor has the right to appeal under the Disputes clause.
(3) Follow the procedures in part 42 to report termination information to the Federal Awardee Performance and Integrity Information System.

question: When would you use a bilateral modification versus an unilateral modification?
answer:
Bilateral modifications are negotiated changes such as delivery schedule change, funding change, significant change to the SOW, etc. A unilateral modification can be issued for administrative changes, change orders within the general scope of the contract, termination notices, etc. If the contract has an option (to extend the contract, to purchase additional supplies or services, etc.) the contract should have an option clause in it and then the option can be exercised unilaterally. Numerous modification authorities (and associated clauses) exist for modifications such as Engineering changes, changes to usage of government property, funding changes, etc. The Changes Clauses (FAR 52.243-1 through 52.243-7) allow for unilateral modifications.

Cite: FAR 52.243-1 through FAR 52.243-7.

answer: The Berry Amendment limits the use of funding appropriated or otherwise made available to DoD from being used to buy certain end items, components, or materials unless they are wholly of US origin or, in some circumstances, sourced from a qualifying country. End items include: Articles of clothing, Fibers, Yarns, Fabrics, Stainless Steel flatware, Hand measuring tools, Specialty Metals

question: Describe the differences between a Statement of Work (SOW) and a Performance Work Statement (PWS). When would each be appropriate?
answer: A SOW details what actions the contractor shall take to meet the contract requirements while a PWS describes the outcome. A SOW is more appropriate where risk exists within the process such that the Government must discretely describe necessary actions. A PWS (preferred) is more appropriate where variance in the process to achieve the outcome does not present risk, i.e. commercial items, services or mature product lines.

question: Explain the legal effect of quotations and how a contractor indicates acceptance of a purchase order?
answer: A quotation is not an offer and, consequently, cannot be accepted by the Government to form a binding contract. Therefore, issuance by the Government of an order in response to a supplier’s quotation does not establish a contract. The order is an offer by the Government to the supplier to buy certain supplies or services upon specified terms and conditions. A contract is established when the supplier accepts the offer. Supplier may indicate its acceptance of an order by notification to the Government, preferably in writing. Supplier may indicate acceptance by furnishing the supplies or services ordered or by proceeding with the work to the point where substantial performance has occurred.

question: OSD recently implemented an annual reporting requirement for bridge contracts. What is your understanding of bridge contracts and why is this a matter of concern?
answer:
Applicants should understand the concerns related to competition and the need to ensure proper acquisition planning to minimize the need for bridges. 

A bridge action describes a non-competitive action requiring a justification to include, but not limited to, a formal justification and approval (FAR Part 6 or 12.201-1), limited sources justification (FAR 8.401; FSS ordering procedures moved to GSAR subpart 538.71), and exception to fair opportunity (FAR 16.507-6), to retain the current or similar product or services as a result of delay in the negotiation and award of a follow-on contract.

The timely re-competition and renegotiation of our continuing DoD product and service requirements represents a critical opportunity for securing the best deals in support of the warfighter. Bridge contracts represent a lost opportunity for savings that could be realized from new, competitively awarded contracts.

question: An unrestricted solicitation with an estimate around $2 Million was issued for 30 days and only one offer was received. In order to determine if the proposal is fair and reasonable, what do you do?
answer:
Certified cost & Pricing threshold increased to $2M, effective for contracts entered into after 30 June 2018. (threshold updated — see Thresholds)

DFARS 215.202-71(c): If only one offer is received when competitive procedures were used and the solicitation allowed at least 30 days for receipt of proposals (unless the 30-day requirement is not applicable in accordance with 215.371-4(a)(3) or has been waived in accordance with section 215.371-5 — old DFARS numbering kept; the RFO renumbering of these two paragraphs could not be verified), the contracting officer shall—

 (1) Determine through cost or price analysis that the offered price is fair and reasonable and that adequate price competition exists (with approval of the determination at a level above the contracting officer) or another exception to the requirement for certified cost or pricing data applies (see FAR 15.403-2(c) and 15.403-3). In these circumstances, no further cost or pricing data is required; or

 (2)(i) Obtain from the offeror cost or pricing data necessary to determine a fair and reasonable price and comply with the requirement for certified cost or pricing data at FAR 15.403-3. For acquisitions that exceed the cost or pricing data threshold, if no exception at FAR 15.403-2(b) applies, the cost or pricing data shall be certified; and

 (ii) Enter into negotiations with the offeror as necessary to establish a fair and reasonable price. The negotiated price should not exceed the offered price.
