question: Please define a Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data and its purpose. What are some of the key things you would expect to see on the certificate before accepting the certificate? There are five exceptions to obtaining a Certificate - please list one of them.
answer:
The definition is as follows: A Certificate of Current Cost or Pricing Data certifies that to the best of the company's knowledge, the cost or pricing data submitted were accurate, complete, and current as of the date of agreement on price or, if applicable, an earlier date agreed upon between the parties that is as close as practicable to the date of agreement on price. The purpose is to have the company commit as to the accuracy, completeness, and currency of submitted data. If the data is later found to be incorrect or appropriate data was not submitted, the government reserves the right to a downward contract price adjustment for any monetary damages incurred.
 Key things we would expect to see or review in a Certificate are:
- The certificate is in the format shown in FAR 15.403-4
- Current as of the date of agreement on price or an earlier agreed upon date
- Signed by an authorized representative of the company and dated as close as practicable to the date when price negotiations were concluded
-Check for qualifications or new information disclosed by the sweep and evaluate its impact on the negotiated price

Exceptions (FAR 15.403-2(b)):
Adequate Price Competition
 Prices set by law or regulation
 Commercial Item
 Waiver has been granted
Modifying contract/subcontract for commercial items

Other Exceptions (FAR 15.403-3(b)(3)(iii) — the RFO reuses the number 15.403-2 for a different section, Prohibitions)
Exercise of pre-priced option 
Certified cost or pricing data are not required for proposals used solely for overrun funding or interim billing price adjustments.

Cite: FAR 15.403-2(b); FAR 15.403-3(b)(3)(iii); FAR 15.403-4.

question: You are working on a competitive RFP and are nearing completion of Sections L containing information and instructions for offerors, and Section M containing evaluation factors for award. You have just completed a cross-check of Sections L and M to make sure that there is correlation between the contents of the two sections and you are satisfied that there is 100% correlation. Your project manager comes into your office very excited and tells you that he wants to include a request for additional information in Sec L. In talking to him you find that this new information request is not related to any other information requested from the offerors in Sec L. You also know from your work on the RFP that there is no corresponding evaluation criterion in Sec M for this information. You ask him why he wants to include the request in the RFP and he states that this is important information that he absolutely has to obtain for the success of the program. What do you tell the project manager?
answer: It is critical that the information requested in Sec L be held to an absolute minimum and then be requested only to the extent that the information will be relevant to the evaluation criteria in Sec M. A sure protest loser is where information is received in a proposal, is not relevant to an evaluation criterion, and is considered in the final source selection decision. This situation is called an "undisclosed evaluation criterion" by the GAO. If the information is so critical to the success of the program, then why isn't there a corresponding evaluation criterion in Sec M that will consider the information in making the final source selection decision?

question: Explain Tradeoff and Lowest Price Technically Acceptable (LPTA). When would each be beneficial to use.
answer:
The LPTA process is appropriate when best value is expected to result from selection of the technically acceptable proposal with the lowest evaluated price. LPTAs may be used in situations where the Government would not realize any value from a proposal exceeding the Government's minimum technical or performance requirements, often for acquisitions of commercial or non-complex services or supplies which are clearly defined and expected to be low risk. The LPTA process does not permit tradeoffs between price and non- price factors. See FAR 15.103-2.

• Tradeoff Source Selection Process (see FAR 15.103-1). This process allows for a tradeoff between non-cost factors and cost/price and allows the Government to accept other than the lowest priced proposal or other than the highest technically rated proposal to achieve a best-value contract award. Further, it describes various rating approaches to evaluating proposals when using a tradeoff process. The application of this process, as well as general source selection principles, is discussed in the body of this document.

Cite: FAR 15.103-1; FAR 15.103-2.

Both verified in the crosswalk against the Part 15 deviation guide. Flagged for a later content pass, not applied here: the RFO adds a third approach at 15.103-3, highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price, which this answer does not mention.

question: Define bundling and consolidation and explain their differences.
answer:
"Bundling," as defined in the FAR, is the term used to describe the act of combing two or more existing requirements into a single solicitation when one of the requirements was or could have been performed by a small business and the solicitation will be unsuitable for award to a small business and the work will be performed in the United States.
"Consolidation" is the term used in the contract arena to describe the act of combining two or more existing requirements into a single solicitation. As recently defined in statute, for a consolidation to exist, a proposed services acquisition must be combining two or more requirements that were previously provided or performed under separate contracts. For construction, consolidation exists if two or more discrete sites are involved.
Although small business participation is not a factor in determining whether a proposed strategy is a contract consolidation, small business participation is the primary factor in determining whether an acquisition is bundled. A bundled requirement is a consolidation that displaces one or more small businesses.
In the most general terms, for DoD, a consolidation is the combining of two or more previous contracts into a single solicitation, and a bundled contract is a consolidation that is unsuitable for award to a small business as a prime contractor even though one or more of the previous contracts was performed (or could have been performed) by a small business. To put it another way, a solicitation that consolidates requirements does not always bundle them, but a solicitation that bundles requirements always consolidates them.

rfo.notes: No regulatory cite in the answer text - 'as defined in the FAR' is not a named part or subpart. Skipped per task rule. Audit flag for a later content pass: the RFO consolidated old 7.107-2 (consolidation), 7.107-3 (bundling) and 7.107-4 (substantial bundling) into 7.107-2 'Policy'.

question: You are the Contracting Officer for a civil construction project in your area of responsibility. The proposals are double the IGE, but only 1% apart. The cost estimator stands by his IGE and refuses to revise it. The SSA decision document discounts the IGE and recommends award without further discussions. As the Contracting Officer, what would you do?
answer:
Delay award until the pricing and other pre-award issues were resolved. IAW UAI 36.205-100 Statutory Cost Limitations – Civil Works Contracts, IAW 33 U.S.C. 622 and 624, no civil works construction contract shall be awarded if the contract price exceeds the Government estimate by more than 25 percent.

question: It is the fourth quarter and fall out money becomes available, the design branch wants to use the money to buy a plotter. Do you have any concerns?
answer:
You have two major concerns. First, you have to ask appropriate office the color of money and year of the funds they want to send you. Do not assume that they are sending you FYXX O&M funds. If they are sending you FYXX O&M funds you can use the funds for "operations and maintenance' but you will have to obligate the money before the end of the fiscal year closes out.
Once you have determined the kind and year of money, you can address the Program Director's request. Since the Program Director is asking you to buy replenishment spares, you can use the money to buy these spares assuming the Program Director can show you a bona fide need for the spares. This means you can buy sufficient spares for a current need (which includes a reasonable inventory) but you cannot stockpile. Even if the contractor cannot deliver the spares in FYXX, you still have a bona fide need of FYXX if the contractor can deliver the spares in a "reasonable" time.
Here the Program Director appears to want you to buy spares sufficient to satisfy his needs for the entire war, a sure indication of his intent to stockpile. You will have to go back to the program director to find out the spares he can actually put on an aircraft right now plus find out what a reasonable inventory is for his program. You cannot use current O&M funds to satisfy a "future" need since that violates the bona fide needs rule.

rfo.notes: No regulatory cite in the answer text. Skipped per task rule.

question: You are the contracting officer on a contract with a sporadic funding stream. When can incremental funding be used and what is the rationale for allowing its use? What safeguards keep the contract from violating the Anti-Deficiency Act? What does the incremental funding amount have to cover?
answer:
Contracts using procurement appropriations must, under most circumstances, be fully funded to ensure stable production runs, lower costs, and the availability of sufficient funds to complete the product. Half an airplane or tank would not be very useful.
Contracts using R&D appropriations are normally incrementally funded, allowing more flexibility and control, to provide funding as needed and as progress in the research project is accomplished. The cost and progress in R&D projects are not as predictable as in more mature production programs. In R&D, even if a program is stopped before full funding is provided, some benefit is gained from the research accomplished to date.
For Fixed Price contracts, incremental funding can only be used if: (see DFARS 232.702 Policy.. Fixed-price contracts shall be fully funded except as permitted by 232.703-1 — old DFARS numbering kept; the RFO renumbering of these sections could not be verified) (1) A fixed-price contract may be incrementally funded only if—(i) The contract (excluding any options) or any exercised option— (A) Is for severable services; (B) Does not exceed one year in length; and (C) Is incrementally funded using funds available (unexpired) as of the date the funds are obligated; or (ii) The contract uses funds available from multiple (two or more) fiscal years and— (A) The contract is funded with research and development appropriations; or (B) Congress has otherwise authorized incremental funding. The Limitation of Funds Clause (FAR 52.232-22 - for Cost Reimbursement contracts) or the Limitation of Government Obligation clause (DFARS 252.232-7007 for Fixed Price contracts) caution the contractor that he is not obligated to incur costs, nor is the Government obligated to pay in excess of the amount allotted. Incremental funding is obligated to cover the amount allotted and any corresponding increment of fee.

Cite: FAR 52.232-22; DFARS 252.232-7007; DFARS 232.702; DFARS 232.703-1 (old numbering retained, unverified)

question: You are the Contracting Officer in Source Selection and dutifully following the FAR and DFARS, etc. on a particular issue. However, your higher leadership is now giving you "direction" which you believe is contrary to your legal guidance. What do you do? Do you comply with the legal guidance or the higher direction of leadership?
answer: Once you determine the legal parameters, if there is still a conflict, discuss it with your supervisor, and possibly others in the chain of command in resolving the issue with higher leadership. The point is you do not have to "go it alone". Worst case scenario, if all this fails, remember that it is your warrant on the line. It is your obligation to ensure the integrity of the procurement system, and if that means that you won't sign off on something, then that may be the answer.

question: On 3 Sep XX the PCO awarded a contract for computer purchases using FYXX O&M funds. The computers were to be delivered upon completion of a new building expected sometime early in CY 09, but the contractor could have delivered the computers almost immediately upon contract award. Are there any fiscal issues here?
answer:
Authority: 31 USC 1502(a) "Bona Fide Needs Rule"
Yes. O&M funds are for one year. You cannot cross FYs unless there is an exception. This could be considered a violation of the bona fide need rule. The lead-time exception does not apply since the delivery delay is based on the government's request and not the reality of when the contractor could actually deliver the computers.

Cite: 31 U.S.C. 1502(a)

question: A small business submitted a proposal for a requirement and is the apparent awardee, but you cannot determine them to be responsible, what do you do?
answer:
FAR 19.602-1 -- Referral (legacy subpart 19.6; under the RFO the Certificate of Competency referral is consolidated at RFO FAR 19.204)

(1) Withhold contract award (see 19.602-3); and

(2) Refer the matter to the cognizant SBA Government Contracting Area Office (Area Office) serving the area in which the headquarters of the offeror is located, in accordance with agency procedures, except that referral is not necessary if the small business concern --

(i) Is determined to be unqualified and ineligible because it does not meet the standard in 9.104-1(g); provided, that the determination is approved by the chief of the contracting office; or

(ii) Is suspended or debarred under Executive Order 11246 or Subpart 9.4.

question: What is a Contracting Officer? What is the authority given to a Contracting Officer? What are the responsibilities of a Contracting Officer?
answer:
A contracting officer is a person with the authority to enter into, administer, and/or terminate contracts and make related determinations and findings. That is the RFO FAR 2.101 definition. It includes authorized representatives acting within the limits the KO delegates to them. In the Army we appoint procuring, administrative, termination and contingency contracting officers, and the warrant policy uses KO for all of them.

Where the authority comes from: only contracting officers may sign, administer or terminate contracts on behalf of the Government, and a KO can bind the Government only within the authority actually delegated (RFO FAR 1.402-1). That authority is in writing on the SF 1402 Certificate of Appointment, with the limits stated on the certificate (RFO FAR 1.403-2). In the Army, ASA(ALT) designated procurement authority to DASA(P), who under RFO FAR 1.403-1(b) delegated warrant-granting to the HCA; the HCA may delegate it to SCOs but no lower than the Chief of the Contracting Office. The warrant is issued at a fixed threshold class, and the cumulative instrument value I sign, base plus options plus ceiling plus the absolute value of a modification, must be at or below my warrant. To hold a warrant above the SAT I must meet 10 U.S.C. 1724 as implemented at RFO DFARS 201.403-70: the required contracting courses for my grade, at least two years in a contracting position, and a baccalaureate degree. If I act outside that authority it is an unauthorized commitment and someone with authority has to ratify it under RFO FAR 1.405.

Responsibilities, from RFO FAR 1.402-2:
- Ensure all requirements of law, executive orders, regulations and other procedures, including clearances and approvals, are met before I sign, and that sufficient funds are available.
- Ensure the contractor complies with the terms of the contract and safeguard the interests of the United States in its contractual relationships.
- Treat offerors and contractors impartially, fairly and equitably.
- Request and consider the advice of specialists in audit, law, engineering, information security, transportation and other fields, as appropriate.

In practice that means I am the business advisor and the accountable official: I lead the acquisition team, I make sure the money is right under purpose, time and amount, I keep an ethical distance from industry, and I build a file that shows a complete history and clear support for every action (RFO FAR 4.101). The warrant is personal; the KO owns the decision and its consequences.

Cite: RFO FAR 2.101; RFO FAR 1.402-1, 1.402-2, 1.403-1(b), 1.403-2, 1.405, 4.101; RFO DFARS 201.403-70 (Class Deviation 2026-O0002 Rev 1; was 201.603-2); 10 U.S.C. 1724; Army Warranting Program Policy v12 (Mar 2026), Authority and Standard Warrant Thresholds.

question: Please explain the contracting process in detail, from cradle to grave.
answer:
I think of it in four phases: planning, solicitation and award, administration, and closeout.

Planning. It starts with a validated requirement and funding. I work with the requiring activity on the requirements document - a performance work statement, statement of work, or specification - the independent government estimate, the acquisition-ready package, and the funding document. I confirm the money is the right color and the right year for the need. I do market research to learn what the commercial market does, who the sources are, and whether small business set-aside is appropriate. Out of that I build the acquisition strategy or acquisition plan: commercial or not, competition approach, contract type and how risk is allocated, evaluation approach, milestone schedule, and the small business and legal coordination. Required approvals, including any justification for limiting competition, get done here, not later.

Solicitation and award. I publicize the requirement, issue the solicitation with the correct provisions and clauses, manage exchanges with industry and answer questions to all offerors at once, and receive offers. Then evaluation strictly against the stated factors, price or cost analysis to establish a fair and reasonable price, discussions and final proposal revisions if I am in negotiations, a responsibility determination including the SAM exclusions check, a documented source selection decision, award, the contract action report in SAM.gov, and notices and debriefings. I stay alert to the protest window before I let performance start.

Administration. This is where most of the money is actually spent and most of the risk actually lives. I appoint the COR in writing with a defined scope - RFO FAR 1.404 and DFARS 201.404-70 - hold the post-award conference, monitor performance and surveillance, administer modifications within scope and issue changes under the Changes clause, handle funding actions and options, do inspection and acceptance, certify and pass invoices for payment, manage government property and any GFP, deal with delays and cure or show-cause notices, and handle claims and disputes. If performance fails, I have the full range of remedies up to termination for cause or default, and I always have termination for convenience.

Closeout. Final delivery and acceptance, final invoice and final payment, settlement of any indirect rates or subcontracts, property disposition, releases, a past performance evaluation that is honest, then de-obligation of residual funds and the completion statement.

Two threads run through all four phases: documentation, because the file is the decision, and integrity, because I am the only person who can obligate the Government and I answer for it.

Cite: RFO FAR Part 7 (acquisition planning), RFO FAR 10.001 (market research), Part 5 (publicizing), Part 6 (competition), Parts 12, 13 and 15 (commercial, simplified, and negotiated procedures), Part 19 (small business), RFO FAR 15.404 (price and cost analysis), RFO FAR 9.104-1 (responsibility), Part 42 (administration), Part 43 (modifications), Part 49 (terminations), RFO FAR 4.308 (closeout), RFO FAR 1.402-1 and 1.402-2 (KO authority and responsibilities), RFO FAR 1.404 and DFARS 201.404-70 (COR designation).

rfo.notes: Reviewed 14 Sep 2026. Part-level cites plus section cites that are verified project crosswalk entries (1.402-1, 1.402-2, 1.404, DFARS 201.404-70, 15.404, 9.104-1); 4.308 closeout and 10.001 read on the RFO Part 4 and Part 10 pages. The substance is process narrative rather than a single regulatory rule.

key_points: Four phases: planning; solicitation and award; administration; closeout.
Planning: validated requirement and correct-color funding, IGE, market research, strategy or acquisition plan, competition approach and required approvals up front.
Award: publicize, solicit, evaluate only against stated factors, establish a fair and reasonable price, responsibility and exclusions check, documented decision, notices and debriefings.

Administration carries most of the risk: written COR appointment (RFO FAR 1.404, DFARS 201.404-70), surveillance, in-scope mods and changes, options, inspection and acceptance, payment, property, delays and remedies.
Closeout: final acceptance and payment, rate and subcontract settlement, property disposition, past performance evaluation, de-obligation, completion statement.
Two constants: the file documents the decision, and the KO is the only one who can obligate the Government.

question: As a contracting officer, your customer comes to you with an urgent change to the current contract that you are working. He comes to you by email and states he needs to include a change to the current scope of work and wants to know what steps need to take place to get the change incorporated into the contract. What is your authority in the contract to issue a change to the scope of work? What are the documents needed from the COR to initiate the change along with the steps to incorporate the change into the contract?
answer:
My authority to change the scope comes from the Changes clause and from my warrant. RFO FAR 43.202 says only a contracting officer acting within the scope of their authority can execute a modification, so the customer's email is a request, not a change - nobody but me directs the contractor. Under RFO FAR 43.301 the Changes clause - 52.243-1 for fixed-price, 52.243-4 for construction above the SAT and 52.243-5 below it, prescribed at 43.305 - lets me issue a unilateral change order within the general scope of the contract; a commercial contract under 52.212-4(d) can only be changed bilaterally. And the change must be in scope: the same general nature of work the offerors competed for. If it is out of scope, it is a new procurement that needs competition or a justification under RFO FAR 6.103-1 approved under 6.104-2, and I tell the customer that up front.

What I need from the COR and requiring activity:
- A written description of the change and why it is needed now, with the revised PWS marked up.
- An in-scope statement, which I confirm with legal if it is close.
- A revised IGE for the changed work, per AFARS 5107.90 above the SAT.
- Certified funding - a PR or MIPR with the right appropriation and fiscal year, because RFO FAR 43.205 requires funds to be available before I execute a modification that adds money.
- The COR's technical evaluation of the contractor's proposal, including schedule impact.

Steps: acknowledge the email and set expectations in writing; confirm scope and funds; request a proposal with a due date; negotiate the equitable adjustment and issue a bilateral supplemental agreement under 43.203 - or, if the mission truly cannot wait, a unilateral change order on SF 30 not-to-exceed available funds, then the equitable adjustment negotiated in the shortest practicable time as 43.304 requires and definitized on a second SF 30; document price reasonableness; update the QASP and COR letter if surveillance changes; distribute the mod. And I remind the COR that under 43.204 the contractor must tell us in writing if it thinks we changed the work without a signed mod - so nobody on our side gives direction by email.

Cite: RFO FAR 43.202, 43.203, 43.204, 43.205, 43.301, 43.302, 43.304, 43.305; FAR 52.243-1, 52.243-4, 52.243-5, 52.212-4(d); RFO FAR 6.103-1, 6.104-2; RFO FAR 1.402-1; AFARS 5107.90.

rfo.notes: Reviewer 14 Sep 2026: RFO Part 43 TOC and text re-read on https://www.acquisition.gov/far-overhaul/far-part-deviation-guide/far-overhaul-part-43 - 43.201 definitions, 43.202 policy (only KOs within their authority execute modifications; price before execution where possible), 43.203 types, 43.204 notification (contractor notifies in writing as soon as possible), 43.205 availability of funds, 43.301 general (SF 30; continue performance), 43.302 authority, 43.304 administration (negotiate equitable adjustments in the shortest practicable time; two SF 30s when a unilateral order is definitized), 43.305 clauses (52.243-1 supplies/services, 52.243-4 construction above the SAT, 52.243-5 below). Part 6 (6.103-1, 6.104-2) and Part 1 (1.402-1) confirmed against the verified crosswalk. Local ACC/411th mod routing and review thresholds are not stated and should be confirmed with the local office.

The change must be within the general scope; out of scope = new procurement (RFO FAR 6.103-1, 6.104-2).
From the COR/requiring activity: written change description with revised PWS, in-scope statement, revised IGE (AFARS 5107.90), certified funds, technical evaluation.

Commercial contracts (52.212-4(d)): bilateral only.
Guard against constructive changes - CORs cannot direct the contractor (43.204).

question: You receive a requirements package for a Polaris 4-wheeler. The customer insists it has to be Polaris. As the KO, how would you advise the customer?
answer:
The first thing I tell the customer is that a brand name is not a requirement, it is one possible solution. My job is to turn what they need into a performance or functional description. So I ask: what does the vehicle have to do? Payload, towing, terrain, range, transportability, host-nation registration and licensing, maintenance and parts support where we are, and compatibility with an existing fleet.

Then market research under RFO FAR 10.001: are there other manufacturers whose machines meet those characteristics? If yes, we compete it as brand name or equal, with the salient characteristics stated in the solicitation. Brand name or equal is still full and open competition, so no limited-competition justification is needed for it; the justification requirement at RFO FAR 6.103-1(d) is for a brand-name-only description that shuts other manufacturers out.

If the customer can genuinely show that only Polaris will satisfy the need, for example standardization with an existing fleet where mixed parts, tooling and training would be unreasonably costly, or a documented interoperability requirement, then a brand-name restriction is possible, but it must be justified and approved. Requirements are not to be written around a brand or a feature of one product unless it is essential and market research confirms nothing else meets the minimum need (RFO FAR 11.204). This is a commercial product, so RFO FAR 12.102 requires me to document the decision to restrict competition; above the SAT that is a written justification approved under 6.104-2, and under the SAT I still document the brand-name or limited-source decision in the file and follow the commercial simplified procedures at 12.201-1. The justification content in 6.104-1 is what the customer has to give me: the need, the authority, the market research, why no other product will satisfy, how the price will be found fair and reasonable, and what we will do to open future buys to competition. The redacted justification is posted with the solicitation notice (RFO FAR 5.201(c)(3)).

What is not a justification: we like Polaris, we always buy Polaris, or the vendor told us so. I say that plainly but as a partner, and I help them write salient characteristics so the equal competition still gets them a machine that works. Ethics note: if the requirement turns out to be written around a vendor relationship, that is an integrity issue I raise, not one I process.

Cite: RFO FAR 6.103-1(d), 6.104-1, 6.104-2; 12.102; 12.201-1; 11.204; 10.001; 5.201(c)(3); 10 U.S.C. 3201 and 3204.

Preference, habit or vendor pressure are not justifications; coach the customer rather than refuse them

question: What do you do if you receive only one offer?
answer:
One offer is not a failure, but it is a trigger. The DoD rule is RFO DFARS 215.202-71, which used to be 215.371, and it has two parts: promote competition, and make sure the price is fair and reasonable.

First question I ask: how long was the solicitation open? If I used competitive procedures and allowed fewer than 30 days for proposals, I must go back to the requiring activity and ask whether the requirement should be revised to open up competition, and then resolicit for at least 30 more days. I would have put the provision at 252.215-7007, Notice of Intent to Resolicit, in the solicitation so offerors expected that. The HCA can waive the resolicitation, and that waiver cannot go below one level above me. The resolicitation rule does not apply at or below the SAT, to contingency or humanitarian support, to small business set-asides including 8(a), HUBZone, SDVOSB and WOSB, to science and technology, A-E services, commercial solutions openings, or commercial products and services bought under Part 12. But an exception never relieves me of seeking maximum practicable competition and getting a fair and reasonable price.

If the solicitation was open 30 days or more, or I have already resolicited, and the action is over the SAT, I cannot treat one offer as adequate price competition. I have to prove the price. I do price analysis first, using the IGE, historical prices, market research and catalog or published prices under RFO FAR 15.404-1. If that is not enough I obtain data other than certified cost or pricing data, and if the action exceeds the certified cost or pricing data threshold and no exception at RFO FAR 15.403-2(b) applies, the data must be certified. For DoD that threshold is 10 million dollars for a prime contract awarded after 30 June 2026, under RFO DFARS 215.403-3(a); it was 2.5 million for earlier awards. If I still cannot determine the price fair and reasonable I enter negotiations, and the negotiated price should not exceed the offered price. If I cannot negotiate a fair and reasonable price, 215.202-71(c)(4) sends me to RFO FAR 15.407(d): I refer the action to a level above me rather than award at a price I cannot support.

Along the way I find out why the others did not bid, especially where more than one company expressed interest, per PGI 215.202-71(b)(2), so the next buy is better. I confirm responsibility, and I document all of it in the price negotiation memorandum.

Cite: RFO DFARS 215.202-71 and PGI 215.202-71(b)(2) (Class Deviation 2026-O0048 Rev 1; was 215.371); DFARS 252.215-7007; RFO DFARS 215.403-3(a); RFO FAR 15.403-2(b), 15.403-3, 15.404-1, 15.404-2, 15.407(d).

question: Name 5 market research techniques utilized in contracting?
answer:
Five I use regularly:

- Contacting knowledgeable people in Government and industry about what the market can actually deliver - program engineers, other KOs who bought something similar, and industry technical representatives.
- Publishing a sources sought notice or request for information, and holding an industry day or one-on-one presolicitation exchanges. That is the technique that most often changes my strategy, because it tells me whether the rule of two is met.
- Querying Government data: the contract award data in SAM.gov - which absorbed FPDS in February 2026 - and our own contract writing data for what was paid before and who won, SAM entity records and the SBA Dynamic Small Business Search for capability and socioeconomic status, and the GSA Multiple Award Schedule and other existing vehicles for available sources and pricing.
- Reviewing published commercial information - catalogs, price lists, product literature, and published market and pricing indices - and reviewing recent market research done for an identical or similar requirement.
- Obtaining source lists and lessons learned from other contracting activities, agencies, or trade associations, including site visits and demonstrations when the item is complex.

The point of any of these is not the technique, it is the three answers I need: is there a commercial solution, is there an existing vehicle, and are there two or more capable small businesses at a fair market price. I document what I did, who I talked to, what I found, and what it means for the strategy, and I do it early enough that the results can still change the strategy.

One RFO note: the overhaul condensed Part 10 and no longer prints the enumerated list of techniques that used to sit at FAR 10.002(b)(2). What 10.001 now requires is market research before I develop new requirements documents and before I solicit or place an order above the SAT, responsible and constructive exchanges with industry inside the procurement integrity rules, no more information from sources than I need, and documentation that fits the size and complexity of the buy. The techniques are now the KO's judgment.

Cite: RFO FAR 10.001(b), (c) and (e) (market research requirements, industry exchanges, documentation); the technique list formerly at FAR 10.002(b)(2) is no longer regulatory.

rfo.notes: Reviewed 14 Sep 2026. 10.001 read in full on the RFO Part 10 page (10.000 / 10.001 / 10.002; no enumerated technique list); the five techniques are carried from legacy 10.002(b)(2) as practice. FPDS.gov decommissioning on 24 Feb 2026 and the move of FPDS access into SAM.gov confirmed on sam.gov announcements.

key_points: Talk to knowledgeable Government and industry people about real market capability.
Publish a sources sought or RFI and hold an industry day or presolicitation exchanges - this is what tests the rule of two.
Query SAM.gov contract award data (FPDS moved into SAM.gov in February 2026), SAM entity records, the SBA Dynamic Small Business Search, and existing vehicles such as the GSA Multiple Award Schedule.
Review catalogs, price lists, published literature and indices, plus recent market research for similar requirements.
Get source lists and lessons learned from other activities, agencies, or trade associations; use site visits and demos for complex items.

The RFO condensed Part 10 - the technique list at old 10.002(b)(2) is gone; 10.001 still requires research before new requirements documents and before any solicitation or order above the SAT, documented to fit the acquisition.

question: What shall a KO do prior to exercising an option?
answer:
RFO FAR 17.204-1 Exercise of options.
(a) If the contract includes an economic price adjustment clause and the contractor requests a price revision, the contracting officer must determine how the adjustment affects option prices before exercising the option.
(b) The contracting officer may exercise options only after—
(1) Providing written notice to the contractor of the Government’s intention to exercise the option, within the time specified in the contract;
(2) Confirming that funds are available; and
(3) Determining that–
(i) The option fulfills an existing Government requirement;
(ii) The option was synopsized as required, unless exempt (see part 5);
(iii) The Contractor does not have an active exclusion record in the System for Award Management (see part 9);
(iv) The contractor’s performance on the current contract has been acceptable (for example, satisfactory or better performance ratings);
(v) After reviewing price and other factors, the option price is fair and reasonable based on current market conditions and exercise of the option is in the Government's best interest; and
(vi) The option exercise complies with the requirements of part 6 for full and open competition, i.e., the option was evaluated as part of the initial competition and is exercisable at an amount specified in or reasonably determinable from the terms of the contract.
RFO DFARS 217.204-170 Exercise of options.
In addition to the requirements at FAR 17.204-1(b), exercise an option only after:
Determining that the contractor’s record in the System for Award Management database is active and the contractor’s unique entity identifier, Commercial and Government Entity (CAGE) code, name, and physical address are accurately reflected in the contract document. See PGI 217.204-170 for the requirement to perform cost or price analysis of spare parts prior to exercising any option for firmfixed-price contracts containing spare parts.
Verifying in the Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS) (https://www.sprs.csd.disa.mil/) that—
The summary level score of a current NIST SP 800-171 DoD Assessment (i.e., not more than 3 years old, unless a lesser time is specified in the solicitation) for each covered contractor information system that is relevant to an offer, contract, task order, or delivery order are posted.
The contractor has a CMMC certificate at the level required by the contract, and that it is current (i.e., not more than 3 years old).
Cite: RFO FAR 17.204-1; RFO DFARS 217.204-170; RFO PGI 217.204-170.

question: Who prepares, reviews, and approves the IGE?
answer:
The requiring activity prepares it, the preparer's supervisor approves it, and I review it and accept it into the file.

The IGE is the Government's own estimate of the price or cost a contractor would incur in successful performance. AFARS 5107.90 requires one for every procurement action over the SAT, and I may require one below the SAT. It is prepared by the requiring activity - the technical people who wrote the PWS, or the cost engineer for construction - independently, before we seek proposals, never by a contractor or from a contractor's quote. The preparer signs and dates it with organization, position, title and telephone number, and the preparer's immediate supervisor signs and dates it as the reviewer. That supervisor signature is the approval.

My review before I accept it, under AFARS 5107.9002:
- Enough detail to test the offerors' proposals - labor categories, hours, rates, materials, ODCs - not just a bottom line.
- Sufficient narrative and analytical detail, with the reference material behind it.
- The certification that the Government developed it independently before seeking proposals.
A bottom-line number with no basis goes back.

For construction, RFO FAR 36.101-6 requires an independent Government estimate for any action expected to exceed the SAT, based on a detailed analysis of the requirement, in my hands before receipt of proposals. I protect it as source selection information.

Then I use it as a price analysis comparison under RFO FAR 15.404-1, as a check on unbalanced pricing, and as an input to my negotiation objective - never as the sole basis for a fair and reasonable determination.

Cite: AFARS 5107.9001, 5107.9002; RFO FAR 36.101-6; RFO FAR 15.404-1.

AFARS does not name the preparing organization; 'requiring activity' is standard Army practice. RFO 36.101-6 (IGE for construction above the SAT, furnished to the KO before receipt of proposals) re-read on the far-overhaul Part 36 page; 15.404-1(b) technique list confirmed in the verified crosswalk. No corrections needed.

Reviewed and approved by the preparer's immediate supervisor, who signs and dates it (AFARS 5107.9002).
KO reviews for detail, supporting narrative and the independence certification before accepting it.
Required above the SAT; KO may require it below (AFARS 5107.9002).

question: What are the elements to the IGE?
answer:
The IGE is the Government's own estimate of the price or cost a contractor would incur to perform successfully, prepared independently by the requiring activity before we see proposals. In the Army, AFARS subpart 5107.90 requires one for every procurement action over the SAT, and I can require one below the SAT. Before I accept it, I check for these elements:
- Detail sufficient to test the offerors' proposals: a breakout by CLIN or task; for services, labor categories, hours, rates, burdens such as fringe, overhead and G&A, profit or fee, materials, ODCs and travel; for construction, quantities, unit costs, labor, material, equipment and contingencies; each period and option priced separately.
- A narrative and analytical basis: the estimating method (historical prices, catalog or market prices, engineering build-up, parametric), the assumptions, and the reference material used.
- A certification that the Government developed it independently before seeking formal proposals (for construction and A-E, within the timeframes AFARS still cites as FAR 36.203 and 36.605, now RFO FAR 36.101-6 for construction).
- Signature and date, by hand or CAC, by the preparer with organization, position, title and telephone number, and by the preparer's immediate supervisor with the same information plus rank or grade.

How I use it: it is one of the price analysis comparison techniques under RFO FAR 15.404-1, it is the funding check against the purchase request, it helps me spot unbalanced or unrealistic pricing and pick the source selection approach, and it drives the thresholds for competition, synopsis and my warrant calculation. For construction, RFO FAR 36.101-6 requires an IGE for any action expected to exceed the SAT, based on a detailed analysis of the requirement, and it must be in my hands before receipt of proposals. The IGE is source selection information: it is protected under RFO FAR 3.104 and never shared with offerors.

Cite: AFARS 5107.9002; RFO FAR 15.404-1; RFO FAR 36.101-6; RFO FAR 3.104.

The itemized cost elements are practice guidance, not a regulatory list. AFARS itself still cross-references legacy FAR 36.203/36.605.

question: What three agencies are protest filed with?
answer:
A bid protest can be filed in three forums: with the agency, with the Government Accountability Office, or with the U.S. Court of Federal Claims. All three are covered in RFO FAR Subpart 33.1.

- Agency protest, RFO FAR 33.104. Filed with me as the contracting officer, or the protester can ask for an independent review at a level above me. It is the fastest and cheapest route; the agency must use best efforts to resolve it within 35 days (RFO FAR 33.104-4(c)(1)). A timely post-award agency protest, within 10 days of award or 5 days after an offered debriefing, requires me to suspend performance unless continued performance is justified in writing.
- GAO protest, RFO FAR 33.105, under the Competition in Contracting Act, 31 U.S.C. 3551 to 3557, and GAO's regulations at 4 CFR Part 21. GAO decides within 100 days (4 CFR 21.9). A timely GAO protest triggers the automatic CICA stay; the agency report is due 30 days after GAO's notice (4 CFR 21.3(c)); and only the HCA, on a nondelegable basis, can override the stay (RFO FAR 33.105-3(b)).
- Court of Federal Claims, RFO FAR 33.106, under the Tucker Act, 28 U.S.C. 1491(b). It is judicial review, there is no automatic stay, the protester has to ask for an injunction, and the court is not bound by the 100-day clock.

A protester can start at the agency and then go to GAO within 10 days of learning of the initial adverse agency action, and can go to the court after GAO. The moment I get anything that looks like a protest in any forum, I notify legal counsel. And for the board's companion question, claims and disputes are Subpart 33.2, the Contract Disputes Act.

Cite: RFO FAR 33.104 and 33.104-4(c)(1), 33.105 and 33.105-3, 33.106; 4 CFR 21.2, 21.3, 21.9; 31 U.S.C. 3551-3557; 28 U.S.C. 1491(b).

Agency: best efforts to resolve within 35 days; independent review above the KO available
GAO: CICA, 4 CFR 21; 100-day decision; automatic stay if timely; agency report due in 30 days; HCA-only override
COFC: Tucker Act 28 U.S.C. 1491(b); judicial; no automatic stay, injunction required

Claims and disputes are Subpart 33.2 (Contract Disputes Act)

question: After the accrual of a claim, how long does a contractor have to file their claim?
answer:
Six years after accrual of the claim. A contractor claim has to be submitted in writing to the contracting officer for a decision within six years after the claim accrues, unless the parties agreed in the contract to a shorter period. The same six-year limit runs against the Government on a Government claim against the contractor.

Two qualifiers a board will want to hear. First, the six-year rule comes from the Contract Disputes Act and applies to contracts awarded on or after 1 October 1995; older contracts do not carry it. Second, accrual is not the same as the event - a claim accrues when all events fixing liability have occurred and the injury or damages are known or should reasonably have been known, even if the exact amount is not yet fixed. That is a fact question, and if the timeliness of a claim is contested I get counsel involved rather than deciding it myself.

What I do when a claim comes in: confirm it is a claim and not a routine request for payment - a written demand seeking a sum certain or other relief as a matter of right; check the certification, which is required when the claim exceeds $100,000; date-stamp receipt, because my clock starts there. For a claim of $100,000 or less I issue a written decision within 60 days if the contractor asked for a decision in that period, otherwise within a reasonable time. For a certified claim over $100,000 I issue the decision within 60 days of receipt or, within that 60 days, tell the contractor the firm date by which I will decide. Interest runs from the date I receive the proper claim. The contractor continues performance, and my decision carries the required appeal-rights language: 90 days to the agency board of contract appeals, or 12 months to the Court of Federal Claims.

Cite: RFO FAR 33.205-1 (contractor claim), 33.205-2 (certification), 33.205-3 (interest), 33.205-6 (contracting officer's decision), 33.205-7 (obligation to continue performance); 41 U.S.C. 7103.

question: You have a contract for cleaning services with a basic period of performance and several one year options for continued performance. The contract states that all options must be exercised by 1 October of each year. The basic period of performance has just expired and on 5 October you realize that you never exercised the option for continued performance. There is still an immediate need for the services. How would you try to rectify this situation?
answer:
First, I own it. An option not exercised in strict accordance with its terms cannot be exercised late - RFO FAR 17.204-1 lets me exercise only within the time specified in the contract, and after 1 October there is no contract to extend. So I do not backdate a modification, and I do not let the contractor keep cleaning on a handshake. 52.217-8 does not rescue me either; it also had to be exercised while the contract was alive. If the COR already has them working, that is an unauthorized commitment and it goes into ratification under RFO FAR 1.405 - the HCA ratifies, and that authority is not delegable below the chief of the contracting office.

Then three tracks at once:
- I notify my chief and legal the same day, in writing, with the facts and my plan.
- I confirm with the customer that the need still exists and that current-year funds are certified.
- I cover the gap.

The cleanest cover is a short sole-source bridge with the incumbent, awarded as a new contract action, not an option. That takes a justification under RFO FAR 6.103-2, unusual and compelling urgency, or 6.103-1 if they are truly the only source, with the content at 6.104-1; for DoD the approval level comes from DFARS 206.104-71 Table 206-1, not FAR Table 6-1 - a bridge at ten million or below is approved by my own certification as contracting officer, above that by the competition advocate. The justification is honest: our lapse created the urgency, but the sanitation need is real, and I limit the bridge to the minimum period needed to compete a replacement. If the services are commercial and under the RFO FAR 12.201-1 ceiling, I use an RFQ and purchase order, and 12.102 governs the competition paperwork: at or below the SAT I record that only one source is available, 12.102(a); above the SAT I still need the written justification approved under 6.104, 12.102(b). I run the SAM and responsibility checks, price the bridge against the lapsed option price and current market, and award.

In parallel I start the competitive replacement immediately so the bridge is defensible, and I tell the incumbent the bridge is not a promise of the follow-on.

Last, I fix the cause: an option suspense tracker keyed to the 52.217-9 notice and exercise dates for every contract, reviewed monthly, and a lessons-learned memo in the file.

Cite: RFO FAR 17.204-1; RFO FAR 1.405; RFO FAR 6.103-1, 6.103-2, 6.104-1, 6.104-2; RFO FAR 12.102, 12.201-1; FAR 52.217-8, 52.217-9; DFARS 217.204-170; DFARS 206.104-71 Table 206-1.

question: When is AT/OPSEC required?
answer:
Antiterrorism and OPSEC review is a requirements-package requirement in the Army, not something I bolt on at award. Under AFARS subpart 5107.91 the requiring activity must include a signed AT/OPSEC cover sheet in every requirements package, with three exceptions: supply contracts below the SAT, field ordering officer actions, and Government purchase card purchases. It also applies to orders under indefinite-delivery contracts unless the orders are for substantially the same products or services already reviewed under the base contract. So for services, construction, and supplies over the SAT, it is required every time.

What the cover sheet documents: that the requiring activity's antiterrorism officer, its OPSEC officer and, as applicable, the information security or cybersecurity, physical security, law enforcement, intelligence and foreign disclosure staff reviewed the SOW or PWS, the QASP and any evaluation criteria for protection matters, and it identifies which standard AT/OPSEC language goes into the contract. Typical items are AT Level I awareness training and iWATCH for contractor employees, installation access and badging, OPSEC training when the contractor will handle sensitive information, cybersecurity or IA training for system access, and for OCONUS the theater-specific requirements.

As the KO: I confirm the cover sheet is complete and signed before I accept the package, I put the required language in the PWS or contract, and if a package arrives without it and no exception applies, it goes back to the requiring activity. In Korea this matters more, not less: contractor and Korean national employee access to installations and the host-nation environment mean the ATO and OPSEC reviews drive the access and training terms we put in the contract. The underlying regulations are AR 525-13 for antiterrorism and AR 530-1 for OPSEC.

Cite: AFARS 5107.9101; AT/OPSEC Desk Reference, Appendix A (Army standard cover sheet); AR 525-13; AR 530-1.

AFARS requires the reviews listed in Appendix A of the AT/OPSEC Desk Reference; the list of standard contract-language items is as commonly implemented and was not re-fetched (SharePoint access required). The Korea paragraph is general practice, not sourced - confirm with C&P. Army supplement; not affected by RFO renumbering.

Drives the standard AT/OPSEC contract language (AT Level I, iWATCH, installation access, OPSEC and IA training)

question: What are factors to consider before terminating for default (T4D)?
answer:
Termination for default is the Government's most severe remedy, so before I use it I confirm the facts, I give the contractor its notice, I weigh the factors the FAR requires, and I get legal review. The factors are listed at RFO FAR 49.402-3(i):

- The terms of the contract and applicable laws and regulations. Do I actually have a failure to deliver, a failure to perform a provision, or a failure to make progress that endangers performance, under the Default clause at 52.249-8?
- The specific failure and the contractor's excuses or explanations. Is any of it excusable delay, beyond the contractor's control and without its fault or negligence, like acts of God, acts of the Government in its sovereign or contractual capacity, fires, floods, epidemics, strikes, or unusually severe weather? Did the Government contribute by late GFP, a constructive change, or a COR giving direction?
- Whether the supplies or services are available from other sources, and how urgently I need them: how long would it take to get them from someone else versus from this contractor if I let it continue?
- The degree of essentiality of the contractor in Government acquisition programs and the effect of a default on other contracts.
- The effect on the contractor's ability to liquidate guaranteed loans, progress payments or advance payments.
- Any other pertinent facts and circumstances.

Process-wise: if the delivery date has not passed I must issue a cure notice with at least 10 days to cure (RFO FAR 49.402-3(d)); after the date I use a show cause notice (formats at RFO FAR 49.607). Before any of it, 49.402-3(a) has me review the case with technical personnel and legal counsel. I check that I have not waived the delivery schedule by accepting late performance without reserving my rights. I consider the alternatives, a no-cost extension with consideration, or a termination for convenience, because if the default is later found wrongful it converts to a T4C and the Government pays convenience costs. For commercial items I use the Part 12 termination for cause under 12.304 and 52.212-4(m), not Part 49. The notice must say the contract is terminated, state the reasons, address reprocurement liability, and note it is a final decision appealable under Disputes. And I report it in CPARS and FAPIIS.

Cite: RFO FAR 49.402-3(i) (factors; was 49.402-3(f)), 49.402-3(a) and (d); RFO FAR 49.401(b), 49.607; FAR 52.249-8; RFO FAR 12.304 and 52.212-4(m) for commercial.

question: We often hear that it is the Contracting Officer's responsibility to determine that a contractor is "Responsible ". In your own words please define what it means for a contractor to be Responsible.
answer:
Responsibility is my forward-looking judgment that this offeror can and will perform this contract. It is about capability and business integrity, not about price and not about whether the proposal scored well. Award can only go to a responsible contractor, and I have to make an affirmative determination - without a clear indication of responsibility, the rule at 9.103 is that I find the offeror nonresponsible.

In plain terms I am asking: do they have or can they obtain the money, the people, the facilities, the equipment and the production or delivery capacity to do this work on this schedule; do they have a satisfactory performance record; do they have a satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics; are they otherwise qualified and eligible - meaning registered in SAM, not excluded, and holding any required license or certification; and do they have the necessary organization, experience, accounting and operational controls, including an adequate accounting system if I am using a cost-reimbursement type.

Three distinctions I keep straight. Responsibility is about the offeror; responsiveness is about whether a sealed bid conforms to the invitation. Responsibility is determined at award, and I can and should consider information that arrives right up to award - it is not frozen at proposal receipt. And I can rely on a prospective contractor's ability to get resources it does not yet own, if it has acceptable evidence of commitment.

Sources I use: past performance records, financial statements and credit information, the SAM exclusions record, the responsibility and qualification record in SAM - which I must check above the SAT under 9.104-6 - information from the cognizant contract administration office, DCAA on accounting system adequacy, and reference checks. The overhaul dropped the formal preaward survey section, so I ask the administration office for the specific information I need under 9.105-1 rather than a form. I document the determination and the basis in the file before I sign, per 9.105-2.

The small business rule is the one candidates miss. If I intend to find a small business nonresponsible, I must refer the matter to SBA, which decides whether to issue a Certificate of Competency under 19.204. If SBA issues a COC, it is conclusive on responsibility and I award.

Cite: RFO FAR 9.103 (policy - nonresponsibility absent a clear indication), 9.104-1 (general standards), 9.104-3 and 9.104-3(d)(1) (application; SBA referral), 9.104-6 (responsibility record above the SAT), 9.105-1 and 9.105-2 (obtaining information; determinations and documentation), RFO FAR 9.404 and 9.405 (exclusions and effect of listing), RFO FAR 19.204 (Certificate of Competency).

rfo.notes: Reviewed 14 Sep 2026. 9.103 ('Without a clear indication of responsibility, make a determination of nonresponsibility'), 9.104-3(d)(1), the 9.105-1 to 9.105-3 structure, 9.104-6 and the reserved 9.106/9.107 read on the RFO Part 9 page; 19.204 Certificate of Competency read on the RFO Part 19 page. The draft's reference to formal preaward surveys was softened because 9.106 is now reserved.

key_points: Responsibility is a forward-looking KO judgment about capability and business integrity; award may only go to a responsible contractor.
It must be an affirmative determination - without a clear indication of responsibility, find the offeror nonresponsible (RFO FAR 9.103).

Standards: financial resources, ability to meet schedule, satisfactory performance record, satisfactory integrity and business ethics, necessary organization/experience/controls, necessary facilities, and otherwise eligible.
Responsibility (the offeror) is different from responsiveness (the bid); it is determined at award using the latest information.
The offeror may rely on resources it does not yet own if it shows acceptable evidence of commitment.
Nonresponsibility for a small business requires referral to SBA (9.104-3(d)(1)); a Certificate of Competency under 19.204 is conclusive and must be accepted.

question: What is your experience in awarding and administering contingency contracts as a Contracting Officer or Contract Specialist? What were your 2 to 4 biggest challenges experienced and how did you resolve or mitigate the challenges?
answer:
Answer from your own record. If you have not deployed, say so in the first sentence and bridge to the closest analog - OCONUS exercise support, disaster or pandemic response, urgent Korea or Germany buys - because the board is testing judgment under pressure, not the stamp in your passport. The shape of a strong answer:

I supported contingency contracting as a contract specialist and later as a CCO, awarding and administering life support, base operations, construction and transportation contracts under the RFO FAR 18.001 and DFARS 218.7001-2 flexibilities. Four challenges stand out.
- Vendor base and responsibility. Local vendors had no past performance, no registration, sometimes ties we could not see. I worked with the theater vendor vetting cell and CID, kept a vetted vendor list, used firm-fixed-price and short periods to limit exposure, and documented responsibility under RFO FAR 9.104-1 even when the file was a folder in a container.
- Speed against discipline. Commanders needed it yesterday, and verbal direction from units created unauthorized commitments. I used the raised contingency thresholds, SF 44s and oral solicitations where allowed, but every action still got a written determination and a fair and reasonable price memo. I ran a weekly requirements meeting with the J4 and unit S4s so requirements reached me before the vendor did, and I processed the ratifications we still had under RFO FAR 1.405 as teaching moments.
- Fiscal and payment friction. Wrong appropriations, currency swings, cash versus EFT, MIPRs that arrived after the need. I paired with the finance office and paying agent, built a funds-certification checklist, and wrote currency and payment terms into the contract so the invoice matched the money.
- Theater rules and continuity. Theater business clearance under DFARS 225.770, contractor accountability under 252.225-7040 and DFARS 225.771, host nation law, and 90-day rotations that took the memory home. I built a handover binder per contract - QASP, COR letters, open issues - and closed out as I went.

What carried across all four: get legal on the phone early, write it down the same day, and remember that an urgency justification under RFO FAR 6.103-2 still has to be true - the protests and claims that follow a contingency come from the files we did not build.

Cite: RFO FAR 18.001; DFARS 218.7001-2 and PGI 218.7001-2; RFO FAR 1.405, 6.103-2, 9.104-1; DFARS 225.770, 225.771, 225.773, 252.225-7040; 10 U.S.C. 101(a)(13); JP 4-10; AR 715-9; Defense Contingency Contracting Handbook.

question: Under a current contract, Contractor A is to do testing, evaluation and validation of items to determine their use in a particular area. You are the KO on a new source selection that will have the successful offeror submitting items to be tested by Contractor A under the current contract. Contractor A is one of many contractors who have expressed interest in the new source selection. As a KO what should you consider when determining if Contractor A may be allowed to bid as a prime contractor on this new source selection?
answer:
An organizational conflict of interest may result when factors create an actual or potential conflict of interest on an instant contract, or when the nature of the work to be performed on the instant contract creates an actual or potential conflict of interest on a future acquisition." In this latter case, some restrictions on future activities of the contractor may be required.

In these cases, under FAR 9.504, the KO shall analyze planned acquisitions in order to identify and evaluate potential conflicts of interests as early in the acquisition process as possible to avoid, neutralize, or mitigate significant potential conflicts before contract award. Obtain the advice of counsel and the assistance of appropriate technical specialists in evaluating potential conflicts and in developing any necessary solicitation provisions and contract clauses. 

Before issuing the solicitation, recommend to the head of the contracting activity a course of action for resolving the conflict to avoid creating unnecessary delays, burdensome information requirements, and excessive documentation.
(FAR 9.502)

Cite: FAR 9.502; FAR 9.504.

question: What is a Blanket Purchase Agreement?
answer:
▪ Not a formal contract
▪ Simplified method of filling anticipated repetitive needs for supplies/services against pre-negotiated price list
▪ Can only be used if no existing requirements contract exists for same supply/service
▪ Avoids writing numerous purchase orders
▪ Establish parameters to limit purchases to individual items or commodity groups or classes, or permit the supplier to furnish unlimited supplies or services
▪ Does not exempt agency/individual from keeping obligations and expenditures within available funds (Money is only obligated upon issuance of "call" rather than when BPA is established

RFO 12.201-1 Simplified Procedures
(3) Blanket purchase agreement. A blanket purchase agreement (BPA) is a method of filling anticipated repetitive needs for supplies or services by establishing "charge accounts" with qualified sources of supply. The Government is only obligated to the extent that authorized orders are placed under BPAs.

(i) BPAs may be established with-

(A) More than one supplier for supplies or services of the same type to provide maximum practicable competition; or

(B) A single firm from which numerous individual purchases at or below the simplified acquisition threshold will likely be made in a given period.

(ii) If, for a particular purchase greater than the micro-purchase threshold, there is an insufficient number of BPAs to ensure maximum practicable competition, the contracting officer shall-

(A) Solicit quotations from other sources and make the purchase as appropriate; and

(B) If practical, establish additional BPAs to facilitate future purchases if recurring requirements for the same or similar supplies or services seem likely and qualified sources are willing to accept BPAs.

(iii) The existence of a BPA does not justify soliciting from only one source or avoiding small business set-asides. The requirements in 12.102 and 12.103 apply to each order under the BPA.

question: What is the main purpose of the post award conference/orientation/start to work meeting? What are some inappropriate purposes?
answer: The main purpose is to help both Government and contractor personnel to achieve a clear and mutual understanding of all contract requirements, and to identify and resolve potential problems. question: Why is it important to fully document the file?
answer:
Because the file is the Government's memory and its evidence. Long after I have rotated out, it is the only thing that shows what was done and why.

RFO FAR 4.101 requires each contracting, administration and paying office to keep a file that comprehensively records the transaction history: a complete background for informed decisions at each step, clear support for every action taken, information for reviews and investigations, and the essential facts if litigation or a congressional inquiry arises. 44 U.S.C. 3101 puts the same records duty on every agency.

A complete file:
- Proves the action was proper - authority, compliance, funds and fair treatment, which is what RFO FAR 1.402-1 and 1.402-2 hold me to. If it is not in the file, a reviewer will treat it as not done.
- Defends the decision. In a protest, GAO gives little weight to new analyses prepared in the heat of the protest and credits later explanations only when they fit the record made at the time; in a claim, the Government's case is built from the file.
- Survives turnover. Files are kept six years after final payment (RFO FAR 4.309), and a claim can be submitted up to six years after it accrues (41 U.S.C. 7103(a)(4)(A)).
- Feeds everything downstream: the FPDS contract action report (4.301), closeout under 4.308, audits and reviews.

In the Army the file lives in VCE (AFARS 5104.101(a)), and I build it as the action happens, not at closeout.

Cite: RFO FAR 4.101, 1.402-1, 1.402-2, 4.301, 4.308, 4.309; AFARS 5104.101(a); 44 U.S.C. 3101; 41 U.S.C. 7103(a)(4)(A).

question: What are IT approval requirements? Who is responsible for providing ITAS approval?

question: On a full and open competitive negotiated acquisition, you have received five proposals and determined that discussions are needed, what is the process of determining which offerors are in the competitive range for these discussions?
answer:
The Government evaluated proposals and determined which were the most highly rated and eligible for inclusion in the competitive range relying on the merits of each offer. The merits of each offer were determined on the basis of: (1) The quality of the technical proposal based on the ratings of each proposal against all evaluation criteria. (2) The proposed cost/prices. Those proposals not included in the competitive range will receive no further consideration and will be notified of this in accordance with FAR 15.206-1.

Cite: FAR 15.206-1.

question: If you have a competitive requirement, how will you determine the Best Value Approach to use in regards to choosing LPTA or Tradeoff? Also, give at least one example when each is appropriate.
answer:
Best value is a continuum, and I choose the approach in acquisition planning with the requiring activity, based on how well we can define the requirement and how much better performance is worth to the Government. I never choose it after proposals arrive.

I go lowest price technically acceptable under RFO FAR 15.103-2 when the requirement is clearly definable, the minimum standards can be written as objective performance measures, the risk of unsuccessful performance is minimal, and there is little or no value in exceeding the minimum. In DoD that is not just judgment: 10 U.S.C. 3241, implemented at DFARS 215.103-2-70, requires me to document in the file that those conditions exist, that the lowest price reflects full life-cycle cost, and why LPTA is justified. It tells me to avoid LPTA for IT and cybersecurity services, systems engineering and other knowledge-based professional services, and for knowledge-based training or logistics services in contingency or overseas operations, and it prohibits LPTA for personal protective equipment and aviation critical safety items where failure could cause death or injury. LPTA because it is easier to evaluate is not a reason.

I go tradeoff under RFO FAR 15.103-1 when it may be in the Government's interest to award to other than the lowest price: the requirement is complex or less defined, technical approach, management or past performance drive success, and we are willing to pay more for the better solution. The RFP states all factors and significant subfactors, their relative importance, and whether the non-price factors combined are significantly more, approximately equal to, or significantly less important than price (15.104). The SSA then documents the comparative assessment and why any higher-priced proposal's benefits merit the extra cost (15.205).

Examples:
- LPTA: a competitively awarded grounds maintenance or refuse collection contract with a measurable PWS, or a buy of commercial items to a clear specification.
- Tradeoff: a base operations support or facilities maintenance services contract where staffing approach, transition plan and past performance matter, or a design-build construction project where design quality drives the outcome.
- The RFO also gives me highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price (15.103-3) and phased acquisition (15.103-4) when technical excellence is the driver and price is secondary.

I document the choice in the acquisition plan and source selection plan, get the SSA's approval, and train the evaluators to use only the stated criteria.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.103, 15.103-1, 15.103-2, 15.103-3, 15.103-4, 15.104, 15.205; 10 U.S.C. 3241; DFARS 215.103-2-70 (DoD RFO Part 15 class deviation 2026-O0048, effective 16 March 2026, as revised); DoD Source Selection Procedures.

question: Please describe what is meant by an “Unsolicited Proposal” according to FAR 15.6, and explain in basic terms the relationship between full and open competition and the acceptance of an unsolicited proposal.
answer:
An Unsolicited Proposal (UP) is a essentially a proposal submitted by industry that is not in response to a US Government request. UPs allow unique and innovative ideas or approaches that have been developed outside the Government to be made available to Government agencies for use in accomplishment of their missions. Unsolicited proposals are offered with the intent that the Government will enter into a contract with the offeror for research and development or other efforts supporting the Government mission, and often represent a substantial investment of time and effort by the offeror. There are many discriminators used in validating a UP. If in the end the UP has received a favorable comprehensive evaluation, providing for full and open competition is still required unless a justification and approval has been obtained under 6.103 / 6.104 [see FAR 15.506]

Cite: FAR 15.506; FAR 6.103; FAR 6.104

question: What would be some of the reasons where the Contracting Officer would need to provide written consent before a prime contractor is allowed to enter into a subcontract?
answer:
The Government has no privity with subcontractors, so consent to subcontract is the tool that lets me look at a prime's buying decisions when the prime's purchasing is my cost or performance risk. RFO FAR 44.201-1 and the clause at 52.244-2 say when my written consent is required.

If the contractor has an approved purchasing system, meaning it passed a contractor purchasing system review under RFO FAR 44.301, consent is required only for the subcontracts I specifically identify in paragraph (d) of 52.244-2. I identify a subcontract, or a class of subcontracts, when I decide an individual consent action is needed to protect the Government because of the subcontract's type, complexity or value, or because it needs special surveillance: critical systems, subsystems, components or services.

If the contractor does not have an approved purchasing system, consent is required under cost-reimbursement, time-and-materials, labor-hour and letter contracts, and for unpriced actions under fixed-price contracts over the SAT, for:
- any cost-reimbursement, T&M or labor-hour subcontract, and
- any fixed-price subcontract that exceeds the greater of the SAT or 5 percent of the total estimated cost of the contract.

Under a priced fixed-price contract, consent applies only to unpriced contract actions such as unpriced modifications or unpriced orders, because on a firm-fixed-price deal the prime already owns the risk.

The reasons behind those triggers are the same reasons I review carefully under RFO FAR 44.201-3(b): the contractor's purchasing system or performance is inadequate; there is a close working relationship or ownership affiliation between prime and sub that could preclude competition or raise prices; the sub is being awarded noncompetitively, at a price that looks unreasonable, or higher than the prime offered the Government; or the sub is cost-type, T&M or labor-hour. When I review, the contractor gives me the description, subcontract type, the proposed subcontractor, the price, its cost or price analysis and negotiation memorandum, and certified data if required, per 52.244-2(e). I check make-or-buy consistency, the small business subcontracting plan, adequate price competition, subcontractor responsibility and exclusions in SAM, an appropriate subcontract type, and no cost-plus-percentage-of-cost. My consent is not a determination that the price or terms are acceptable and does not relieve the prime of responsibility (RFO FAR 44.201-4).

Cite: RFO FAR 44.201-1, 44.201-2, 44.201-3(b), 44.201-4, 44.301; FAR 52.244-2(b), (c), (d), (e); 10 U.S.C. 3322(c); RFO DFARS Part 244 (Class Deviation 2026-O0015 Rev 1).

question: When should performance based payments and progress payments be utilized and what is the difference between the two?
answer:
Performance Based Payments are financing payments based upon the achievement of specific, measurable events or accomplishments that are defined and valued in advance by the parties to the contract. Payments under performance based payments are made on the basis of performance measured by objective quantifiable methods, accomplishment of defined events or other quantifiable measures of results. Customary contract financing to large businesses may be provided on contracts valued at $2.5 million or more where deliveries will not begin until six months after contract award. In determining whether or not PBPs are practical for use on a contract, the contracting officer should first consider whether the benefits associated with PBPs outweigh the time and effort required to establish and administer them. Therefore smaller contracts are generally not good PBP candidates as the administrative effort can easily exceed any financial benefits attained.
Progress payments can be made on the basis of costs incurred, or on the basis of completed work. Progress Payments Based on Costs Incurred are made on the basis of costs incurred by the contractor as work progresses under the contract. This form of contract financing does not include: payments based on the percentage or stage of completion accomplished; payments for partial deliveries accepted by the Government; partial payments for a contract termination proposal; or performance-based payments. (FAR 32.102(b)). Progress Payments Based on a Percentage or Stage of Completion. For DoD, progress payments based on percentage or stage of completion are authorized only for contracts for construction (as defined in FAR 2.101 — the RFO moved the definition of 'construction' out of 36.102, which is now Architect-Engineer Services), shipbuilding, and ship conversion, alteration, or repair. Payments must be commensurate with work accomplished, and meet quality standards established under the contract. If the contractor’s performance is not satisfactory, the Contracting Officer may suspend or withhold up to 10% of the progress payment until corrective action is implemented (FAR 32.103).
Reference/s: Performance Based Payments Guide The Better Buying Power Initiative Performance Based Payments Guide (osd.mil)

Cite: FAR 32.102(b); FAR 32.103; FAR 2.101.

question: Explain the difference between severable and non-severable services.
answer: A severable service is a service that can be separated into components that independently meet a separate need of the government. As a general rule, severable services are the bona fide needs of the fiscal year in which performed, however, DoD agencies may award severable services contracts that cross fiscal years, provided they do not exceed one year in duration. A non-severable service is a service that produces a single or unified outcome, product, or report that cannot be subdivided for separate performance in different fiscal years. Thus, the government must fund the entire effort with dollars available for obligaton at the time the contract is executed, and the contract performance may cross fiscal years.

question: How do you determine whether or not a change is within the scope of the contract?
answer: In general, a modification is considered to be outside the scope of an existing contract when there is a "material difference" between the contract as modified and the contract as it existed before the modification. The rule is to examine any changes in the type of work, performance period and costs between the contract as awarded and as modified. The PCO must look at the Acquisition Plan, the Scope of Work (SOW), the Pricing Negotiation Memorandum (PNM), Justification & Approval (J&A), to determine if the change was contemplated by the parties at the time of contract award. Neither dollar amount nor quantity of changes is sole determinantions deciding whether a change is in or out of scope. The proposed change must also be evaluated with the consideration as to whether it would have significantly affected the original competition (more or different offerors, different technical approaches in the proposals, use of commercial items, etc.).
