question: Describe Performance Based Payments and Progress Payments. When should they be utilized? How does Government financing differ for commercial products/services?
answer:
Progress Payments and Performance Based Payments are both forms of customary financing. They may be used in any procurement that meets the requirements of FAR 32.104. Progress based on cost incurred, evidence of some progress, 80% of costs covered, and contractor must have approved accounting system. PBP based on value of events, evidence of specific progress, provides for tailoring, accounting system to support incurred costs. Commercial financing, FAR 32.2, is more flexible and allows advanced and installment payments. If a general practice of the commercial market. Commercial financing only applies to purchases under FAR Part 12.

Cite: FAR 32.104; FAR 32.2; FAR 12.

question: What are liquidated damages and when can they be used?
answer: Liquidated damages are an express provision in a contract stating a sum for which one of the parties will be liable upon breach of contract or failure to perform. They are used to compensate the Government for probable damages for the harm that is caused by late delivery or untimely performance of the particular contract. Use liquidated damages only when: the time of delivery or timely performance is so important that the Government may reasonably expect to suffer damage if the delivery or performance is delinquent, and the extent or amount of such damage would be difficult or impossible to estimate accurately or prove. question: Currently there is a non-Government contractor employee who is working in a unique technical area. A new source selection is planned and the Commander wants to make this contractor employee chief of the technical evaluation team. As such, this employee would be a voting member of the source selection board. Is it permissible to have a non-Government contractor employee as chief of the technical evaluation team and a voting member of the source selection board?
answer: It is not permissible to have a non-Government employee as a voting member of any source selection board. FAR policy states that contracts shall not be used for the performance of inherently governmental functions. OMB may review Agency decisions to determine whether a function is or is not an inherently governmental function. They include: control of criminal investigations or prosecutions, command of military forces, determination of agency policy and application of regulations, determining budget priorities, and direction and control of federal employees. Specifically, included in this list are determining what supplies or services shall be acquired by the Government on a prime contract and being a voting member of any source selection boards.

question: Who is responsible for the cost of repair of Government Furnished Property?
answer:
Unless otherwise provided for in the contract, the Contractor shall not be liable for loss of Government property furnished or acquired under this contract, except when any one of the following applies: 1) The risk is covered by insurance or the Contractor is otherwise reimbursed. 2) Loss of Government property that is the result of willful misconduct or lack of good faith on the part of the Contractor's managerial personnel. 3) The Contracting Officer has, in writing, revoked the Government's assumption of risk for loss of Government property due to a determination that the Contractor's property management practices are inadequate, and/or present an undue risk to the Government, and the Contractor failed to take timely corrective action. (FAR 52.245-1(h))

question: Once proposals are received in response to a competitive source selection, the government can conduct exchanges with the offerors. Explain the difference between the 3 types of exchanges identified in FAR 15.
answer: Clarifications are limited exchanges, between the Government and offerors, which may occur when award without discussions is contemplated. Clarifications can be used to address minor aspects of the proposal and may be used to resolve minor or clerical errors. Clarifications can be do not have to occur with all offerors. Communications are exchanges between the Government and offerors that lead to establishment of the competitive range. These communications are limited to offerors whose past performance information is the determining factor preventing them from being placed in the competitive range; and for those offerors whose exclusion or inclusion from the competitive range is uncertain. Communications may also be conducted to enhance Government understanding of proposals; allow reasonable interpretation of the proposal; or facilitate the Government’s evaluation process. Communications shall not provide an opportunity for the offeror to revise its proposal. Discussions occur after establishment of the competitive range. Discussions are tailored to each offeror’s proposal, and must be conducted by the KO with each offeror within the competitive range. KOs should discuss with, each offeror deficiencies, significant weaknesses, and adverse past performance information to which the offeror has not yet had an opportunity to respond and other aspects of the offeror’s proposal that could be altered or explained to enhance the proposal’s potential for award. At the conclusion of discussions, each offeror still in the competitive range shall be given an opportunity to submit a final proposal revision.

question: As a contracting officer there will be situations where you will disagree with the decisions/direction/strategies of your customer. How would you reconcile these situations and continue to instill a sense of customer support? How do you prepare yourself for these challenges? Give an example.
answer:
My starting point is that the customer and I want the same outcome - the mission supported, on time, without putting anyone at legal risk. Disagreement is almost never about the goal. It is about the route. So I separate the two things: what is a preference, where I should bend, and what is a legal or regulatory limit, where I cannot. I am the only person who can bind the Government, and I am required to safeguard its interests, so on the second category the answer is no - but the answer is never just no. It is no, and here is the path that gets you what you need.

How I handle it in practice. I go early and in person before positions harden. I lead with the mission effect, not the citation, then produce the citation. I bring at least one executable alternative to the table. I put the agreed way ahead in writing the same day. And if we still do not agree and it is a matter of law, I document my position and elevate through my chain and legal counsel rather than negotiating a compliance question in a hallway.

Three examples of the kind of situation I mean.

- A requiring activity insisted on a brand-name sole source for a maintenance requirement because the incumbent was known and comfortable. I did not argue the merits in the meeting. I asked the engineer to write down the salient physical and functional characteristics that actually drive the need. Market research against those characteristics surfaced two capable sources. We competed it, got a better price, and the customer got a stronger statement of work out of the exercise. Had market research confirmed only one source, I would have supported the justification - the discipline was in testing it, not in refusing it.
- A customer wanted work started before funds were available, on the strength of a promise that money was coming. That is a bright line. I explained the Antideficiency Act exposure in terms of personal consequence to the person who would direct the work, and I offered the lawful options: a smaller scope funded now, a phased schedule, or - because this was an operation and maintenance service that is normal, consistently funded work - an award conditioned on the availability of funds under RFO FAR 32.703-2 with the Availability of Funds clause, which obligates nothing and accepts no work until I give written notice that funds are available. We phased it. Nobody signed an unauthorized commitment.
- A program office pressed for a delivery schedule my market research said industry could not meet, and wanted to keep it in the solicitation to signal urgency. I showed them the likely outcome - either no offers, or priced-in risk, or a default fight in month nine. We ran an industry day, revised the schedule with incentives on the milestones that actually mattered to the mission, and awarded on time.

How I prepare. I know the requirement and the regulation before the meeting so I am not improvising. I build the relationship before I need it - regular touchpoints with the requiring activity so the first substantive conversation is not a refusal. I keep counsel and my Chief of Contracting informed early, not after a position hardens. And I am honest with myself about when I am defending the rule versus defending my own preference.

Cite: RFO FAR 1.402-1 and 1.402-2 (contracting officer authority and responsibilities - bind the Government only within delegated authority, safeguard the Government's interests, request assistance from specialists); RFO FAR 1.102(b)(4) (a strategy is permissible if it is in the best interests of the Government and is not prohibited); RFO FAR 3.104 (procurement integrity); 31 U.S.C. 1341 (Antideficiency Act); RFO FAR 32.703-2 and clause 52.232-18 (contracts conditioned upon availability of funds).

rfo.notes: Reviewed 14 Sep 2026. The four FAR cites are verified crosswalk pairs. The draft offered an 'undefinitized action' as a way to start work before funds were available; a UCA still requires funds to be obligated at award, so it was replaced with 32.703-2 / 52.232-18 (fiscal-year O&M and continuing services, no acceptance until the KO notifies funds availability), read on acquisition.gov (FAC 2026-01) and confirmed retained as 32.703-2 on the RFO Part 32 page. Examples are illustrative - a candidate should substitute real experience.

key_points: Separate preference (bend) from legal or regulatory limit (cannot bend) - and never answer with a bare no.
Engage early and in person, lead with mission effect then the citation, bring an executable alternative, confirm in writing the same day.
Brand-name pressure: force the salient characteristics into writing and let market research decide; support the justification if it holds up.

Unfunded start: explain Antideficiency Act exposure in personal terms and offer lawful options - reduced scope, phasing, or an award conditioned on availability of funds (RFO FAR 32.703-2, clause 52.232-18) with no work until funds are notified; an undefinitized action is not a cure for unavailable funds.
Unrealistic schedule: show the downstream outcome, use industry engagement, then incentivize the milestones that matter.
Prepare by knowing the requirement and the rule cold, building the customer relationship before the conflict, and involving counsel and the chain early.

question: In a competitive source selection environment, there will be disagreements between the contracting officer, Source Selection Evaluation Board (SSEB) members, legal advisor, and/or other advisors regarding decisions/direction/strategies pertaining to the source selection process. Describe how you will reconcile such differences in a productive, cooperative manner.
answer:
Disagreement in a source selection is healthy as long as it stays inside the process, inside the record, and inside the RFP. As the contracting officer I am the business advisor and the process owner, so I manage it in three moves.

First, common ground. Most fights are really about facts or about what the RFP says. I pull the team back to the evaluation criteria and the source selection plan, because RFO FAR 15.202(a)(1) requires that proposals be evaluated solely on the factors and subfactors in the RFP - the anchor nobody can argue with - and 15.201 makes me the focal point for the process. If the SSEB wants to credit something the RFP did not ask for, the answer is no, explained as protest risk, not personality.

Second, roles. The SSEB owns technical findings; I own the process and the business judgment; legal owns legal sufficiency; the SSA owns the decision. When an evaluator and legal disagree, I do not vote. I make sure each position is written with its rationale, add my recommendation, and put it in front of the SSA, or the SSAC on a large action. Under the DoD Source Selection Procedures and the Army Source Selection Supplement the SSA may accept or reject any recommendation, but the record must show independent judgment. A documented disagreement the SSA resolves is a strength in a protest; one that vanishes from the file is a weakness.

Third, tone. Private conversations first, never in front of offerors or the whole board; assume competence; ask what risk the other person is protecting against.

Three examples:
- An SSEB chair wanted to eliminate an offeror for a page-limit violation; legal said the RFP was ambiguous. We documented both views and the SSA treated excess pages as unread for every offeror, consistently. No protest.
- An evaluator kept rating the incumbent higher for familiarity. I showed the team that was not an evaluation factor and we re-ran consensus on the stated criteria under RFO FAR 15.202.
- A program office pushed to skip discussions to hit an award date. I laid out the competitive range and negotiation options under RFO FAR 15.204 with the schedule and risk of each; the SSA chose discussions, and the award survived a protest.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.201, 15.202, 15.204, 15.205; RFO FAR 1.402-2; DoD Source Selection Procedures; Army Source Selection Supplement (AFARS Appendix AA).

question: In your opinion, what are the keys to ensuring that the integrity of the competitive source selection process is maintained and that the overall acquisition is conducted in a fair and impartial manner?
answer:
In my opinion it comes down to four things: set the rules before the game, protect the information, treat every offeror the same, and be able to show your work.

Set the rules first. A clear PWS, evaluation factors and subfactors with their relative importance in the RFP, a source selection plan approved by the SSA before release, and evaluators trained on it. We evaluate only against what we published. Example: on a services recompete a technical evaluator wanted to credit an offeror for a capability we never asked for. I stopped it. If it matters, we amend the RFP and let everyone respond; otherwise it is an unstated criterion and a sustainable protest.

Protect the information. Non-disclosure and conflict-of-interest certifications from every board member and advisor, need-to-know handling of proposals and source selection information under RFO FAR 3.104, screening for personal and organizational conflicts under RFO FAR subpart 9.5, and no non-Government employee as a voting member. Example: a board member's spouse worked for an offeror's subcontractor; we replaced the member before evaluations started and documented why.

Treat offerors the same. One point of contact for offerors, and that is the KO. Exchanges are consistent: clarifications, communications and discussions follow RFO FAR 15.202 and 15.204, discussions are meaningful and not misleading, and every offeror in the competitive range gets them. No favoritism toward the incumbent and no back channel through the customer. Example: the incumbent asked the COR about a transition detail; I redirected it, answered through an amendment to everyone, and reminded the requiring activity that only the KO talks to offerors.

Show your work. Consensus evaluations with strengths, weaknesses, deficiencies and risks tied to the stated criteria; a source selection decision by the SSA that reflects independent judgment and the comparative assessment (15.205); and debriefings that are honest and complete (preaward under 15.206-2, postaward under 15.301), because a good debriefing is the best protest prevention we have.

As a leader I model it: I do not discuss the competition outside the team, I bring legal in early, and I make it safe for the most junior evaluator to say that is not in the criteria.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.201 (source selection responsibilities and safeguards), 15.104, 15.202, 15.204, 15.205, 15.206-2, 15.301; RFO FAR 3.104 and 41 U.S.C. chapter 21 (Procurement Integrity); RFO FAR subpart 9.5; DoD Source Selection Procedures.

question: Describe the trade-off process as envisioned by FAR Part 15, and how it is implemented to determine the best value offeror(s) in a competitive source selection.
answer:
A tradeoff process is appropriate when it may be in the best interest of the Government to consider award to other than the lowest priced offeror or other than the highest technically rated offeror. This process permits tradeoffs among cost or price and non-cost factors and allows the Government to accept other than the lowest priced proposal. The perceived benefits of the higher priced proposal shall merit the additional cost, and the rationale for tradeoffs must be documented in the file in accordance with 15.408 (the RFO moved documentation from 15.406 to 15.408; 15.406 is now 'Data to support proposal analysis').
Reference/s: FAR 15.103-1

Cite: FAR 15.103-1; FAR 15.408.

Citing 15.406 for documentation would now be wrong, hence the short parenthetical. question: In the performance of your duties as a contracting officer you will be required to use your discretion in making critical decisions. Describe the decision-making process you will employ and the manner in which you will prepare to defend your decisions should they be challenged, whether by others at the time and/or in a future review/investigation.
answer:
My decision process has six steps, and the sixth one is what lets me defend the first five.

One, frame the decision. What exactly am I deciding, is it within my warrant and my authority, and what is the real deadline? If it is above my authority I elevate early, I do not stretch.

Two, get the facts and the rules. I go to the requirement, the market research, the COR, the contractor and the data, and I find the governing rule in order: statute and fiscal law, then FAR, DFARS, AFARS and local policy. If a practice is in the Government's interest and is not prohibited by law, regulation or executive order, RFO FAR 1.102(b)(4) says I may use it; I do not invent prohibitions and I do not invent permissions.

Three, consult. RFO FAR 1.402-2 requires me to request and consider the advice of specialists, so legal, pricing, the small business specialist, policy and the requiring activity are in the room before I decide, not after.

Four, analyze alternatives and risk: mission impact, fiscal risk under purpose, time and amount, competition and protest risk, and contractor performance risk. I pick the course that best serves the Government, not the easiest one.

Five, decide and communicate. I tell the affected parties what I decided and why, in plain language, including the customer who did not get the answer they wanted.

Six, document contemporaneously. The file must show a complete history and clear support for every action (RFO FAR 4.101): the D&F, the J&A, the price negotiation memorandum, and for a source selection the decision document with the rationale for every business judgment and tradeoff (RFO FAR 15.205). I write it the day I decide, never after the fact.

How I defend it. In the moment, when a commander or customer pushes, I explain the rule, offer a lawful alternative, and put my position in writing. Later, in a protest, audit, IG inquiry or investigation, the standard is whether my decision was reasonable, consistent with the solicitation and regulation, fair to all parties and made in good faith on the record I had at the time. A well-documented file answers that without me having to remember anything. If the record shows I was wrong, I take corrective action rather than defend an error.

Three examples:
- A commander wants a sole source for a $40K maintenance job. I run market research, and if only the OEM can do it I document the limited-source decision under RFO FAR 12.102 if it is commercial, or RFO FAR 13.101(b) if it is not; if not, I compete it and I tell the commander why in writing.
- A customer sends a September purchase request with this year's O&M for services starting next July. I reject it, cite the bona fide needs rule at 31 U.S.C. 1502, explain severable services, and keep the email.
- In a best-value tradeoff I pick a higher-priced offeror. The SSDD explains specifically what the extra strengths buy and why they are worth the price difference, so GAO can follow my reasoning.

Cite: RFO FAR 1.102(b)(4), 1.402-2, 4.101, 15.205 (was 15.308), 12.102, 13.101(b); RFO FAR Part 3 standards of conduct; 31 U.S.C. 1341 and 1502.

rfo.notes: Reviewer 14 Sep 2026: crosswalk entries 1.102-4(e)/1.102(b)(4), 1.602-2/1.402-2, 4.801-4.803/4.101, 15.308/15.205, 12.102 (RFO meaning: restricting competition, at/below SAT record that only one source exists) and 13.106-1(b)/13.101(b) are all 'verified' in regulations.json. The $40K sole-source example now distinguishes commercial (12.102) from noncommercial (13.101(b)). Leadership question; structure is the drafter's. Facts and rules in order: statute and fiscal law, FAR, DFARS, AFARS, local policy; RFO FAR 1.102(b)(4) permits what is not prohibited
Consult specialists before deciding (RFO FAR 1.402-2): legal, pricing, small business, policy, customer

Decide, communicate plainly, document contemporaneously (RFO FAR 4.101; SSDD rationale RFO FAR 15.205)

question: When should a COR be assigned to a contract and what criteria is required by the individual in order to be appointed as a COR? What procedures are involved?
answer:
Contracting Officers shall designate a COR for all service contracts, and supply contracts with cost-reimbursable line items including both firm-fixed-price and other than firm-fixed-price contracts, awarded by a DoD component or by any other Federal agency on behalf of DoD within 3 business days of contract award. The surveillance activities performed by CORs should be tailored to the dollar value/complexity of the specific contract for which they are designated. Contracting officers may exempt service contracts from this requirement when the following three conditions are met:
Awarded using SAP procedures;
Requirement is not complex; and
Contracting Officer documents the file reasons why the appointment of COR is unnecessary.

Follow the guidance of DoDI 5000.72 for general COR appointment and training requirements. (DFARS PGI 201.602-2 no longer exists under the RFO DFARS; COR designation guidance is now at DFARS PGI 201.404-70, with the DFARS rule at 201.404-70.)

Cite: DFARS PGI 201.404-70(e); DFARS 201.404-70; DoDI 5000.72.

The surveillance activities performed by CORs should be tailored to the dollar value and complexity of the specific contract for which they are designated. For geographically dispersed large contracts with multiple task orders, contracting officers should consider appointing multiple or alternate CORs to assist with surveillance duties. These CORs should have specific duties based on criteria, such as geographic region or distinct task areas, to avoid conflicting or duplicative direction. question: When is a Services Acquisition Strategy required?
answer:
Short answer: in the Army, a written acquisition strategy for a service acquisition is required whenever the acquisition meets the review thresholds delegated in AFARS Appendix GG, and it has to be approved before I release the final solicitation. It is also required, regardless of dollar value, for any service acquisition designated special interest - the AFARS names the Under Secretary of Defense for acquisition (still styled USD(AT&L) in the text), the ASA(ALT), the Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army (Procurement), and the Senior Services Manager as the officials who can designate one.

The framework has three layers and I would lay them out that way.
- DoD. DoDI 5000.74, Defense Acquisition of Services, puts services into categories by total planned value and assigns a decision authority to each; the higher the category, the higher the approval and the more formal the review. The AFARS applies except where DoDI 5000.74 itself carves something out.
- Army. AFARS 5137.890, Oversight of services acquisition, reissued in June 2026 for the FAR overhaul. Oversight is shared by the requiring activity, the contracting activity and ASA(ALT). 5137.890-2 points to Appendix GG for the review thresholds and delegations and says the final solicitation may be released only after the strategy is approved - and then still subject to the peer review process in DFARS 201.170 and AFARS 5101.170 and any local reviews. 5137.890-3 has the HCA set the review procedures for the levels delegated to it, and for USD, DASA(P) or SSM level reviews the strategy goes to the addressee in AFARS PGI 5101.290(b)(4). Task orders under a strategy that was already reviewed do not need a separate strategy if I issue them consistent with the decision authority's conditions. AR 70-13 is the companion Army regulation.
- Local. My contracting activity will have its own routing, suspense timelines and template, and the requirement normally clears a Services Requirements Review Board before the strategy is approved.

What the strategy has to contain is listed in AFARS PGI 5137.890-4. The elements I would expect: the requirement and the outcomes, written performance-based where possible; a risk assessment and mitigation; the competition approach and rationale; the socioeconomic and small business approach; the business arrangement - funding, contract type, incentives, period and existing vehicles considered; multiyear budgeting if used; and the metrics for cost, schedule and performance.

Separately, do not confuse this with the general acquisition plan. The written acquisition plan rules in RFO FAR 7.102 and AFARS Part 5107 still apply on their own terms; the services acquisition strategy is the services-specific overlay.

Board-honest caveat: the dollar tiers and approval levels sit in Appendix GG and change with AFARS and DoDI 5000.74 revisions. I would state the framework and then say I confirm the current threshold and routing in Appendix GG and with my policy branch - at the 411th, the Chief, C&P - before I commit to a date.

Cite: AFARS 5137.890-1 (applicability and special interest designation), 5137.890-2 (review thresholds via Appendix GG; approval before solicitation release; peer review), 5137.890-3 (review procedures and routing), 5137.890-4 with AFARS PGI 5101.170-3 (independent management reviews); AFARS PGI 5137.890-4 (strategy content); AFARS Appendix GG; DoDI 5000.74; AR 70-13; RFO FAR 7.102 and Part 37.

DFARS 201.170 peer review is cited as referenced by 5137.890-2(b), not independently verified against the RFO DFARS Part 201 deviation.

question: Your contractor is seriously defaulting on a contract. What factors do you need to take into consideration prior to termination for default?
answer:
Before I terminate for default I make sure the Government is on solid ground, because a bad default converts to a termination for convenience with costs against us.

RFO FAR 49.402-3(a) starts me with a review of the situation with my technical people and legal counsel - default, convenience, or no-cost cancellation - and the factors at 49.402-3(i) drive the decision:
- The terms of the contract and applicable law. Is the failure actually a breach, and have we followed the Default clause?
- The specific failure and the contractor's excuses. Excusable delay under 52.249-8 - acts of God, acts of the Government, strikes, unusually severe weather, subcontractor delay beyond both parties' control - defeats a default, and under 49.402-3(m) if the failure is excusable I may not default.
- Whether the supplies or services are available from other sources.
- The urgency of the need and how long another source would take compared with the delinquent contractor.
- The contractor's essentiality to Government programs and the effect of a default on its other contracts.
- The effect on the contractor's ability to repay guaranteed loans, progress or advance payments.
- Any other pertinent facts.

I also check our own house. Did the Government waive the schedule by letting them keep performing past the date? If so, 49.402-3(c) makes me set a new date and reserve our rights before I can default. Did a COR give direction, was GFP late, was the specification defective? Has the contractor had the cure notice under 49.402-3(d) with at least ten days when the failure endangers performance, or the show cause under (f) when time has run - formats at 49.607? Have I notified the surety under (g), and for a small business sent the notices to the small business specialist and SBA under (h)? Will the file support a final decision that will be appealed under the Disputes clause?

Then I weigh the alternatives at 49.402-4 - a revised schedule with consideration, completion by the surety or a subcontractor, or convenience if that is in our interest. If default is still right, the notice under 49.402-3(j) states the failures, the excess reprocurement cost liability under 49.402-6, and appeal rights; under (k) I distribute the notice, send the surety a copy and ask whether it wants to arrange completion, and tell the disbursing officer to stop payments; and I record the default in the past performance and integrity systems. For a commercial contract I terminate for cause under RFO FAR 12.304 and 52.212-4(m), not Part 49.

Cite: RFO FAR 49.402-3(a), (c), (d), (f), (g), (h), (i), (j), (k), (m); 49.402-2, 49.402-4, 49.402-6, 49.607; FAR 52.249-8; RFO FAR 12.304; FAR 52.212-4(m); 41 U.S.C. chapter 71.

RFO 12.304 and 52.212-4(m) confirmed against the verified crosswalk. The legacy paragraph letters in the crosswalk are from memory and remain the least certain element.

key_points: Review with technical and legal first (RFO FAR 49.402-3(a)); a default is a final decision that will be appealed.
Factors at 49.402-3(i): contract terms and law; the failure and excuses; other sources; urgency vs time to reprocure; contractor essentiality; effect on loans and payments; other facts.
Excusable delay (52.249-8) bars default; if excusable, no default (49.402-3(m)).
Check Government fault: waiver of schedule (49.402-3(c)), COR direction, late GFP, defective spec.

question: Before the award of the contract, you as the Contracting Officer received a protest. Can you proceed with the award, why or why not?
answer:
Generally no. I do not award over a pending protest on my own authority, and the rule depends on where the protest was filed.

Agency-level protest, RFO FAR 33.104-2(b)(1): a contract may not be awarded until the agency resolves the protest, unless a written justification is made for urgent and compelling reasons, or award is determined in writing to be in the best interest of the Government. Who signs that is set by agency procedure, so I go through legal and my chief and SCO, and I confirm the current approval level locally.

GAO protest, RFO FAR 33.105-2: if the agency receives notice from GAO before award, the contract may not be awarded. That is the statutory stay under 31 U.S.C. 3553(c). The only way through is the head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, making a written finding that urgent and compelling circumstances which significantly affect the interests of the United States will not allow waiting for GAO's decision, and that award is likely to occur within 30 days of the finding. The override is reported to GAO, and the protester can challenge it at the Court of Federal Claims.

Court of Federal Claims, RFO FAR 33.106: no automatic stay, but the court can enjoin award, so I act on legal's direction.

What I actually do the day it lands: notify legal and my chain immediately; confirm it is timely and that it really is a protest (a letter objecting to the award without the word protest may still be one, and legal decides); stop the award action; preserve the record; notify the apparent awardee if appropriate; and start building the agency report, which for GAO is due 30 days after notice. If the protest has merit, early corrective action is cheaper than losing at GAO and rebuilding the competition anyway. If the mission truly cannot wait, I build the urgent and compelling package for the right official. I do not decide it myself.

Cite: RFO FAR 33.104-2(b)(1); 33.105-2(a) and (b); 33.106; 31 U.S.C. 3553(c); 4 CFR 21.3(c).

rfo.notes: RFO Part 33 subpart 33.1 structure (33.104-2 Preaward agency protest, 33.105-2 Preaward GAO protest with the HCA urgent-and-compelling finding, 33.106 Protests at the U.S. Court of Federal Claims) re-confirmed on the acquisition.gov Part 33 page (updated 28 Jul 2026) on 14 Sep 2026; 33.105-2(b) 30-day award condition and 4 CFR 21.3(c) were read 13 Sep 2026. The agency-level approval official is set by agency procedure and must be confirmed locally.

key_points: Agency protest: no award until resolved unless a written urgent-and-compelling justification or best-interest determination (RFO FAR 33.104-2(b)(1))
GAO protest before award: no award; only the HCA's nondelegable written finding (urgent and compelling, award likely within 30 days) overrides (33.105-2; 31 U.S.C. 3553(c))
Court of Federal Claims: no automatic stay, but the court can enjoin award (33.106)
Immediate actions: legal and chain of command, timeliness check, stop award, preserve the record, agency report due in 30 days
Consider early corrective action; the KO never overrides a protest alone

question: Ali & Sons Cleaning Service has filed a protest with the agency after award of the camp janitorial contract. How long does the agency have to resolve the protest?
answer:
There is no statutory deadline for an agency protest, but the FAR sets the standard: the agency must make its best efforts to resolve it within 35 days after the protest is received by the contracting officer or by the official conducting an independent review. That is RFO FAR 33.104-4(c)(1).

Here is what I do with Ali and Sons. First, I check timing. It is post-award, so if the protest came in within 10 days after award, or within 5 days after a debriefing date I offered under a timely request, whichever is later, I must immediately suspend performance on the janitorial contract pending resolution, unless I justify continued performance in writing on urgent and compelling reasons or best interest of the Government (RFO FAR 33.104-3). For a camp janitorial contract, a break in service may well support that written finding, but it is a finding, not an assumption.

Second, I consult legal as soon as practicable, which AFARS 5133.103(d)(3) requires. Third, I find out whether the protester wants me to decide it or wants an independent review at a level above me; for an ACC contracting office that review is routed under AMC procedures (AFARS 5133.103(d)(4)(i)), so I confirm the current routing with my Chief of Contracting. Fourth, I resolve it on the merits: pull the evaluation record, answer each ground, and issue a written decision that explains the basis. If they are right, I take corrective action; if they are wrong, I say why.

Two clocks I keep in mind: my 35-day best-efforts target, and the protester's GAO clock, which is 10 days from when they learn of the initial adverse agency action, so a prompt, well-reasoned decision is also my best protection against a follow-on GAO protest.

Cite: RFO FAR 33.104-4(c)(1) (was 33.103(g)); RFO FAR 33.104-3(a); AFARS 5133.103(d)(3) and (d)(4)(i) (AFARS still carries legacy section numbers); 4 CFR 21.2(a)(3).

rfo.notes: Reviewer 14 Sep 2026: RFO Part 33 page re-read: 35-day best-efforts rule at 33.104-4(c)(1); 10-day/5-day postaward suspension with written urgent-and-compelling or best-interest justification at 33.104-3(a). AFARS Part 5133 on acquisition.gov (revised 01 Oct 2024, change 2025-0711) read: 5133.103(d)(3) 'As soon as practicable, the Contracting officer must consult with the legal office'; (d)(4)(i) AMC contracting officers use AMC procedures for independent review. question: What is the requirement for obligating funds when awarding indefinite-quantity contracts?
answer:
An obligation to meet the minimum guarantee amount must be executed at the time of award.
Reference/s: GAO case B-318046; Principles of Federal Appropriations Law, Volume II, Chapter 7, p. 7-21

alt_answers.text:
An obligation to meet the minimum guarantee amount must be executed at the time of award.

Reference/s: GAO case B-318046; Principles of Federal Appropriations Law, Volume II, Chapter 7, p. 7-21

RFO 16.504 Indefinite-quantity contracts.
16.504-1 Description.

(a) An indefinite-quantity contract provides for an indefinite quantity, within stated limits, of supplies or services during an ordering period. The Government places orders for individual requirements. Quantity limits may be stated as number of units or as dollar values.

(b) The contract must require the Government to order and the contractor to furnish at least a stated minimum quantity of supplies or services. To ensure that the contract is binding, the minimum quantity must be more than a nominal quantity, but it should not exceed the amount that the Government is fairly certain to order.

question: When the contracting officer properly issues a unilateral change under the Changes clause, what responsibility, if any, does the contractor have to continue performance?
answer:
The contractor must continue performance of the contract as changed, except that in cost reimbursement or incrementally funded contracts the contractor is not obligated to continue performance or incur costs beyond the limits established in the Limitation of Cost or Limitation of Funds clause. In the case contractor and Contracting Officer cannot agree to the terms of the change order, the contractor is permitted to submit a dispute under the disputes clause. question: What is the Defense Base Act, when does it apply and how is it implemented? What are the conditions for a country waiver?
answer:
The Defense Base Act extends the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act to civilian employees working overseas on U.S. Government contracts. In plain terms it is the workers' compensation regime for contractor employees performing outside the United States, paid for by insurance the contractor buys and prices into the contract.

When it applies. It covers employment on U.S. military bases overseas and on lands outside the continental United States that the United States occupies or uses for military purposes, on public-work contracts - construction, alteration, repair and service contracts - performed outside the United States, on certain Foreign Assistance Act contracts, and for employees of contractors providing welfare or similar services overseas for the benefit of the armed forces. Benefits are payable regardless of nationality: U.S. citizens, U.S. residents, third-country nationals and local nationals alike, unless a waiver applies. A supply contract with no employees performing overseas does not carry it.

How it is implemented. The contractor buys Defense Base Act insurance from a carrier authorized by the Department of Labor, or is authorized by Labor to self-insure. I put the clause at 52.228-3, Workers' Compensation Insurance (Defense Base Act), in the solicitation and contract when the Act applies, and I require proof of coverage before performance begins. The premium is an allowable, priced cost, and the contractor must flow the requirement down to every subcontractor at any tier performing overseas. Claims are administered by the Department of Labor's Office of Workers' Compensation Programs, not by me; my job is to make sure coverage is in place, priced and flowed down, and to work with the requiring activity and counsel if a claim arises. War-hazard injuries are covered through the War Hazards Compensation Act, which reimburses the carrier.

Country waiver. Only the Secretary of Labor - not the contracting agency, and not the contracting officer - can waive the Act, and only on the written recommendation of the head of the agency. A waiver can cover a contract, a subcontract, a work location, or a classification of employees, and in practice Labor grants them for specified classes of employees in specified countries. Two conditions always ride with a waiver: it never reaches U.S. citizens, U.S. legal residents, or anyone hired in the United States, and it is valid only if the waived employees receive workers' compensation benefits under the local law. When a waiver applies to a public-work contract performed outside the United States, I use the alternate clause, 52.228-4, Workers' Compensation and War-Hazard Insurance Overseas, instead of 52.228-3 - and under it the contractor still has to provide the local-law benefits and war-hazard coverage.

Practical OCONUS point: whether a waiver is in effect for your country and your class of employees is a fact you confirm - through your legal office and the Department of Labor - before you pick the clause.

Cite: 42 U.S.C. 1651-1654 (Defense Base Act) and 42 U.S.C. 1701 et seq. (War Hazards Compensation Act); 33 U.S.C. 901 et seq. (Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act); RFO FAR 28.305 (overseas workers' compensation and war-hazard insurance, including the agency-head recommendation and Secretary of Labor waiver); RFO FAR 28.309(a) and (b) (clause prescriptions); FAR 52.228-3 and 52.228-4; Department of Labor OWCP Defense Base Act guidance (waiver conditions).

question: Discuss the differences in FAR Part 12 commercial procurements and non-commercial procurements under FAR Part 15.
answer:
Part 12 is how we buy what the commercial marketplace already sells; Part 15 is how we negotiate for what it does not. The differences run through the whole life cycle.

Applicability. Part 12 applies only after a commerciality determination - the product or service is of a type sold or offered to the general public, or evolved from one - and RFO FAR 12.101 makes commercial acquisition mandatory when commercial items meet the need, implementing 10 U.S.C. 3453. Part 15 is the default for everything else that is not sealed bidding.

Solicitation. Part 12 uses the SF 1449, the streamlined provisions 52.212-1 and 52.212-2 and the single clause 52.212-4, tailorable except where statute controls, with combined synopsis and solicitation under 12.202. Part 15 uses the uniform contract format at 15.109, full instructions and evaluation sections, and the RFP process.

Procedures and thresholds. Under RFO FAR 12.201-1, commercial buys up to nine million dollars, fifteen million for contingency and emergency support, use simplified procedures: RFQ and purchase order. Above that, 12.201-2 uses this subpart together with the Part 15 RFP or Part 14 procedures, and 12.203 says commercial evaluation factors need not be more detailed than technical, price and past performance. Part 15 has no ceiling but carries the source selection machinery: the evaluation approach at 15.103, competitive range and negotiations at 15.204, a source selection decision at 15.205, and formal debriefings.

Contract type. RFO FAR 12.104 requires firm-fixed-price or fixed-price with EPA to the maximum extent practicable, with time-and-materials or labor-hour for commercial services only within the limits that section sets; cost-reimbursement is not an authorized commercial contract type. Part 15 can use any Part 16 type the risk justifies.

Pricing. Commercial buys rely on price analysis and market prices; certified cost or pricing data is prohibited for commercial products and services under 15.403-2, and price reasonableness rests on competitive quotes under 12.204. Part 15 requires certified cost or pricing data above the threshold at 15.403-3 - two and a half million governmentwide, but ten million for DoD prime contracts awarded after 30 June 2026 under DFARS 215.403-3(a) - unless an exception applies, with cost analysis and profit analysis under 15.404.

Terms and administration. Commercial contracts flow fewer laws and clauses - the list is at acquisition.gov/inapplicablelaws under 41 U.S.C. 1906 and 1907; changes under 52.212-4(c) are bilateral only; terminations are for cause or convenience under RFO FAR 12.304 using 52.212-4, not Part 49. Non-commercial contracts carry unilateral change orders under RFO FAR 43.301, Part 49 terminations, and the full clause set.

Bottom line: Part 12 trades Government-unique protections for speed and commercial pricing; Part 15 keeps the protections and pays for them in time and cost.

Cite: RFO FAR 12.101, 12.102, 12.104, 12.201-1, 12.201-2, 12.202, 12.203, 12.204, 12.205, 12.304; RFO FAR 15.103, 15.109, 15.204, 15.205, 15.403-2, 15.403-3, 15.404; RFO FAR 43.301; DFARS 215.403-3; 10 U.S.C. 3453; 41 U.S.C. 1906, 1907; FAR 52.212-1, 52.212-2, 52.212-4.

question: What are the essential elements the Contracting Officer must analyze when making a Scope Determination? What would be considered the scope tests?
answer: Is there a change to; the type of work or function of an item, change to quantity, especially of major items or portions of the contract?, change to the performance period? Change to costs? Was the procurement historically acquired under a separate contract? Once the nature of a change is identified, consider followings: Does the modification change the contract so much that different offerors would have submitted proposals than those who actually offered? Would potential offerors have reasonably anticipated this kind of change prior to award? Do material differences exist between the modified and originally awarded contract? Would the contractor have reasonably contemplated the modification at the time of award? Does the modified contract required the same work for which the parties originally bargained?

Was the procurement historically acquired under a separate contract? Would potential offerors have reasonably anticipated this kind of change prior to award? Do material differences exist between the modified and originally awarded contract? Would the contractor have reasonably contemplated the modification at the time of award? Does the modified contract required the same work for which the parties originally bargained?

GAO Material Difference Assessment:
“[T]he extent of any changes in the type of work, performance period, and costs between the modification and the original contract, as well as whether the original solicitation adequately advised offerors of the potential for the change or whether the change was the type that reasonably could have been anticipated, and whether the modification materially changed the field of competition for the requirement.”

DAU Tests

Cotemplation of the Parties Test: An “In scope” determination can be made if the change would have been fairly & reasonably contemplated by the contracting parties when the contract was entered into, related directly to MATERIAL DIFFERENCE (type of work, costs, and performance period). 

Scope of the Competition Test: GAO/courts will deem a change “in scope” if it would have been fairly and reasonably contemplated by potential bidders to the original competition.

Self-Answer: To make a scope determination, the KO must analyze 

(1) [CONTEMPLATION OF PARTIES TEST] whether the modification creates a material difference in the type of work, cost, or performance period, that would have been reasonably contemplated by contracting parties and 

(2) [SCOPE OF THE COMPETITION TEST] whether the change would have altered the field of competition. 

RFO 43.203, FAR 43.3, the Changes clauses (FAR 52.243‑1 through 52.243‑4), and FAR Part 6 (CICA) provide the regulatory basis for these determinations. A modification is out of scope if it materially changes the contract or would have attracted different competitors had it been included originally.

question: The COR has noticed that the contractor may be acquiring "Contractor Acquired Property" (CAP) that was authorized for purchase in the contract. The contractor reportedly told the COR that they were not tracking the purchase or the location, etc., of the property because they (contractor) purchased it, not the Government. What would you do in this instance?
answer: Would have to review the contract to determine what type of contract it is, ie: FFP or cost. In accordance with the FAR, typically the Government has title to the contractor acquired property, but it depends on contract type and what is in the contract. See below for the different scenarios based on contract type. Government-furnished property also includes contractor-acquired property if the contractor-acquired property is a deliverable under a cost contract when accepted by the Government for continued use under the contract. Under fixed -price type contracts, in the absence of financing provisions or other specific requirements for passage of title in the contract, the contractor retains title to all property acquired by the contractor for use on the contract, except for property identified as a deliverable end item. If a deliverable item is to be retained by the contractor for use after inspection and acceptance by the Government, it shall be made accountable to the contract through a contract modification listing the item as Government-furnished property. Under cost type and time-and-material contracts, the Government acquires title to all property to which the contractor is entitled to reimbursement. If it is FFP and there was no deliverable, it may not matter that they are not tracking it for our purposes because we don't have title to it, however we paid for it, so there should be some record of it for invoicing purposes. Otherwise, if it is cost, we should have the rights. Would probably also set up a telecom with the customer, COR, legal, and the contracts to discuss and would follow up with a PCO letter to advise them that it is their responsiblity to track the equipment, etc.

question: Describe the difference between an OTA vs. a FAR based contract.
answer:
A FAR-based contract is a procurement contract: under 31 U.S.C. 6303 we use it when the principal purpose is to acquire supplies or services for the direct benefit of the Government. It carries the Competition in Contracting Act, the FAR, DFARS and AFARS, the Contract Disputes Act, cost accounting standards, certified cost or pricing data rules, the Bayh-Dole and DFARS data-rights framework, and the mandatory clause set. An Other Transaction is a legally binding agreement issued under a specific statutory authority that is, by definition, not a procurement contract, grant or cooperative agreement, so those procurement statutes and the FAR do not apply unless we write them in.

Authorities: 10 U.S.C. 4021 for basic, applied and advanced research OTs; 10 U.S.C. 4022 for prototype projects; and 4022(f), which allows a follow-on production contract or transaction without further competition if the prototype OT was competitively awarded and the prototype was successfully completed. Approval under 4022: above $100 million the head of the contracting activity or agency director; above $500 million the senior procurement executive plus 30 days notice to Congress.

The practical differences:
- Who signs: an Agreements Officer with an AO warrant, not a KO. Army Warranting Policy v12 requires the OT courses, working knowledge of data rights and intellectual property, and a prior commensurate KO or GO warrant, and the OT's cumulative value counts against the AO's warrant threshold.
- Competition: 4022 requires competitive procedures to the maximum extent practicable, not CICA; commercial solutions openings and consortia are the usual vehicles.
- Eligibility under 4022(d): at least one nontraditional defense contractor or nonprofit research institution participating to a significant extent, or all significant participants small businesses or nontraditionals, or at least one third of the cost from non-federal sources, or exceptional circumstances documented by the senior procurement executive.
- Terms: negotiated, not prescribed. Payment milestones, IP and data rights, termination, audit and accounting are whatever the parties agree to. No CAS, no TINA, no Christian doctrine reading in missing clauses.
- Remedies: the Contract Disputes Act does not apply; disputes go where the agreement says. GAO protest jurisdiction is limited to whether the agency properly used an OT instead of a procurement contract (4 CFR 21.5(m)); otherwise the Court of Federal Claims.
- Risk: fewer built-in protections for the Government. The AO has to negotiate what a KO gets for free, so market research, a clear statement of the prototype, and a payment schedule tied to outcomes matter more.

What does not change: fiscal law, the bona fide need rule, the purpose statute, ethics and procurement integrity, and Army warrant limits all apply to OTs. I would recommend an OT when the FAR would keep a commercial or nontraditional innovator from working with us, speed matters, and the deliverable is a prototype or research result. I would not use it to buy commodity supplies or recurring services. The other non-FAR instruments, grants and cooperative agreements, are governed by the DoDGARs at 32 CFR and 2 CFR part 200 and are for assistance, not acquisition.

Cite: 10 U.S.C. 4021 and 4022; 31 U.S.C. 6303 through 6305; DoD Other Transactions Guide (2023); 4 CFR 21.5(m); Army Warranting Program Policy v12 (MAR 2026) sections 2 and 3; 32 CFR chapter I subchapter C (DoDGARs).

rfo.notes: 10 U.S.C. 4022(a)(2) re-read on law.cornell.edu 14 Sep 2026: over $100M to $500M the head of the contracting activity (or the DARPA, DIU or MDA director); over $500M the senior procurement executive (or those directors) plus 30 days written notice to the congressional defense committees; (d)(1) conditions and (f) follow-on production confirmed. AO qualifications (CON 0660 and CON 2880V or equivalent, data-rights and IP knowledge, hold or have held a commensurate KO or GO warrant; warrant threshold applies to FAR and non-FAR instruments) confirmed against the Army Warranting Program Policy v12 source file. Statutes are unchanged by the RFO. The DoD OT Guide edition date (2023) was not re-verified.

OT = statutory non-procurement instrument: 10 U.S.C. 4021 (research), 4022 (prototype), 4022(f) follow-on production without further competition
Signed by a warranted Agreements Officer; Army AO qualifications include OT courses, IP and data-rights knowledge, and a prior KO or GO warrant; value counts against the warrant

Negotiated terms, no CDA, limited GAO review (4 CFR 21.5(m)); fiscal law, ethics and warrant limits still apply

question: What are the differences between Grants and Contracts?
answer:
A grant or cooperative agreement’s principal purpose is to transfer a thing of value to the recipient to carry out a public purpose of support or stimulation authorized by a law of the United States. A contract’s principal purpose is to acquire property or services for the direct benefit or use of the Federal Government.
----------------------------
Grant agreement: 
(1) The principal purpose is to stimulate or support a public purpose, is authorized by statute; and

(2) Substantial involvement is not expected between the agency and the recipient. 

Procurement contract:
The principal purpose is to acquire (by purchase, lease, or barter) property or services for the direct benefit or use of the United States Government.

question: What are the various types of Other Transactions?
answer:
Three types of OT agreements: Research, Prototype, and Production

a. Research OTs (sometimes referred to as “original” or science and technology (S&T) OTs) are authorized under 10 U.S.C. §4021 for basic, applied, and advanced research projects. These OTs were intended to spur dual-use research and development (R&D), taking advantage of economies of scale without burdening companies with Government regulatory overhead, which would make them non-competitive in the commercial (non-defense) sector. Traditional defense contractors were also encouraged to engage in Research OTs, particularly if they sought to adopt commercial practices or standards, diversify into the commercial sector, or partner with non defense contractor.

**When using Technology Investment Agreements (TIAs), be sure to read this guide in conjunction with the DoD Grant and Agreement Regulations (DoDGARs) — see Part 21 of Title 32 of the Code of Federal Regulations (32 CFR Part 21).

b. Prototype OTs (sometimes referred to as “2371b” or “prototype project” OTs) are authorized under 10 U.S.C. §4022 to acquire prototype capabilities and allow for those prototypes to transition into Production OTs. Both dual-use and defense specific projects are encouraged under section 4022. Per statute, successful Prototype OTs offer a streamlined method for transitioning into follow-on production without competition.
Note: The solicitation and original Prototype OT agreement shall include notice that a follow-on Production OT is possible to allow greater flexibility to those Government organizations planning to leverage production efforts without re-competing. This should also increase competition and reduce the risk of future protest.

c. Production OTs are authorized under 10 U.S.C. §4022(f) as noncompetitive, follow-on OTs to a Prototype OT agreement that was competitively awarded and successfully completed. 
Note: This statute requires that advanced consideration be given and notice be made of the potential for a follow-on OT; this is a necessary precondition for a follow-on Production OT. As such, solicitation documents and the Prototype OT agreement shall include notice that a follow-on Production OT is possible.

Cite: 10 U.S.C. 4021; 10 U.S.C. 4022; 10 U.S.C. 4022(f); 32 CFR Part 21 (DoDGARs).

question: How would you describe the business acumen needed to negotiate, award and administer OTs?
answer:

question: What is a Non-Traditional Defense Contractor?
answer:
Section 815 of the 2016 NDAA defines A nontraditional defense contractor, with respect to a procurement or with respect to a transaction authorized under section 4021(a) or 4022 of this title, means an entity that is not currently performing and has not performed, for at least the one-year period preceding the solicitation of sources by the Department of Defense for the procurement or transaction, any contract or subcontract for the Department of Defense that is subject to full coverage under the cost accounting standards prescribed pursuant to section 1502 of title 41 and the regulations implementing such section.

question: What is the difference between a grant and a cooperative agreement? Provide an example of when a grant and cooperative agreement are most appropriate.
answer:
Grant: 31 USC 6304 (Grants) states the principal purpose of the relationship is to transfer a thing of value to the state or local government or other recipient to carry out a public purpose of support or stimulation. Additionally, substantial involvement is not expected between the executive agency and the state, local government or other recipient when carrying out the activity contemplated in the agreement.
Cooperative Agreement: 31 USC 6305 (Cooperative Agreements) states the principal purpose of the relationship is to transfer a thing of value to the State, local government, or other recipient to carry out a public purpose of support or stimulation authorized by a law of the United States instead of acquiring (by purchase, lease, or barter) property or services for the direct benefit or use of the United States Government. Substantial involvement is expected between the executive agency and the State, local government, or other recipient when carrying out the activity contemplated in the agreement.

Cite: 31 U.S.C. 6304; 31 U.S.C. 6305.

question: What do you envision is the role of the Program Manager/GOR? What authorities does the Program Manager/GOR have vs. the authority of the Grants Officer?
answer:
The GOR/PM serves as the technical point of contact with the recipient and maintains a current and informed of the progress of the award to ensure that the work being performed is consistent with what was proposed in the application. The GOR also advises and assists the Grants Officer in administering the award as it pertains to technical issues. The GOR must advise the Grants Officer in a timely manner on all matters relating to the recipient’s performance, especially work scope or funding issues that arise which may require modifications to the award. Other aspects include, but are not limited to, reviewing reports and other products, coordinating program management decisions as they bear on the award, and assisting with the review of final closing documents.

The Grants Officer is the person delegated with the authority to officially issue and modify awards, as well as grant approvals for exceptions (i.e. extended time for report submission). While the GOR advises the GO, the GO has the ultimate authority for decisions related to the award.

question: Describe how you would deal with a recipient that is failing to meet the reporting requirements as well as other technical requirements outlined in the terms of the award?
answer: Determine the contact that has been made by the specialist and the GOR/PM regarding delinquent reports and or other technical issues. Official notification, in writing, should be send to the recipient outlining the failures to meet the T&C, what actions must be taken to come into compliance, and a time frame to do so. The notification should also state the enforcement action that will be taken if compliance is not achieved (i.e. suspension of payments). If the recipient continues to be non-compliant the Government can terminate for material failure to comply.

question: Describe the steps you would take to assist a Grants Specialist in determining if a recipient meets the risk review criteria outlined in 2CFR200?
answer:
Review the requirements outlined in 2 CFR 200. 206, Federal awarding agency review of risk posed by applicants. Consider all of the information available through FAPIIS. Has the organization or PI been suspended or debarred? Is there other negative information included in FAPIIS, regarding termination and reason for termination?
Other areas to consider for review include (these are specifically pulled from 2 CFR 200):
Financial stability. Financial stability;
Management systems and standards. Quality of management systems and ability to meet the management standards.
History of performance. The applicant's record in managing Federal awards, if it is a prior recipient of Federal awards, including timeliness of compliance with applicable reporting requirements, conformance to the terms and conditions of previous Federal awards, and if applicable, the extent to which any previously awarded amounts will be expended prior to future awards;
Audit reports and findings. Reports and findings from audits performed under subpart F of this part or the reports and findings of any other available audits; and
Ability to effectively implement requirements. The applicant's ability to effectively implement statutory, regulatory, or other requirements imposed on non-Federal entities.
Risk-based requirements adjustment. The Federal awarding agency may adjust requirements when a risk-evaluation indicates that it may be merited either pre-award or post-award.
Suspension and debarment compliance. These provisions restrict Federal awards, subawards and contracts with certain parties that are debarred, suspended or otherwise excluded from or ineligible for participation in Federal programs or activities.
After a review of all information, if there is question of risk, consider discussion with leadership, advising attorney and policy. If the risk is too serious we can opt to not make the award. If the risk can be mitigated with award specific conditions, apply those as appropriate (i.e. more frequent reporting, reimbursement of payments)

Cite: 2 CFR 200.206; 2 CFR 200 subpart F.

question: Explain what strategic sourcing is. Are you aware of any strategic sources? How is this related to recent policy to conduct and submit a Business Case Analysis (BCA) for review and approval? What dollar thresholds apply to this requirement?
answer:
Strategic sourcing is the collaborative, structured process of analyzing what an organization spends and using that spend data to buy commodities and services more effectively: aggregate common requirements across the enterprise, standardize them, compete them once with the Government's full buying power, cut duplicate contract vehicles, manage the supplier relationship, and measure the savings. Today it lives inside category management, OMB Memorandum M-19-13 and DoD's category management roles and responsibilities, which measure spend under management and push us to Best-in-Class vehicles before we create our own. The newest Government-wide policy is Executive Order 14240 of 20 March 2025, Eliminating Waste and Saving Taxpayer Dollars by Consolidating Procurement, which directs GSA to consolidate domestic procurement of common goods and services and makes the GSA Administrator the executive agent for all information technology GWACs; OMB implemented it by memorandum in 2025. For a KO that raises the bar even higher for standing up a new Army vehicle for common goods, services or IT.

Strategic sources I use or steer customers to:
- GSA Federal Strategic Sourcing Initiative BPAs and the Best-in-Class solutions built on the Multiple Award Schedule, plus GWACs like OASIS+, Alliant 2 and NASA SEWP.
- Army CHESS, the Army's designated source for commercial IT hardware, software and services, and the DoD Enterprise Software Initiative.
- DLA supply chains and prime vendor programs, and the mandatory sources at RFO FAR 8.102 and 8.103: agency inventory, excess, Federal Prison Industries and AbilityOne. RFO FAR 8.104 tells me to use an existing government-wide contract when it is designated required use.
- Our own enterprise vehicles: Army multiple-award IDIQs for services and base operations, and in an OCONUS brigade like the 411th, theater-wide BPAs and IDIQs, which I would confirm with the local policy shop.

The BCA connection: before an agency stands up a new contract vehicle it has to show that the vehicle beats what already exists. Section 865 of the FY2009 NDAA requires a business case for any multi-agency contract, addressing administration, all direct and indirect costs, and the effect on the Government's ability to leverage its purchasing power; that is now RFO FAR 17.502-1(b). OFPP's 29 September 2011 memorandum on business cases set the thresholds: a business case for every new or renewed GWAC regardless of value, and for covered multi-agency contracts, agency-specific contracts and BPAs that would create significant usage by other agencies or significant overlap, defined as roughly 25 percent, with FSSI, SmartBUY or an existing GWAC, when the estimated value is 250 million dollars or more for solicitations released in fiscal 2012, 100 million in fiscal 2013, and 50 million from fiscal 2014 on. The business case is approved no lower than the Senior Procurement Executive, posted to OMB MAX, and GWAC cases go to OMB itself. In the Army, AFARS 5137.590-6, acquisition strategy content, requires a services acquisition strategy to address opportunities for strategic sourcing, describe how category management was applied and analyze existing spend-under-management contracts; it does not use the term business case analysis. The related consolidation and bundling analysis is RFO FAR 7.107: a written determination for consolidation over 2 million and substantial bundling at 8 million for DoD, with AFARS 5107.107-2 putting consolidation approvals at the HCA from 2 million up to 500 million and at DASA(P) at 500 million and above.

What I would confirm before I quote a number at the board: whether ASA(ALT) or ACC has a current Army-specific BCA threshold and routing for new enterprise vehicles, because that policy has changed more than once and I could not verify a current Army dollar figure.

question: You receive a pricing report (inclusive of the technical evaluation) for a government recommended position on direct labor costs which reflects an amount that is significantly lower than the proposed amount. What might you rely upon in the development of your objective position and/or what you might seek during negotiations to support a movement towards an objective position?

The Contracting Officer should consider the data source for direct labor costs in the pricing report before making a decision concerning the objective position. The Contracting Officer may want to check other data sources (Bureau of Labor Statistics, Global Insight, etc..) for direct labor costs. Ideally, the Contracting Officer required the company to submit a spreadsheet and cost narrative for the Government to analyze/validate during proposal evaluation. question: What is CONSOLIDATION?
answer:
Consolidation is combining two or more requirements that were previously provided or performed under separate smaller contracts, or that are reasonably likely to be, into a single solicitation for a single contract or a multiple-award contract. It is a statutory concept from 15 U.S.C. 657q, and it exists because combining requirements shrinks the field to the firms big enough to do all of it - which is usually bad for small business and, over time, bad for the industrial base.

I keep three terms distinct.
- Consolidation is about combining previously separate requirements, whatever the reason; the written-determination trigger is dollar-based, above $2 million.
- Bundling is the subset where the combined requirement is likely to be unsuitable for award to a small business because of its diversity, size or specialized nature, its aggregate value, its geographic dispersion, or a combination. Any bundling needs the determination, regardless of value.
- Substantial bundling is bundling at or above $8 million for DoD, including options, and it carries extra strategy documentation and the solicitation provision.

The rule I have to satisfy. Before I consolidate or bundle, RFO FAR 7.107-1(a) makes me do market research, identify alternatives with less consolidation, coordinate with the Office of Small Business Programs, identify any negative impact on small business, and take steps to include small business in the strategy. Then, above $2 million for consolidation or for any bundling, the senior procurement executive or chief acquisition officer has to determine in writing that it is necessary and justified - meaning the benefits substantially exceed the benefits of each alternative approach. Substantial is defined: financial benefits equal to ten percent of the estimated contract or order value including options when that value is $94 million or less, or five percent or $9.4 million, whichever is greater, above $94 million. Benefits that cannot be quantified in dollars still have to be specifically identified. Reduced administrative or personnel cost alone is not enough unless the savings are substantial. If the benefits are not substantial but the requirement is mission-critical and the strategy maximizes small business participation, only the SPE - for DoD, non-delegably - can make the determination.

I also owe notifications and coordination: notify each incumbent small business at least 30 days before the solicitation, publish the determination in SAM.gov, work early with the small business professional and the SBA procurement center representative, give SBA the justification on request, and put the provision at 52.207-6 in a multiple-award solicitation above the substantial bundling threshold. The DoD supplement adds a SAM.gov notice of intent to bundle at least 30 days before release. Any subcontracting plan expectations and any line-item or multiple-award structure should let small businesses compete for a piece.

Leadership angle. Consolidation is often the right answer for the Government - fewer interfaces, better leverage, one accountable prime. My responsibility is not to prevent it, it is to make sure the decision is made on analysis rather than convenience, that the alternatives were genuinely tested, and that the determination would survive a protest and a look from SBA.

Cite: RFO FAR 7.107-1 (required steps; written-determination triggers at (b): consolidation above $2 million, any bundling, substantial bundling at $8 million or more for DoD), RFO FAR 7.107-2 (SPE/CAO determination at (a), benefit tests at (c)(3), administrative-cost rule at (d), mission-critical exception at (e)), RFO FAR 7.107-3 (notifications), RFO FAR 7.107-4 (provision 52.207-6), RFO FAR 2.101 (definitions), RFO FAR 19.102 (coordination with SBA and procurement center representatives); DFARS 207.107-370 (DoD bundling notice, RFO Class Deviation 2026-O0020 Rev. 1); 15 U.S.C. 657q and 644(e).

The draft described substantial bundling only as 'the agency's published threshold' - the DoD figure is now stated - and had not mentioned the 7.107-1(a) preconditions or the 7.107-2(e) exception. DFARS 207.107-370 read from the RFO DFARS Part 207 deviation PDF (2026-O0020 Rev. 1, 2 Sep 2026; text extracted locally); that deviation has no DoD consolidation-approval section (legacy 207.170 is now public-private competitions), so no DoD approval authority beyond FAR 7.107-2 applies. The legacy DFARS 205.205-70 origin of the bundling notice is stated from the deviation memo's 'relocates bundling notification criteria from DFARS part 205' wording.

Distinguish consolidation (determination above $2 million) from bundling (unsuitable for small business; determination at any value) and substantial bundling ($8 million or more for DoD, including options) - RFO FAR 7.107-1(b).

Before consolidating: market research, alternatives, OSBP coordination, small business impact and inclusion (7.107-1(a)); then a written SPE or CAO determination that benefits substantially exceed each alternative (7.107-2(a)).

'Substantial' is defined at 7.107-2(c)(3): 10 percent of value including options at $94 million or less; 5 percent or $9.4 million, whichever is greater, above $94 million; unquantifiable benefits must still be identified.
Administrative or personnel savings alone do not justify it (7.107-2(d)); the mission-critical exception belongs to the SPE only, non-delegable in DoD (7.107-2(e)).

Notify incumbent small businesses 30 days before solicitation, publish the determination in SAM.gov, coordinate with the SB professional and SBA PCR, use 52.207-6 above the substantial bundling threshold (7.107-3, 7.107-4); DoD adds a 30-day SAM.gov notice of intent to bundle (DFARS 207.107-370).

question: How can CONSOLIDATION be beneficial to the Government?
answer:
Consolidation is combining two or more requirements previously performed under separate, smaller contracts into one solicitation. It is beneficial when the whole is genuinely worth more than the parts, and the FAR makes us prove it.

The benefits to the Government are the ones RFO FAR 7.107-2 lists and expects us to quantify:
- Cost savings or price reduction through volume, one set of overhead, and fewer transitions.
- Quality improvements that save time or enhance performance or efficiency.
- Shorter acquisition cycle time - one competition instead of five.
- Better terms and conditions.
Beyond the statutory list, consolidation gives me one accountable contractor instead of seams between vendors on the same installation, a single QASP and COR structure, standardized performance across sites, real leverage in negotiations, less workload for an office that cannot run five source selections, and fewer expiring options and bridges to manage. One base operations contract with clear performance standards is easier to hold to account than five contracts that point at each other.

The discipline. Under RFO FAR 7.107-1 I must conduct market research first, identify the alternative contracting approaches, coordinate with the small business specialist and SBA, assess the impact on small business participation, and for a consolidation over two million dollars obtain a written determination that it is necessary and justified, 7.107-1(b). Under 7.107-2 the senior procurement executive or chief acquisition officer, or the Army official delegated that authority, determines that the benefits substantially exceed those of the alternatives - ten percent of the estimated value up to ninety-four million, five percent or nine point four million above that, 7.107-2(c)(3) - and the benefits are quantified from the market research, not asserted; under 7.107-2(d) administrative or personnel savings alone do not carry the determination. If the consolidated requirement is also bundling, meaning it is unsuitable for award to a small business that was doing or could do part of it, substantial bundling at the DoD threshold of eight million or more, 7.107-1(b)(3), adds the 7.107-2(c)(6) analysis of the small business impact and mitigation, and under 7.107-3 I notify the incumbent small businesses thirty days before the solicitation and the determination is published in the GPE.

As a leader I look at the other side of the ledger. Consolidation concentrates risk: one default takes out everything, entry barriers rise, and small firms lose work. So my mitigation is deliberate: set aside the consolidated requirement or a portion for small business where the market supports it; include the 7.107-4 provision so small business teams and joint ventures can compete; structure CLINs or a multiple-award vehicle so partial set-asides remain possible; and put teeth in the subcontracting plan. Consolidation is a tool; the justification is the check that it serves the mission and the industrial base, not just our convenience.

Cite: RFO FAR 7.107-1(b), 7.107-2(c)(3), (c)(6), (d), 7.107-3, 7.107-4; 15 U.S.C. 657q; 15 U.S.C. 644(e); 13 CFR 125.2(d); RFO FAR Part 19.

Practical benefits: one accountable contractor, one QASP/COR structure, fewer seams, negotiation leverage, less workload and fewer bridges.
