question: When can a Contractor request a debriefing and what consists of the debriefing? What cannot be disclosed in the debrief?
answer: An offeror, upon its written request received by the agency within 3 days after the date on which that offeror has received notification of contract award, shall be debriefed. The debriefing should include: 1) overall evaluated cost or price and applicable ratings, 2) description of strengths, deficiencies, weaknesses and past performance rating, 3) Overall evaluated Cost or Price, including unit prices, and applicable ratings of successful offeror, 4) strengths, weaknesses and past performance ratings of successful offeror, 5) overall ranking, 6) Redacted Source Selection Decision Document, 7) For commercial items, the make and model of successful offeror’s item. The debriefing should not include: 1) Cost/price of other unsuccessful offerors, 2) Names of unsuccessful offeror, 3) Point by point comparison with other offerors, 4) Trade secrets, privileged, confidential information, commercial, financial information that is privileged or confidential such as cost breakdowns, profits, rates, any other proprietary information, etc., names of individuals providing past performance information.

rfo.notes: No FAR/DFARS/AFARS/PGI/U.S.C./CFR citation and no FAR part or subpart named in words in the answer text; nothing to renumber. Included for coverage audit only. Paraphrases debriefing rules (RFO FAR 15.301) but names no section, so it is left alone per the skip rule.

question: What is the protest decision time period for GAO?
answer:
GAO must issue its decision within 100 days after the protest is filed. That is statutory, 31 U.S.C. 3554(a)(1), and it is in GAO's bid protest regulations at 4 CFR 21.9(a). Under the express option, which GAO may use for protests suitable for quick resolution, the decision is due within 65 days (31 U.S.C. 3554(a)(2); 4 CFR 21.10). Days are calendar days, and a deadline that falls on a weekend or federal holiday rolls to the next business day.

Inside that 100 days, here is the clock that drives me as the KO:
- Filing: solicitation challenges before the closing date; other grounds within 10 days after the basis was known or should have been known, or, where a debriefing is requested and required, within 10 days after the debriefing (4 CFR 21.2).
- The stay: notice from GAO before award means no award; notice within 10 days after award or 5 days after the offered debriefing date, whichever is later, means I suspend performance or terminate, unless the HCA makes the nondelegable override finding (RFO FAR 33.105-2 and 33.105-3).
- Agency report: due 30 days after GAO's notice of the protest (4 CFR 21.3(c)); protester comments 10 days after the report (21.3(i)), and failure to comment means dismissal. Supplemental protests are usually decided inside the original 100 days.
- Outcome: sustain, deny, or dismiss. GAO's recommendations are not binding, but if the agency does not fully implement them within 60 days, the HCA must report the failure to GAO within 5 days after that, and GAO reports to Congress (RFO FAR 33.105-4(b); 31 U.S.C. 3554(e)). GAO can also recommend payment of protest costs and proposal preparation costs.
- Corrective action: if we find a defect early, taking corrective action gets the protest dismissed as academic, which beats a sustain.

Practical point for the board: 100 days is the outside limit, but with a stay in place the requirement waits three-plus months. So on day one I get legal engaged, confirm the stay status, and work bridge coverage or the HCA override package with the customer. Under the RFO, the 100-day and 65-day figures live in statute and 4 CFR part 21, not in FAR part 33.

Cite: 31 U.S.C. 3554(a)(1), (a)(2), (e); 4 CFR 21.2, 21.3(c) and (i), 21.9, 21.10; RFO FAR 33.105-2, 33.105-3, 33.105-4(b).

question: Does the Govt incur interests on claims? Explain
answer:
Yes. Under the Contract Disputes Act, 41 U.S.C. 7109, the Government pays interest on a contractor's claim from the date the contracting officer receives a proper claim, or from the date payment would otherwise be due if that is later, until the date of payment. The FAR implementation is RFO FAR 33.205-3, which used to be 33.208. The rate is the one the Secretary of the Treasury sets and publishes every six months for CDA purposes; it is simple interest, and it keeps running through the KO's decision period, the appeal at the ASBCA and any litigation at the Court of Federal Claims.

The details a Class III KO should know:
- Interest only runs on a proper claim: a written demand, as a matter of right, for a sum certain, and certified if it is over 100,000 dollars (RFO FAR 33.205-2). A request for equitable adjustment or an undisputed invoice is not a claim; the day the contractor converts it into a claim is the day the interest clock starts.
- A defective certification does not stop interest. If the contractor corrects it, interest still runs from the date I originally received the claim (RFO FAR 33.205-3(c), carrying legacy 33.208(c); the correction rule itself is 41 U.S.C. 7103(b)(3)).
- My 60-day decision window under RFO FAR 33.205-6(c) does not pause interest, so slow-rolling a claim costs the Army money. That is a real incentive to resolve legitimate claims quickly, ideally through negotiation or ADR under 33.205-8.
- If the claim goes to judgment, principal and interest are paid from the Judgment Fund under 31 U.S.C. 1304 and the Army then reimburses the fund from its own appropriations (41 U.S.C. 7108); if I settle it, it is paid from the contract's funds. Either way it is a cost of the dispute.
- CDA interest is different from Prompt Payment Act interest. Prompt Payment interest under 31 U.S.C. 3901 and RFO FAR 32.907 is an automatic penalty for paying a proper, undisputed invoice late. Once an amount is in dispute and becomes a claim, the CDA interest rules apply instead; the contractor does not collect both on the same dollars.

And it runs the other way too. On a Government claim, a contract debt, RFO FAR 32.608-1 and the Interest clause at 52.232-17 charge the contractor simple interest on any amount still unpaid 30 days after my demand, computed from the date of the demand, at the same Treasury rate under 41 U.S.C. 7109; it is not a different rate.

Cite: 41 U.S.C. 7109, 7103(b)(3) and 7108; RFO FAR 33.205-3 and 33.205-3(c) (was 33.208), 33.205-2, 33.205-6(c), 33.205-8; RFO FAR 32.907; 31 U.S.C. 3901; RFO FAR 32.608-1 and FAR 52.232-17; 31 U.S.C. 1304.

question: A KO is notified that a protest has been filed with GAO, what steps shall the KO and agency take in response to the protest?
answer:
The first thing I do is note the date and time GAO notified the agency, because every other clock runs from it - and I log the protest in the PIEE Protest Tracker, which DoD requires.

Preaward. If GAO notifies the agency of a protest before award, I do not award while the protest is pending. The only exception is a written finding by the head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, that urgent and compelling circumstances significantly affecting the interests of the United States will not permit waiting for GAO's decision and that award is likely to occur within 30 days of the finding. Best interests of the Government is not a preaward ground. The agency notifies GAO of the finding before award.

Postaward. If GAO's notice arrives within the stay window, I immediately direct the contractor to suspend performance, or I terminate the award. In DoD the window is the latest of: 10 days after award; 10 days after an order over $35 million is issued; 5 days after the debriefing date offered under a timely debriefing request, whether or not the protester accepted that date; or 5 days after an enhanced postaward debriefing concludes. Performance may continue or resume only on a written HCA finding, again nondelegable, that performance is in the best interests of the United States or that urgent and compelling circumstances will not permit waiting, with notice to GAO. I brief my chain before recommending an override, because overrides get challenged in the Court of Federal Claims.

Then the agency actions.
- Notify the awardee, or the offerors with a reasonable prospect of award if there is no award yet, that a protest was filed, and put the suspension direction to the contractor in writing.
- Preserve the record immediately - lock the evaluation materials, tell evaluators and the source selection authority to retain everything including emails and notes, and suspend routine destruction.
- Work with counsel to produce the agency report, due 30 days after GAO's notice under 4 CFR 21.3, including the contracting officer's statement of facts and the relevant documents; GAO may set a shorter schedule under the express option.
- Consider corrective action honestly and early. If the protest has merit, reevaluating, amending the solicitation, or terminating and reawarding is cheaper and faster than defending a bad record, and I make that recommendation to the chain rather than defending my own work out of pride.
- Track the outcome: GAO decides within 100 days of filing, or 65 under the express option. If GAO sustains, it recommends a remedy, and may recommend the protester recover protest and proposal preparation costs. If the agency has not fully implemented the recommendation within 60 days, the HCA reports to GAO within 5 more days, and GAO reports non-compliance to Congress.
- For a protested acquisition of $1 billion or more, DoD also requires a briefing to DPCAP within 10 days of filing.

One Class III note on orders: GAO's jurisdiction over orders under multiple-award contracts is limited. For DoD, a protest of an order is allowed only if the order exceeds the scope, period or maximum value of the contract, or the order is valued over $35 million - and on that second ground GAO has exclusive jurisdiction. So the first question on an order protest is whether GAO can hear it at all.

Cite: RFO FAR 33.105-2 (preaward: nondelegable HCA finding, urgent and compelling plus award within 30 days), 33.105-3 (postaward stay, 10-day / 5-day window, nondelegable HCA override on best-interests or urgent-and-compelling grounds), 33.105-4 (other procedures; 60-day implementation report); RFO FAR 33.104 series for agency-level protests; DFARS 233.105-70 (DoD stay windows, including orders over $35 million and enhanced debriefings) and 233.170 (Protest Tracker; $1 billion briefing), per RFO Class Deviation 2026-O0026 Rev. 1; 31 U.S.C. 3551-3556 and 4 CFR Part 21 (21.3 agency report, 21.8 costs, 21.9 and 21.10 decision periods); 10 U.S.C. 3406(f) (order protests).

rfo.notes: Reviewed 14 Sep 2026. 33.105-2 and 33.105-3 override text quoted from the RFO Part 33 page (HCA, nondelegable; preaward = urgent and compelling AND award likely within 30 days; postaward = best interests OR urgent and compelling). The draft's preaward override wrongly included a 'best interests' ground and allowed an HCA 'designee' - both corrected. DoD stay windows, the $35 million order figure, the Protest Tracker and the $1 billion briefing read from the RFO DFARS Part 233 deviation PDF (2026-O0026 Rev. 1, 24 Aug 2026; text extracted locally). The 30-day report and 100-day / 65-day periods rest on 4 CFR 21 (the RFO FAR text does not restate them per the project crosswalk note); the 60-day / 5-day implementation report was read on the RFO page.

key_points: Record the date and time of GAO's notice - every deadline runs from it - and log the protest in the PIEE Protest Tracker (DFARS 233.170(c)).

Preaward: no award while the protest is pending unless the HCA, nondelegably, finds in writing urgent and compelling circumstances AND that award is likely within 30 days; 'best interests' is not a preaward ground (RFO FAR 33.105-2).

Postaward: immediately suspend performance if GAO's notice arrives in the stay window - in DoD the latest of 10 days after award, 10 days after an order over $35 million, 5 days after an offered debriefing date, or 5 days after an enhanced debriefing concludes (RFO FAR 33.105-3; DFARS 233.105-70); override only by a nondelegable HCA finding of best interests or urgent and compelling circumstances.
Immediately preserve the record - lock evaluation materials, direct evaluators and the SSA to retain notes and emails, suspend routine destruction; notify the awardee or prospective awardees.
Agency report with counsel within 30 days of GAO notice (4 CFR 21.3), shorter under the express option; GAO decides within 100 days, 65 under express (4 CFR 21.9, 21.10).

Evaluate corrective action early and honestly; on a sustain GAO recommends a remedy and possibly costs; if not fully implemented within 60 days the HCA reports to GAO within 5 days and GAO reports to Congress (RFO FAR 33.105-4; 31 U.S.C. 3554(e)).

question: What are the differences between apparent, implied and express authority?
answer:
Apparent authority is the power of an agent to act on behalf of a principal, even though not expressly or impliedly granted. This power arises only if a third party reasonably infers, from the principal's conduct, that the principal granted such power to the agent.
Implied authority refers to an agent with the jurisdiction to perform acts that are reasonably necessary to accomplish the purpose of an organization. Under contract law, implied authority figures have the ability to make a legally binding contract on behalf of another person or company.
Express authority is agent's power to act on behalf of a principal, explicitly granted by an agreement between the agent and principal.

question: As the Contracting Officer on a source selection you recently sent out the notice to unsuccessful offerors and have received several requests for debriefings. Some of the requests are for pre-award debriefs and some are for post award debriefs. What are the things you may/may not tell the offerors in the debriefings?
answer:
The rule of thumb: I can tell an offeror everything about its own proposal and the outcome, and nothing about the other offerors' proposals except the summary results the FAR specifically allows.

Preaward debriefings under RFO FAR 15.206-2 are for offerors excluded from the competitive range or otherwise eliminated before award. They must request within three days of the exclusion notice. I may delay the debriefing until after award if the offeror asks or if delay is in the Government's interest, and it then becomes a postaward debriefing. What I may say: the agency's evaluation of the significant elements in that offeror's proposal, a summary of the rationale for eliminating it, and reasonable answers to questions about whether the source selection procedures in the RFP and regulations were followed. What I may not say: the number of offerors, the identity of the other offerors, the content of their proposals, the ranking of the other offerors, the evaluation of the other offerors, or anything barred from a postaward debriefing.

Postaward debriefings under RFO FAR 15.301-1 are for offerors that stayed in the competition. Request within three days of the award notice; I debrief within five days where practicable. What I may say: the Government's evaluation of the significant weaknesses or deficiencies in that offeror's proposal; the overall evaluated cost or price and technical rating of the successful offeror and of the debriefed offeror, plus the debriefed offeror's past performance information; the overall ranking of all offerors when one was developed; a summary of the rationale for award; for commercial products, the make and model of the successful offeror's item; and reasonable answers to relevant questions. What I may not say: point-by-point comparisons with other proposals; trade secrets and proprietary manufacturing processes; cost breakdowns, profit, indirect cost rates and similar confidential financial data; and the names of the individuals who gave past performance references.

For DoD there is more, and under the RFO DFARS the debriefing rules moved from 215.506 to 215.301. question: You receive a letter from a contractor requesting a no cost time extension. The contractor states that he is behind schedule due to his subcontractor’s slow progress. He says it is an “Excusable Delay” because the delay is not the fault of the prime contractor. How would you respond?

▪ A subcontractor’s slow progress is not an excusable delay.

question: Address which federal statutes or regulations apply to Other Transactions.
answer: OT authorities are authorized by law with clear statutory guidelines. Generally, the statutes and regulations applicable to acquisition and assistance do not apply to OTs. Since OTs are defined in the negative—they are NOT procurement contracts, grants, or cooperative agreements—any statute, regulation, or policy that applies solely to these types of contractual arrangements will not apply to OTs. However, statutes and regulations applicable to acquisition and assistance are only a subset of all federal statutes or regulations. Laws and regulations that are unrelated to the acquisition or assistance process will still apply to OTs. These can include, but are not limited to, appropriations, security, export control, socio-economic, and criminal laws.

question: What are some benefits of Partnering?
answer: Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs) are broadly defined in the DoD as, “voluntary, noncontractual collaborations between DoD and non-federal entities (NFEs) through which both parties leverage the expertise, resources and incentives of the other to achieve mutually agreed goals.”3 In the arena of integrated product support, a public-private partnership is defined as a cooperative arrangement between an organic product support provider and one or more privatesector entities to perform defense-related work, utilize DoD facilities and equipment, or both. Other government organizations, such as program offices, inventory control points, and sustainment commands, may be parties to such agreements. 4 There is a key distinction between partnerships and defense contracts. All partnerships are implemented within the framework and business arrangements established by a contract between the DoD and a private-sector entity (e.g., an original equipment manufacturer [OEM], small business, or other third-party logistics provider [3PL]). Defense contracts specify the work tasks, articles, services, and outcomes to be provided by the private-sector entity. They are generally one-sided in their directive requirements—from the government to the contractor. Partnerships enable a more collaborative relationship in which parties from both public and private-sectors are able to leverage and maximize the use of their resources in ways that were not specified in their underlying contracts. Resources may include goods, services, infrastructure, products, personnel, or processes employed to more efficiently and effectively accomplish product support. Examples range from allowing contractors to utilize depot maintenance facilities, to workshare agreements in which joint organic-contractor teams join forces on a common workload, to contractor purchase of government-provided products and services. The parties may be separately funded by defense contracts or work orders. Depending on the type of cooperative arrangement, the partnership may entail payment between the partners for goods and services produced, when authorized by law.

question: Who funds the depot/arsenal in a Direct Sale and when?
answer: Direct Sale (sales of articles and services)─An arrangement, currently authorized primarily for depot maintenance activities designated as centers of industrial and technical excellence (CITEs), arsenals and ammunition plants, and other working capital–funded industrial facilities under specified circumstances, whereby military and commercial entities enter into a business relationship for the sale of depot maintenance articles or services to an outside (non-government) entity, usually a contractor. A direct sale agreement begins with a government contract that funds a commercial activity. In turn, after development of a partnership agreement with an appropriate implementing agreement, the contractor pays an organic depot maintenance activity (or other industrially funded activity as authorized) for goods and services provided to the contractor. Depending on the legal authority applied, the funds may be paid to the U.S. Treasury or directly to the depot’s working capital fund. The contractor may also supply materiel to the depots in support of the partnership. The purchase of articles or services by the commercial entity establishes a quasi-subcontract relationship for the depot, which ensures (as authorized by law) the depot can be held accountable for willful misconduct, gross negligence, or the failure of the government to comply with cost, schedule, or performance requirements in the contract agreement.

question: Please explain about the Defense Base Act and it's requirement for insurance.
answer:
The Defense Base Act provides workers' compensation protection to civilian employees working outside the United States on U.S. military bases or under a contract with the U.S. government for public works or for national defense. Federal law requires all U.S. government contractors and subcontractors to secure workers' compensation insurance for their employees working overseas. The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) also sets out the workers' compensation insurance requirements for all overseas contracts at 48 CFR 28.305 (FAR 28.305), and at FAR 52.228-3 and FAR 52.228-4. Companies are required to purchase insurance to cover worker’s compensation benefits, disability, medical and death benefits before commencing performance. If an employer who fails to secure the payment of compensation when required shall be guilty of a misdemeanor and, upon conviction thereof, shall be punished by a fine of not more than $10,000 or by imprisonment for not more than one year, or both. And if the employer is a corporation, the president, secretary, and treasurer shall be also severally liable for such fine and imprisonment. Wavers must be approved by the Department of Labor. Waivers may be approved for a contract, subcontract, subordinate contract, work location, or classification of employee. question: What is the Logistics Cost Sharing Program?
answer: The Logistic Cost Sharing Program is a portion of the overall Special Measures Agreement (SMA), which is a defense cost-sharing program between the US and the ROK. Through this SMA, the ROK provides financial support for the expenses incurred in the stationing of United States Forces - Korea (USFK) on the peninsula. The LCS Program is a portion to partially offsets the logistical costs of USFK operations. Some of these logistical costs include, but not limited to, costs associated with the movement of personnel and assets, repair and maintenance of services, and purchase of non-tactical vehicles.

question: What are some unique aspects of LCS funds?

question: What is the Invited Contractor (IC) Program? Describe the four exceptions and the steps taken to obtain SOFA Invited Contractor (IC) status designation?
answer: All US Contractors supporting USFK contracts are required to obtain SOFA Designation through the FKAQ Invited Contracting Program. It is a two-step process. The first step, which is the KO's responsibility, is to obtain SOFA designation for the contract/order. The contracting officer must submit a request for contract SOFA designation to USFK/FKAQ. The contracting officer must review Article XV of the SOFA Agreement and USFKI 4901.01 for unique requirements for contract performance in the ROK. The second step, which is the RA's responsibility, is to obtain SOFA designation for individual contractor. There are four unique requirements for US contractor to perform in the ROK: security considerations, technical qualifications, unavailability of materials/services required by US standards, and limitations of US laws.

question:
Under FAR 12.603, when a written solicitation will be issued, the contracting officer may use what procedure to reduce the time required to solicit and award contracts for the acquisition of commercial items?

Under FAR 12.202, when a written solicitation will be issued, the contracting officer may use what procedure to reduce the time required to solicit and award contracts for the acquisition of commercial items?
answer:
Combined synopsis/solicitation procedure combines the synopsis required by 5.201(d) and the issuance of the solicitation into a single document. When using the combined synopsis/solicitation procedure, the SF 1449 is not used for issuing the solicitation. Synopsis prepared as described at 5.201(c).

RFO 12.202 Publicizing.
(a) Publicize in accordance with part 5.

(b) To reduce the time required to solicit and award contracts for acquisitions valued over the SAT, combine the presolicitation notice and solicitation notice required by part 5.

(1) Format. Select the “Combined Synopsis/Solicitation” format in the GPE, and include the following information:

(i) In the “Description” section, include the following statements:

This is a combined synopsis/solicitation for commercial products or commercial services prepared in accordance with part 12. This announcement constitutes the only solicitation. Offers are being requested and a separate written solicitation will not be issued.

Solicitation number [insert solicitation number] is issued as a [insert request for quotation (RFQ), request for proposal (RFP), or invitation for bid (IFB)] for [provide a brief description of the requirement].

This acquisition [is/is not] set-aside for small business concerns. This solicitation incorporates provisions and clauses by reference. The full text of provisions and clauses may be accessed electronically at www.acquisition.gov.

[If applicable, insert a statement regarding the Defense Priorities and Allocations System (DPAS) and assigned rating.]

(ii) A list of line-item number(s) and items, quantities, and units of measure (including option(s), if applicable).

(iii) Description of requirements for the items to be acquired, including documentation supporting any brand name descriptions (see 12.102).

(iv) Date(s) and place(s) of delivery and acceptance and f.o.b. point (see part 47).

(v) A list of solicitation provisions that apply to the acquisition (see 12.205(a)).

(vi) A list of contract clauses that apply to the acquisition (see 12.205(b)).

(vii) The date, time, and place for receipt of offer and point of contact.

(viii) Any other additional information required by 5.101(c).

(2) Response times. Set a response time that gives offerors a reasonable opportunity to respond, unless the acquisition is subject to the minimum time period for acquisitions covered by the World Trade Organization Government Procurement Agreement or a Free Trade Agreement (see subpart 5.2 and part 25).
Cite: RFO FAR 12.202; RFO FAR 12.202(b); RFO FAR 5.201(c); RFO FAR 5.201(d).

question: On a late Saturday evening at Osan Air Base, a major water line bursts in a motor pool. The facility manager panics and directly calls an off-base Korean plumbing company to fix the pipe immediately to prevent flooding. The company completes the work and submits an invoice for $18,000 (equivalent in KRW) on Monday morning. The facility manager brings you the invoice and asks you to "just pay it."
answer:
I do not just pay it, and I do not lecture the facility manager either; the pipe had to be fixed. But this is an unauthorized commitment. The facility manager had no authority to bind the Government, so the agreement is not binding until an official with authority ratifies it, and paying the invoice as if it were a contract would itself be improper. The $18,000 is above the micro-purchase threshold, and in any case the purchase card is a buying method for a cardholder with authority, not a way to pay for a commitment somebody made without authority.

What I do:
- Get the facts. Who called whom, what was ordered, what was done, and that the Government received the benefit: a repaired water line. Get the itemized invoice in KRW: weekend and emergency labor, hours, materials.
- Tell the facility manager the path is ratification and what he owes the package under AFARS 5101.602-3-90: a signed statement describing the circumstances and why normal contracting procedures were not followed, plus all orders and invoices. His commander verifies the facts, endorses it, and describes the measures taken to prevent recurrence.
- The package comes to the contracting office; the chief of the contracting office assigns a KO to review the facts and prepare a summary with a recommendation. That is my job. I determine whether the price is fair and reasonable, comparing it to our existing BOS or DPW emergency repair rates, an IGE, or a quick quote, and I check all six criteria in RFO FAR 1.405(c): the Government accepted the work or benefit, the ratifying official has authority to contract, the contract would otherwise have been proper if a KO had made it, the price is fair and reasonable, I recommend payment and legal concurs, and funds are available now and were available at the time. The resource manager certifies the funds; if they were not available then, this is potentially an Anti-Deficiency Act issue and I say so.
- Ratification authority: under RFO FAR 1.405(b)(2) the HCA may ratify and may delegate no lower than the chief of the contracting office; the Army's delegation levels are in AFARS Appendix GG. I confirm with the Chief, C&P which official ratifies an $18,000 action in the 411th.
- Once ratified, I issue the purchase order or contract to document the obligation and the invoice is paid through the servicing finance office. A Korean local firm is fine for this kind of local repair; the SOFA invited contractor program is for U.S. contractors, not Korean companies, but I confirm the vendor's registration and payment requirements with C&P and finance. If it cannot be ratified, RFO FAR 1.405(d) governs nonratifiable commitments and the vendor's remedy runs through legal as a claim under 31 U.S.C. 3702 authority, not my signature.
- Fix the root cause. The right call on Saturday night was the installation emergency service order channel, the existing DPW or base operations maintenance contract, or the contracting office's after-hours duty number. I offer the facility manager and his unit training on who has authority and what emergency options exist. And because Osan is an Air Force installation, I confirm which contracting activity actually has cognizance over that facility before I process the package.

Cite: RFO FAR 1.405; AFARS 5101.602-3 and 5101.602-3-90, Appendix GG; 31 U.S.C. 1341 (Anti-Deficiency Act) and 31 U.S.C. 3702; 411th CSB local ratification procedures (confirm with C&P).

rfo.notes: RFO FAR 1.405 (ratification authority at 1.405(b)(2), six criteria at 1.405(c), nonratifiable actions at 1.405(d)) is a verified crosswalk entry; AFARS 5101.602-3 and 5101.602-3-90 (HCA may ratify, see Appendix GG; individual's signed statement and invoices, commander endorsement with preventive measures and funding, KO summary and recommendation, ratifying official decision, HCA compliance monitoring) re-read on acquisition.gov 14 Sep 2026 (effective 11 Jul 2025). MPT $15,000 per the project thresholds file. The 411th's current ratification approval level, Osan installation contracting cognizance, and Korean-vendor registration and KRW payment mechanics are not in the sources and must be confirmed with C&P.

key_points: It is an unauthorized commitment: not binding until ratified; do not pay it as if it were a contract; above the MPT so the GPC is out
Package per AFARS 5101.602-3-90: individual's signed statement and invoices, commander's endorsement with prevention measures, KO summary and recommendation, legal concurrence
Check all six RFO FAR 1.405(c) criteria, especially fair and reasonable price and funds available then and now (ADA exposure if not)
Ratifying official: HCA or delegate, no lower than the chief of the contracting office (1.405(b)(2)); Army levels in AFARS Appendix GG; confirm the 411th level with C&P
After ratification, issue the order to obligate, then pay; if not ratifiable, the vendor's remedy is a 31 U.S.C. 3702 claim
Root cause: emergency service order channel, existing DPW contract or after-hours contracting; train the unit; confirm installation contracting cognizance at Osan

question:
You have just awarded a $150,000 contract for IT network equipment to Company A. You notify the unsuccessful bidder, Company B, of the award.
Three days after you notify them, Company B files a formal protest with the Government Accountability Office (GAO). They claim your evaluation of Company A's technical proposal was unfair and that Company A does not meet the requirements.
Immediate Actions: What is the very first thing you must do when you receive notice of the GAO protest?
Stop-Work Order: Are you required to stop the winning company (Company A) from performing the work? What dictates this timeline?
Agency Report: How long does your office have to pull together the official Agency Report to submit to the GAO?
answer:
Immediate actions. GAO notifies the agency within one day of the filing, and under RFO FAR 33.105-4(a) the very first thing I do on that notice is notify legal counsel and start assembling the record. In the 411th that means the supporting legal office and my Chief of Contracting, so the protest gets into the ACC and Army legal channel the same day; I confirm the exact routing with C&P. At the same time I give notice of the protest to Company A, the awardee, as 4 CFR 21.3(a) requires, I put a litigation hold on the file and the evaluators' notes, and I identify whether the protest is timely for the stay. I also take an honest early look at whether Company B has a point, because corrective action on day two is far cheaper than a sustained protest on day ninety.

Stop work. Yes, I am required to stop performance, and the statute dictates the timeline. Under 31 U.S.C. 3553(d) and RFO FAR 33.105-3(b)(1), if the agency receives GAO's notice within 10 days after contract award, or within 5 days after a debriefing date offered under a timely request, whichever is later, I must immediately suspend performance or terminate the award. For DoD, RFO DFARS 233.105-70 replaces those periods with four and uses whichever is latest: 10 days after award; 10 days after issuance of a task or delivery order over 35 million dollars; 5 days after a debriefing date offered under a timely request; or 5 days after a postaward debriefing is concluded, which under RFO DFARS 215.301-71 is not until the agency answers the follow-up questions the offeror may submit within 2 business days. Company B filed three days after my notice, so we are inside the 10-day window and the CICA stay applies; I issue a stop-work order under 52.242-15 to Company A. At 150,000 dollars this was below the SAT, so it was likely a simplified acquisition where a formal Part 15 debriefing was not required, which is why the 10-days-after-award clock governs. The only way around the stay is the head of the contracting activity, on a nondelegable basis, making a written finding that performance is in the best interests of the United States or that urgent and compelling circumstances will not permit waiting for GAO, and GAO must be told. For network equipment on a camp in Korea I would build that case only if the mission truly cannot wait.

Agency report. The agency report is due to GAO 30 days after GAO's telephone notice of the protest (4 CFR 21.3(c)). It contains my contracting officer's statement of facts, counsel's memorandum of law, and all relevant documents, redacted or produced under a protective order. Company B then has 10 days to comment, and GAO issues its decision within 100 days of filing, or 65 days under the express option (4 CFR 21.9). If GAO sustains, the HCA must report to GAO if the recommendation is not implemented within 60 days (RFO FAR 33.105-4(b)).

Cite: RFO FAR 33.105-3(b) and 33.105-4(a)-(b) (was 33.104); RFO DFARS 233.105-70(a)-(d) (Class Deviation 2026-O0026 Rev 1; was 233.104(c)); RFO DFARS 215.301-71 (Class Deviation 2026-O0048 Rev 1); 4 CFR 21.3(a), 21.3(c), 21.9; 31 U.S.C. 3553(d); FAR 52.242-15.

DFARS Class Deviation 2026-O0026 Rev 1 (24 Aug 2026) text extracted and 233.105-70(a)-(d) read verbatim: 10 days after award; 10 days after a task/delivery order over $35 million (10 U.S.C. 3406(f)); 5 days after an offered debriefing date; 5 days after a postaward debriefing is concluded 'in accordance with 215.301-2' - the Part 215 deviation numbers that rule 215.301-71 (2-business-day questions, 5-business-day answers, debriefing not concluded until the written response), a numbering mismatch between the two deviations. SAT $350,000 'verified' in regulations.json. 411th legal and C&P routing for GAO protests is not in the source files; korea-verify-cp and verify-locally stay.

Stay: GAO notice within 10 days of award or 5 days after offered/concluded debriefing, whichever later, requires immediate suspension or termination (31 U.S.C. 3553(d); RFO FAR 33.105-3(b)(1))

DoD (RFO DFARS 233.105-70): latest of 10 days after award, 10 days after a task/delivery order over $35M, 5 days after offered debriefing date, or 5 days after the debriefing is concluded incl. follow-up questions (215.301-71)

question:
You are the Contracting Officer for a base operations support contract. In August 2026 (FY26), the requiring activity submits a purchase request to fund a one-year janitorial services contract with a period of performance from 1 July 2027 to 30 June 2028. The requiring activity wants to use current year (FY26) Operations & Maintenance (O&M) funds, citing concerns that next year’s budget may be reduced.
Question:
Is it permissible under the bona fide need rule and fiscal law to use FY26 funds for a janitorial services contract with a period of performance beginning in July 2027? Why or why not?
What actions should you take as the Contracting Officer if you receive a purchase request funded in this manner?
What are the potential consequences of violating the bona fide need rule in this scenario?
answer:
1. No, it is not permissible. Under the bona fide need rule (31 U.S.C. § 1502), appropriated funds may only be used for goods and services that meet a legitimate need arising in the fiscal year for which the appropriation was made. In this scenario, the janitorial services contract is for a period of performance starting in July 2027, which is in FY27. Since janitorial services are considered severable services (recurring services that can be separated by fiscal year), the bona fide need arises in the year the services are performed, not when the contract is awarded or the funds are available. Therefore, FY26 funds cannot be used for services performed in FY27.
2. As the Contracting Officer, you should:
Reject the purchase request as currently funded and explain to the requiring activity that FY26 funds cannot be used for a period of performance that begins in FY27.
Educate the requiring activity on the bona fide need rule and the distinction between severable and non-severable services.
Advise the requiring activity to submit a new purchase request using the correct fiscal year’s funds (i.e., FY27 funds for services performed in FY27).
Document your actions and communications to ensure compliance with fiscal law and to protect the integrity of the acquisition process.
3. Violating the bona fide need rule can result in:
Antideficiency Act (ADA) violations: Using funds for purposes other than those for which they were appropriated is a violation of the ADA, which can lead to administrative and disciplinary actions.
Audit findings and negative reports: The agency may be cited in audits (e.g., by the GAO or DoD IG) for improper use of funds.
Requirement to correct the funding: The agency may be required to deobligate the improper funds and re-fund the contract with the correct fiscal year’s appropriation, which can delay the requirement and disrupt services.
Personal liability: In severe cases, individuals responsible for the violation may be held personally liable for the improper obligation of funds.

Cite: 31 U.S.C. 1502

rfo.notes: Only a Cite line was added (task rule 5); no cite changed. 31 U.S.C. 1502 is a statute in the regulations.json 'unchanged' list - the RFO does not touch statutes. The Antideficiency Act is named in words only (no 31 U.S.C. 1341 cite), so nothing else to convert. Status 'n/a' because nothing required conversion. No dollar thresholds stated.

question: Your customer has a service requirement for maintenance to some power conditioners with an estimated cost of $40K. They inform you the power conditioners are produced in the U.S. and the maintenance can only be completed by the manufacturer due to proprietary information and specialized parts. What do you need to consider and what are the steps you need to take to award this contract?
answer:
Forty thousand dollars for maintenance of power conditioners, with the customer telling me only the original manufacturer can do it. Three things are true at once: it is above the $15,000 micro-purchase threshold, it is below the $350,000 simplified acquisition threshold, and it is a restriction on competition that I have to justify in writing. So this is a simplified acquisition with a documented sole-source decision - Part 6 and the J&A approval tables do not apply below the SAT.

What I consider, in order.

First, the requirement, not the answer. I ask the requiring activity for the salient physical, functional and performance characteristics of the maintenance actually needed, in writing, signed by a technical authority. Proprietary information and specialized parts is a conclusion; I need the facts under it. Is the restriction a technical data rights issue, a warranty or safety certification condition, or a preference? Is there an authorized service network or distributor - including one in Korea? Would OEM parts plus a qualified third-party technician meet the need? Does an existing contract or vehicle already cover it?

Second, market research. Even for a sole source I have to do it, and it is what makes the decision defensible: SAM.gov contract award data for what was bought before and from whom, SAM entity search and the SBA Dynamic Small Business Search, a sources sought notice if the schedule allows, the GSA Multiple Award Schedule and existing installation support vehicles. If market research turns up an authorized service provider, this becomes a competition.

Third, the competition decision and the paperwork. Manufacturer maintenance is normally a commercial service, so I use the commercial simplified procedures - an RFQ and a purchase order - and I document under 12.102(a) that only one source is available and the basis for that. If the service is not commercial, I use Part 13 and sign a determination and findings under 13.101(b) that only one source is reasonably available. If I describe the work by brand name, 11.204 requires me to show the brand is essential and that market research found nothing else that meets the need. The decision is mine as the contracting officer; I confirm any local review or routing with the Chief, C&P rather than assume a threshold. Then I publicize: at $40,000 I am over the SAM.gov notice threshold and a sole source is not exempt, so the RFQ or a notice of intent goes on SAM.gov with the redacted justification attached and a reasonable response time - and if someone answers, I take it seriously.

Fourth, the rest of the award package. Fair and reasonable price with one quote - price analysis against historical prices paid, published price lists, the requiring activity's estimate, or similar services; if that is thin I ask for cost information short of certified data. Responsibility determination and the SAM exclusions check before award. Correct funding - operations and maintenance, the right fiscal year, a bona fide need in that year. Small business: above the micro-purchase threshold the rule of two normally requires a set-aside if two capable small businesses exist, but Part 19 is mandatory only in the United States and its outlying areas and discretionary overseas, so for performance in Korea I follow the 411th practice and document the reason if it is not set aside. Then the right commercial clauses, confirmation that this is a nonpersonal service, a COR appointed in writing, and a surveillance approach sized to a $40,000 action.

Fifth, because this is 411th CSB in Korea, the OCONUS overlay. Where the work is performed and who performs it drives real requirements: the Defense Base Act clause for contractor employees working in Korea unless a Department of Labor waiver applies, SOFA Invited Contractor status through USFK and base access if the OEM sends technicians in, Korean labor law, and whether a Korean authorized service agent or a host-nation program changes the picture. I confirm all of that with the C&P shop and local counsel rather than reasoning from stateside habit.

The steps, plainly: validate and document the requirement with salient characteristics; do and document market research; make and document the sole-source or brand-name decision; publicize on SAM.gov; solicit, evaluate, determine price reasonableness and responsibility; verify funding; award with the right clauses; appoint the COR and put surveillance in place; and file everything in PCF as I go.

Cite: RFO FAR 2.101 (micro-purchase threshold $15,000; SAT $350,000); RFO FAR 12.201-1 (commercial simplified procedures), 12.102(a) (documenting restricted competition at or below the SAT) and 12.204 (fair and reasonable price); RFO FAR 13.101(b) (noncommercial single-source determination and findings); RFO FAR 11.204 and DFARS 211.204 (items peculiar to one manufacturer); RFO FAR 6.001 and 6.103-1(d) (the Part 6 justification applies above the SAT); RFO FAR 5.101 and 5.201(c)(3) (SAM.gov notice; posting the justification); RFO FAR 10.001 (market research); RFO FAR 15.404-1 (price analysis); RFO FAR 9.104-1 and 9.405(e) (responsibility; exclusions check); RFO FAR 19.000(b) and 19.104-1 (set-aside rule and overseas applicability); RFO FAR 37.201-2 (personal services); RFO FAR 1.404 and DFARS 201.404-70 (COR); RFO FAR 28.305 (Defense Base Act). Confirm the current justification review routing and any 411th requirements with your Chief, C&P.

rfo.notes: Reviewed 14 Sep 2026. All FAR/DFARS cites are verified project crosswalk entries or were read on the RFO Part 5, 6, 11, 12, 13 and 19 pages (12.102(a) at/below-SAT documentation; 13.101(b) determination and findings; 11.204 text; 6.001 exclusion of Part 13 actions; 5.101(b)(2) no notice exemption for 6.103-1 sole sources; 19.000(b) 'may apply' outside the U.S.; 19.104-1(a) rule of two above the MPT). MPT $15,000 and SAT $350,000 were re-read verbatim by the project verifier on FAR 2.101 (FAC 2026-01) and the RFO Part 2 page. FPDS references replaced with SAM.gov contract award data (FPDS.gov decommissioned 24 Feb 2026; reporting continues in SAM.gov Contract Awards Management). The RFO 5.101(a) notice figure read as $20,000 on two fetches of the RFO Part 5 page (legacy 5.101(a)(1) was $25,000), so the answer says only that $40,000 is over the threshold. Korea items (DOL waiver status, SOFA IC processing, 411th set-aside practice, local review routing) are not in the project sources and carry korea-verify-cp; the invented role name 'Chief, Policy and Compliance' was replaced with 'Chief, C&P'.

key_points: At $40K you are above the $15,000 MPT and below the $350,000 SAT: simplified acquisition procedures with a documented sole-source decision; Part 6 and the J&A approval tables apply only above the SAT.

Do not accept 'only the OEM can do it' - get salient characteristics in writing from a technical authority and identify whether the restriction is data rights, warranty, safety certification, or preference; ask about authorized service agents, including in Korea.

Market research is still required and is what makes the decision defensible - SAM.gov contract award data, SAM and DSBS, sources sought, GSA MAS and existing vehicles; an authorized service network turns this into a competition.

Commercial path: RFQ and purchase order under 12.201-1 with a 12.102(a) record that only one source is available; noncommercial path: 13.101(b) determination and findings; brand-name descriptions need the 11.204 showing; then publicize on SAM.gov with the redacted justification (5.101, 5.201(c)(3)).
With one quote, establish a fair and reasonable price by price analysis against history, price lists, or the estimate (15.404-1, 12.204); request uncertified cost information if analysis is thin.

Complete the package: responsibility and exclusions check, O&M funds of the right year and a bona fide need, the set-aside decision documented (Part 19 is discretionary outside the U.S. - follow 411th practice), nonpersonal services confirmation, written COR appointment and surveillance.

Korea overlay: Defense Base Act clause unless a DOL waiver applies, SOFA Invited Contractor status and base access for OEM technicians, Korean labor law, and whether a Korean service agent or host-nation program applies - confirm with C&P and counsel.

question: Why is it important to fully document the contract file?
answer: So whenever anyone else picks up your file, they can find out exactly what the status is and pick up the work from there. Additionally, you have to document the file so that 1) you comply with law and regulation, 2) you can defend your decision making in the future to either the Army or the German government, and 3) so that in the event of litigation, the Army's interests can be protected.

question:
You are a 411th CSB contracting officer at Camp Humphreys. USFK J4 sends you an approved Logistics Cost Sharing (LCS) requirement from the garrison DPW to replace rooftop HVAC units on three barracks, IGE $1.8 million, funded from the current ROK program year. Before you post anything, a U.S. HVAC company with an office in Pyeongtaek calls and asks to be put on the bidders list, and the DPW engineer says he would prefer the U.S. firm because it installed the original units. You must decide how to set up this competition.

1. What authority lets you restrict this competition to Korean firms, and what do you document?
2. How does the Korean-firm restriction change your market research?
3. What do you publicize, where, and what do you tell the U.S. firm?
4. What changes in your evaluation and award process compared with an O&M action of the same size?
answer:
This is ROK money, not a U.S. appropriation. LCS is the logistics portion of the Special Measures Agreement; the funds are held by ROK MND, USFK J4 manages the program, and the program is limited to Korean businesses using Korean material and labor. That is the rule I start from.

Authority and documentation. The Korean-firm limitation is a rule of the LCS program under the SMA, not a FAR set-aside, and the contract is awarded by MND, not by me. If a FAR competition cite is needed in my file, the closest fit is RFO FAR 6.103-4, international agreement: full and open competition is not required when precluded by the terms of an international agreement or the written directions of a foreign government reimbursing the agency, and under 6.103-4(c) a DoD contract under that authority does not need the written justification and approval of 6.104. That mapping is my analysis, though. Whether the 411th documents LCS actions under 6.103-4 or treats them as outside FAR Part 6 altogether is set by the 411th LCS SOP, and I confirm it with C&P before I write anything. Either way I put a short determination in the file that names the SMA/LCS authority, the J4-approved requirement and the Korean-firm limitation, in whatever format the LCS SOP prescribes. I do not invent one.

Market research. RFO FAR 10.001 still applies, but the universe is Korean industry. I look at prior LCS awards for like work, J4 and DPW vendor knowledge, Korean vendor registrations and vendor-day contacts, and I issue a sources-sought aimed at Korean HVAC installers. Two things I settle early: whether Korean-manufactured units meet the spec, because the offshore-versus-local materials memo has to go with the package to J4, and what vendor registration MND and the LCS SOP require of offerors. Because MND, not the United States, awards and pays, I do not assume the U.S. SAM rule applies; if the 411th does require SAM registration for LCS offerors, the foreign-vendor exception in RFO FAR 4.203-1(b)(7) only reaches actions at or below $40,000, so at $1.8 million it would not help. I confirm the registration rule with C&P.

Publicizing. Where and how LCS actions are advertised is an LCS SOP question that I confirm with C&P, because the award is MND's and the U.S. publicizing rules were written for U.S. awards. What I know from the FAR side: RFO Part 5 requires GPE notices for actions over $20,000, and the RFO 5.101(b) exemption list no longer carries the old overseas-only-local-sources exemption, so if the 411th posts LCS actions on SAM.gov I post the presolicitation and solicitation notices and state plainly that competition is limited to Korean firms under the LCS program; I also ask C&P whether the DFARS Part 205 deviation restores an OCONUS exemption. Whatever channel the SOP names, including any Korean-language channel, I use it. I tell the U.S. firm the truth: this action is LCS-funded and by program rule limited to Korean firms, it is not eligible here, and I keep its capability statement on file for O&M requirements.

Evaluation and award. The mechanics stay FAR-based: LCS contracts are prepared under standard U.S. contracting procedures for MND and the USFK LCS program manager to approve and sign. What changes:
- Eligibility becomes a gate: I verify each offeror is a Korean firm using the method the LCS SOP prescribes, and I document it.
- At $1.8 million I am above the SAT ($350,000) but below the $9 million commercial ceiling, so if the work is commercial I can use RFO FAR 12.201-1 simplified procedures; otherwise Part 15. I confirm with C&P which of those U.S. procedures the 411th applies to LCS packages at this value. Price reasonableness rests on adequate price competition among Korean firms plus the IGE (AFARS 5107.90).
- Buy American does not bite: RFO FAR 25.100(b) applies the subpart to supplies acquired for use in the United States, and here the buyer is MND in any case.
- The SOFA invited contractor program is irrelevant to Korean firms; it is for U.S. contractors.
- Pricing is likely in won because MND pays; I confirm the currency convention with C&P.
- I do not award. I make the recommendation for award through USFK J4, MND approves and awards, and the vendor invoices MND. MND approval adds time, so I build that into the schedule and tell DPW now.

Cite: RFO FAR 6.103-4 and 6.104(a); RFO FAR 10.001; RFO FAR 5.101, 5.101(b), 5.201; RFO FAR 4.203-1(b)(7); RFO FAR 12.201-1; RFO FAR 25.100(b); AFARS 5107.90; U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS); USFK Reg 37-5 (2007; confirm currency with C&P); 411th CSB LCS SOP (confirm current procedure with C&P).
key_points: LCS is ROK MND money under the SMA; program rule limits award to Korean firms with Korean material and labor; KOs recommend award through USFK J4 and MND awards and pays

The limitation is an LCS program rule and MND awards; if a FAR cite is needed the closest fit is RFO FAR 6.103-4 (international agreement), which under 6.103-4(c) needs no 6.104 J&A for DoD, but whether the 411th documents LCS actions that way is an LCS SOP question; write the file determination in the SOP format (confirm with C&P)

Market research (RFO FAR 10.001) targets Korean industry; settle the offshore-versus-local materials question and the vendor registration MND/the LCS SOP require early (do not assume the U.S. SAM rule applies; if it does, the foreign-vendor exception stops at $40,000)

Where LCS actions are advertised is an LCS SOP question (confirm with C&P); if SAM.gov is used, RFO Part 5 applies over $20,000 and the old overseas local-sources exemption is not in RFO 5.101(b) (check the DFARS 205 deviation); tell the U.S. firm it is ineligible for this LCS action

Evaluation stays FAR-based (12.201-1 if commercial and under $9M, else Part 15); Korean-firm eligibility is a gate; Buy American reaches only supplies for use in the U.S. (25.100(b)); no IC program for Korean firms
Build MND approval time into the schedule and tell the customer up front

question:
You are the KO for an LCS-funded purchase of twelve non-tactical vehicles for a transportation motor pool in Area II, evaluated price 3.1 billion won (about $2.4 million at the rate you used for evaluation). Evaluation is complete, the apparent successful offeror is a Korean dealer, and the winter driving season starts in six weeks. The transportation officer walks in and asks you to sign the award tomorrow so the vehicles can be delivered before the first snow. You have to decide what you can sign, what goes where, and what to promise.

1. Who awards this contract, and what exactly is your signature on?
2. What is in the package you route, and through whom?
3. How does the dealer get paid, and what do you tell it about invoicing?
4. What do you tell the transportation officer about the timeline and your role after award?
answer:
I cannot award this tomorrow, and I would not sign it as an award at all. 411th CSB KOs do not award LCS contracts. The procurement runs through 411th contract vehicles and procedures, but the funds are ROK funds held by MND, so my product is a recommendation for award that goes through USFK J4, the LCS program manager, and ROK MND approves and awards. So I tell the transportation officer that today, before he leaves my office, so nobody calls the dealer and tells it to start delivering. An LCS vendor that starts on a verbal from the customer has no contract with anyone, and that is the same unauthorized commitment problem we have on the O&M side.

What I sign and route. I prepare the contract document under standard U.S. contracting procedures for MND and the USFK LCS program manager to approve and sign, and I sign the recommendation for award. The package that goes to J4 includes, at minimum:
- The recommendation for award with the evaluation record, the eligibility check showing the dealer is a Korean firm, and my price reasonableness determination (competition among Korean dealers plus the IGE).
- The memo documenting offshore or local materials. Since January 2022 MND does not require an offshore waiver before submission, but the memo must accompany every LCS package to J4. For vehicles, that memo has to say honestly where the vehicles are built.
- The J4 requirement approval showing this is on the current program-year LCS list, and whatever routing sheet the 411th LCS SOP requires.
I confirm the current checklist with C&P rather than guess at forms.

Payment. Invoices go to ROK MND and MND pays. Because no U.S. funds are involved I do not expect a U.S. obligation, a DFAS payment or a WAWF invoice on this action, and I confirm the actual invoice mechanics with C&P and J4. I tell the dealer that in the solicitation and again at award so it does not send invoices to me or to the customer. I make sure the contract states the currency and the invoice address and acceptance documentation MND expects, and I confirm that language with C&P and J4.

Timeline and my role afterward. MND approval takes more time than a U.S. award; I give the transportation officer the realistic window J4 and C&P give me, not the window he wants. If the mission truly cannot wait, the honest alternatives are a smaller interim O&M action on a separate solicitation, because O&M and LCS cannot be mixed, or accepting the LCS timeline. After MND approves, the 411th's role in coordinating delivery and administering the contract is whatever the LCS SOP assigns it; I expect to stay the contracting point of contact for questions of scope and performance, and I confirm that with C&P, but the award and the money are MND's. I document every conversation with the customer in the file.

Cite: U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS); USFK Reg 37-5 (2007; confirm currency with C&P); 411th CSB LCS SOP (confirm current procedure with C&P); RFO FAR 1.405 (unauthorized commitments, for the warning); RFO FAR 6.103-4.
key_points: 411th KOs do not award LCS contracts: the KO signs a recommendation for award, routes it through USFK J4 (LCS program manager), and ROK MND approves and awards

Package: recommendation for award, evaluation and Korean-firm eligibility record, price reasonableness, the offshore/local materials memo (required with every LCS package since Jan 2022), J4 requirement approval; confirm the checklist with C&P
Invoices go to ROK MND and MND pays; no U.S. obligation is expected (confirm the invoice mechanics with C&P and J4); say so in the solicitation and at award
MND approval adds time; do not promise delivery dates the ROK approval cycle cannot support; no verbal starts by the customer (unauthorized commitment risk)
O&M cannot be added to the LCS action; an urgent interim buy would be a separate O&M solicitation
After MND approval the 411th's post-award role is set by the LCS SOP; expect to remain the contracting point of contact (confirm with C&P)

question:
You are assembling an LCS package for repair of the walk-in refrigeration at a Camp Casey dining facility, evaluated price about 850 million won (roughly $650,000). The successful Korean offeror's technical proposal shows the replacement compressors are manufactured in Japan; the rest of the parts and all labor are Korean. The DPW engineer tells you to write 'local materials' on the memo that goes to J4 because 'MND never checks and the offshore question just slows things down.' The package is due to J4 on Friday. You must decide what the memo says and what else you do.

1. What is the memo, and what changed in January 2022?
2. What do you write, and how do you answer the engineer?
3. Does the offshore compressor make the offer ineligible, and who decides?
4. What do you put in the file?
answer:
The memo is the offshore-versus-local materials memo that must accompany every LCS package to USFK J4. The LCS program expects Korean material and labor. Before January 2022 an offshore waiver had to be approved by ROK MND before the package could be submitted; since January 2022 MND no longer requires the waiver up front. Instead a memo documenting whether the materials are offshore or local goes with every LCS package to J4; who prepares and signs it is set by the LCS SOP, and in this scenario it is coming to me. So the memo replaced a pre-approval, it did not remove the requirement to disclose.

What I write. The compressors are made in Japan, so the memo says offshore materials, identifies the compressors, and states that the balance of materials and all labor are Korean, with the reason the offeror gave for the offshore component and what my market research showed about Korean-made alternatives that meet the spec. I say that to the engineer plainly: the memo is a written representation from the 411th, over my signature or my office's, to J4 and to a partner government that is paying the bill, I will not put a false statement in it, and neither will anyone else on this package. Whether MND checks is not the standard; my integrity and the Government's credibility with MND are. RFO FAR 1.402-2 puts safeguarding the interests of the United States on me, and the Joint Ethics Regulation does not have a 'nobody checks' exception. If a false memo were discovered, the likely results are MND rejecting the package, the 411th losing credibility on every LCS package after it, and a personal integrity problem for me and the engineer.

Eligibility. The Korean-firm and Korean-labor rules are met. Whether an offshore component is acceptable inside an LCS award is an MND and LCS program decision, not mine. I do not reject the offer on my own, and I do not assume MND will accept it. I ask J4 now, before Friday, how MND is treating offshore components in the current program year, and I put the market-research evidence in the memo so MND can approve it on the facts if no Korean compressor meets the requirement. If MND requires a Korean-made compressor, the path is a proposal revision or resolicitation, not a mislabeled memo.

File. The memo, the market research on Korean-made compressors, the offeror's statement of origin, my note of the conversation with the engineer and what I told him, and the J4 response. If the engineer escalates, I brief my Chief of Contracting the same day. I confirm the current memo format and MND's current position with C&P and J4; I do not rely on my memory of the 2022 change.

Cite: 411th CSB study material on LCS limitations (offshore/local materials memo, January 2022 change); U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS); USFK Reg 37-5 (2007; confirm currency with C&P); RFO FAR 1.402-2; DoD 5500.07-R Joint Ethics Regulation; 411th CSB LCS SOP (confirm current procedure with C&P).

question:
You are one week from releasing an LCS-funded solicitation for grounds maintenance across Camp Casey and Camp Hovey, IGE about $3.2 million for the program year. The DPW chief asks you to add three line items for hazardous tree removal and stump grinding, about $400,000, funded with FY27 O&M, 'so we only run one competition and the same contractor does everything.' The RM has already certified the O&M funds. You must decide whether to add the line items.

1. Can O&M and LCS line items go in one solicitation? Why or why not?
2. What are the practical differences that would break even if the competition rules allowed it?
3. What alternatives do you offer the customer?
4. How do you handle the already-certified O&M funds?
answer:
No, and this one I can answer without checking a local SOP. U.S. O&M actions must be solicited using full and open competition unless a FAR exception applies, while ROK LCS actions must be solicited under competitive procedures limited to Korean contractors. One solicitation cannot carry two contradictory competition requirements, so O&M and LCS funds cannot be combined in a single solicitation. I would be either illegally restricting the O&M work to Korean firms or opening LCS work to non-Korean firms in violation of the program rule.

Even if the competition rules lined up, the two actions would still break apart:
- Different awarding official and payer. I recommend award on the LCS portion, MND approves, awards and pays; on the O&M portion I award and DFAS pays. Two award signatures and two invoice paths in one document is not a contract anyone can administer.
- Different fiscal rules. The O&M line items carry the bona fide need rule, the one-year availability of O&M and the 12-month severable-services authority; LCS follows the ROK program year and MND approval. A single period of performance cannot serve both.
- Different clauses and pricing. The O&M portion needs the full U.S. clause set and dollar pricing; the LCS portion follows the LCS package rules and, in practice, won pricing.

Alternatives. First, I ask whether tree removal is actually an LCS-eligible logistics requirement; repair and maintenance services are within LCS scope, so if J4 will approve it as an LCS requirement in the program year, it can ride in the LCS solicitation with LCS money and the O&M funds go back. Second, if it stays O&M, it is a separate action: $400,000 is above the SAT ($350,000), so it is a full and open competitive acquisition on its own solicitation, or an order under an existing base operations or DPW services contract if in scope. Part 19 set-aside rules do not reach performance outside the United States, so I do not run a small-business analysis for it. Third, if the customer's real goal is one contractor on the ground, the honest answer is that we cannot buy that with mixed money; the LCS awardee can compete for the O&M work if it is otherwise eligible.

The certified funds. The O&M certification stays with the RM until I have an O&M action to obligate against. I do not park it on the LCS solicitation, and if the requirement moves to LCS, the RM withdraws the certification. I document the customer's request and my answer, offer the two options in writing, and keep the LCS release date.

Cite: 411th CSB study material (O&M and LCS cannot be combined in one solicitation); RFO FAR 6.101 and 6.103; RFO FAR 6.103-4 (closest FAR authority for the LCS limitation, if one is needed; confirm with C&P); 31 U.S.C. 1502; 10 U.S.C. 3133; RFO FAR 2.101 (SAT); FAR 19.000(b); U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement (LCS); 411th CSB LCS SOP (confirm current procedure with C&P).
key_points: O&M requires full and open competition (or a FAR exception); LCS must be limited to Korean contractors; contradictory competition requirements cannot share one solicitation

Even apart from competition: different awarding official and payer (KO/DFAS vs MND), different fiscal rules (bona fide need and 12-month severable authority vs ROK program year), different clauses and currency

Option 1: ask J4 whether the tree work is LCS-eligible and fund it as LCS; Option 2: separate O&M action, full and open at $400,000 (above the $350,000 SAT), or an order under an existing in-scope services contract
Part 19 set-asides do not apply to performance outside the U.S. (FAR 19.000(b))
Do not hold certified O&M funds against an LCS solicitation; RM withdraws or re-certifies as the path is chosen
Document the request and the answer; keep the LCS release date

question:
USFK J4 sends you an approved LCS requirement for custodial and grounds maintenance services across Area III installations, IGE $14 million for a base period plus four option periods, each option subject to MND approval in its program year. The last three LCS actions you worked were all under $2 million using simplified procedures. Your Chief of Contracting asks for your acquisition approach by Monday. You must decide the procedures, the source selection structure and the schedule.

1. Which acquisition procedures apply at $14 million, and why can you not use what you used at $2 million?
2. What source selection planning is required, and who approves it?
3. What Korea-specific limits and package items still apply at this size?
4. What does your schedule look like, and what do you tell J4 about timing?
answer:
At $14 million this is a formal source selection, not a simplified buy. The commercial simplified procedures in RFO FAR 12.201-1 stop at $9 million, and the SAT is $350,000, so neither route I used on the $2 million actions is available. I use RFO FAR Part 15 procedures, with Part 12 commercial terms if the services are commercial, and I plan it as a competitive negotiated acquisition.

Source selection planning. Two things drive this. First, the DoD Source Selection Procedures apply to competitively negotiated Part 15 acquisitions with an estimated value greater than $10 million, and they require a written source selection plan. Second, RFO DFARS 215.201(b)(2) says that for high-dollar acquisitions, as prescribed by agency procedures, the source selection authority must approve the source selection plan before the solicitation is issued. So my sequence is: appoint the SSA at the level Army and 411th procedures require, and I confirm that level with C&P rather than guess; write the SSP with the evaluation approach, factors, rating method and team; get SSA approval; then release the RFP. Evaluation approach under RFO FAR 15.103: for custodial and grounds work I would lean to lowest price technically acceptable or the highest-technically-rated-with-fair-and-reasonable-price approach if the requirement is well defined, with past performance evaluated as RFO FAR 15.104 and DFARS 215.202-70 require. I also need a written acquisition plan under RFO FAR 7.102 and the Army services acquisition strategy review at the AFARS threshold, an IGE under AFARS 5107.90, and a performance work statement with a quality assurance surveillance plan under RFO FAR Part 37. Certified cost or pricing data: the DoD threshold is $10 million for prime contracts awarded after 30 June 2026, but adequate price competition is an exception under RFO FAR 15.403-2, so I plan for competition and price analysis under 15.404-1.

Korea-specific items that do not go away at $14 million:
- Competition is still limited to Korean firms under the LCS program; if the file needs a FAR cite, RFO FAR 6.103-4 is the closest fit and under 6.103-4(c) needs no 6.104 J&A for DoD, but how the 411th documents it is an LCS SOP question I confirm with C&P.
- The offshore-versus-local materials memo still goes with the package to J4.
- I still recommend award through J4; MND approves and awards, and MND pays. That includes each option period in its ROK program year, so I write the option structure the way J4 and C&P tell me MND will accept, and I do not assume U.S. option rules alone control.
- Protests and debriefings: I offer debriefings under RFO FAR 15.301, and I ask legal before release how protest procedures apply to an MND-awarded action so I am not surprised later.
- My warrant: whether a warrant is required to sign an LCS recommendation for award, and at what level, is 411th policy that I confirm with C&P; if the action value governs, $14 million is above the $10 million Class III level, so a KO holding a $25 million or higher Class III warrant would sign.

Schedule. Acquisition plan and SSP approval, sources-sought and industry engagement with Korean firms, RFP with at least 30 days for proposals, evaluation with an SSEB, clarifications or negotiations, SSA decision, then the package to J4 and MND approval, which is the step I cannot compress. I give J4 a schedule that starts from when MND needs services to begin and works backward, and I tell them now that MND approval time is the long pole and that the requirement has to be in the approved program year before I release.

Cite: RFO FAR 12.201-1 and 2.101 (SAT $350,000; commercial ceiling $9 million); RFO FAR 15.103, 15.104, 15.201, 15.301, 15.403-2, 15.404-1; RFO DFARS 215.201(b)(2) and 215.202-70 (Class Deviation 2026-O0048 Rev 1); DoD Source Selection Procedures (20 Aug 2022) paras 1.2 and 2.2; RFO FAR 7.102; AFARS 5107.90; RFO FAR Part 37; RFO FAR 6.103-4; Army Warranting Program Policy v12 Table 1; 411th CSB LCS SOP and Army source selection supplement (confirm SSA level and templates with C&P).
citations: Army Warranting Program Policy v12 Table 1
key_points: $14M is above the $9M commercial simplified ceiling (RFO FAR 12.201-1) and far above the $350K SAT, so RFO FAR Part 15 competitive negotiation applies
DoD Source Selection Procedures apply above $10M and require a written SSP; RFO DFARS 215.201(b)(2): SSA approves the SSP before the solicitation is issued; confirm SSA level with C&P
Pick the approach under RFO FAR 15.103 (LPTA / tradeoff / HTRFRP), evaluate past performance (15.104, DFARS 215.202-70); AP under 7.102, IGE under AFARS 5107.90, PWS/QASP under Part 37
Certified data threshold is $10M (DoD, after 30 Jun 2026) but adequate price competition is an exception (15.403-2)

Korea rules survive: Korean firms only (6.103-4 if a FAR cite is needed; confirm with C&P), materials memo, recommendation through J4, MND awards and pays each program year; ask legal about protest procedure on an MND award

Warrant level for an LCS recommendation for award is a 411th policy question (confirm with C&P); if action value governs, $14M is above the $10M Class III level; MND approval is the schedule long pole

question:
It is 14 September 2026. The Area I DPW submits an LCS purchase request for snow and ice removal services, estimated 1.2 billion won (about $900,000), with a requested period of performance of 1 November 2026 through 31 March 2027. The cover email says 'please award before 30 September so we do not lose the FY26 money.' J4 has not yet confirmed whether the requirement is on this program year's approved LCS list. You must decide how to advise the customer and how to plan the action.

1. Does the U.S. fiscal year end drive this LCS action? Why or why not?
2. Which calendar does drive LCS timing, and what do you need from J4?
3. The performance period crosses 31 December. What does that mean for LCS, and what would it mean if the requirement were O&M instead?
4. What do you tell the customer, in writing?
answer:
The 30 September deadline does not exist for this action. LCS money is not a U.S. appropriation; it is ROK cost-sharing money held by ROK MND under the Special Measures Agreement. It never transfers to the U.S., so U.S. fiscal-year end, the one-year availability of O&M and the year-end obligation push have nothing to do with it. The customer is applying O&M instincts to ROK money.

What does drive it. The ROK Government's fiscal year is the calendar year, 1 January through 31 December, and the National Assembly passes the budget in early December. LCS is planned on an annual cycle that J4 runs (USFK material refers to annual LCS submissions; I say 'program year' here and J4 and C&P will confirm the current term and calendar), and MND approves and awards each action. So my two questions to J4 are: is this requirement on the approved LCS list for the current program year, and if not, is there a supplemental path or does it wait for the next program year. Until J4 confirms, I do not have an LCS requirement, only a request.

Crossing 31 December. For LCS, a 1 November to 31 March period crosses the ROK fiscal year, and how MND treats performance that straddles its program years is an MND and J4 question; I ask J4 whether MND will approve the full period on the current program year's funds or expects a split. I confirm the current practice with C&P and I do not assume the U.S. cross-year rules apply to ROK money. If instead this were O&M, the analysis flips to U.S. fiscal law: snow removal is a severable service, the bona fide need arises when the service is performed, and FY26 O&M cannot fund services that begin in November of FY27. An FY26 award for a November start would be the same violation as the janitorial case we all know. The 12-month severable-services authority in 10 U.S.C. 3133 lets a contract cross fiscal years, but only from funds current when the period starts, so an O&M version would be awarded with FY27 money on or after 1 October.

What I tell the customer, in writing:
- This is an LCS request; there is no 30 September deadline and no FY26 money to lose.
- The controlling dates are the ROK program year and MND approval; I have asked J4 to confirm program-year approval and how MND handles the December crossing.
- MND approval takes time, so a 1 November start is at risk; I give the realistic date once J4 answers, and if the mission cannot wait I discuss an O&M interim buy with FY27 funds, on its own solicitation, because O&M and LCS cannot be mixed.
- Competition will be limited to Korean firms, the materials memo goes with the package, and I recommend award while MND awards and pays.
And I tell the DPW that the fastest way to have snow removal in November is to get LCS requirements to J4 early in its annual cycle, by whatever cutoff J4 sets, not in September.
